# Voice guide

This guide explains the voice already used by Neon Pairs and how that voice supports play, recovery and accessible feedback.

The game speaks briefly because the player's attention belongs on the cards. Controls name actions, status text reports facts, and help explains the next useful interaction. The small amount of personality sits around those jobs. This page is about that balance; exact number presentation is covered in [Numbers style](numbers-style.md), and failure messages have their own [error message guide](error-message-style.md).

## The voice in the current screen

`src/game/Game.tsx` opens with the eyebrow “A little focus. A perfect pair.” The title is simply “Neon Pairs”. The introduction then becomes practical: “Reveal two cards. Match their shape and marker to keep the pair.” Those lines do different work. The eyebrow sets a mood; the introduction tells a new player what to do. Reading only the introduction is enough to begin.

The board help is equally direct: “Use a pointer or Tab to enter the board. Arrow keys move between cards. Enter or Space reveals a card.” It names the supported interactions without requiring a player to know terms such as roving focus, keydown handlers or native activation. Those implementation terms are useful in engineering documents, but they would make the board instructions harder to use.

The tone is friendly and restrained. Interface text has no exclamation marks. The completion banner closes with “Well played.” after reporting the result, so encouragement follows something that actually happened. There is no running commentary on the player's skill or on the quality of a particular miss.

That division gives copy review a useful starting point. A phrase that explains a control belongs near the control. A phrase that describes the latest turn belongs in feedback. A phrase that merely adds atmosphere has to earn its space alongside the existing eyebrow and title.

## Labels name the action

The literal labels live in `src/game/controls/control-labels.ts`. They are short enough to recognize while scanning and specific enough to distinguish actions with different consequences.

| Current label | What the wording tells the player |
| --- | --- |
| Grid size | The select changes the board dimensions. |
| New Game | Start a fresh deal at the selected size. |
| Restart | Begin the current deal again. |
| Reproduce a game | Open the tools for repeating a deal or restoring progress. |
| Board code | The nearby field contains a deal identifier. |
| Load board | Use the entered code to start its deal. |
| Snapshot JSON | The larger field contains serialized progress. |
| Export snapshot | Put the current progress into that field. |
| Load snapshot | Restore the progress entered in that field. |
| Resume | Continue the unfinished game loaded from a snapshot. |

“New Game” and “Restart” are especially easy to blur in explanatory prose. The first changes the deal; the second repeats it. A sentence such as “restart for a different arrangement” would misdescribe the existing button. [New game and restart](../gameplay/new-game-and-restart.md) explains the behavior in detail. In a writing review, the important question is whether the reader can predict the button's result from the surrounding sentence.

The mix of capitalization is part of the current interface, rather than evidence of one universal casing scheme. “New Game” has two capitals, while “Load board” has one. Quoting the real control name makes instructions easier to follow than silently regularizing those labels in prose.

## Outcomes are facts, not judgments

`src/game/session/session.ts` constructs the turn feedback. A successful nonfinal turn begins “Pair found.” and follows with the matched-pair count. An unsuccessful turn says “No match. Cards close after a short pause.” Neither message blames the player. Both identify what happened, and the second explains the temporary state of the board.

The word “short” in that message describes the experience rather than asking the player to read a technical timer value. Engineering prose can name the `MISMATCH_MS` constant and the active-time behavior. The player needs to know why the cards remain visible and that they will close. That is a useful example of the same behavior needing different levels of detail in different places.

The final turn's feedback combines the pair result with completion: “Pair found. All pairs found in N moves and time.” The visible banner uses a related sentence: “Every pair found in N moves and time. Well played.” Here `N` and `time` describe substitutions, not literal interface text. The banner and turn feedback serve different reading situations; copying one into the other without checking the component would lose that distinction.

“Perfect” in the eyebrow is an atmospheric phrase about pairs. It is not a score classification. The implementation has moves, matched pairs, elapsed time and a local best move count, rather than grades such as excellent, average or poor. A release note or help paragraph that describes a “perfect rating” would create a feature the game does not have.

## Help uses the player's vocabulary

In player-facing explanations, “card”, “pair”, “board” and “move” carry most of the meaning. “Activate” is useful when discussing the shared action behind click, tap and keyboard input. In the board help, the implementation instead says “reveals a card”, which describes the visible effect. The [glossary](glossary.md) records both vocabularies and the places where they differ.

“Click” alone is too narrow for a description intended to cover every input route. The actual help names a pointer and the keyboard. Other prose can say “select Load board” without assuming a particular device. A reproduction report can be more specific when the distinction matters: for example, whether Enter submitted the board-code form or a pointer selected its submit button.

The phrase “shape and marker” in the introduction is deliberately economical. The complete face model also includes solid or outline fill. That detail matters when discussing the full face catalogue, especially the largest board. It does not mean the short introduction is a complete definition of identity. A technical explanation can link to [Card artwork](../visuals/card-artwork.md) instead of expanding every piece of introductory copy into an implementation reference.

## Accessible names tell the same story

The visual card and its accessible name describe the same available information. `src/game/board/card-state.ts` builds a position first, then the state, then a face label when a face is available. The first hidden card is named “Row 1, column 1, closed”. With face 0 revealed at that position, the name becomes “Row 1, column 1, revealed, cyan solid circle, marker top”.

These are functional descriptions. Adding a playful nickname for a hidden card would make it harder to compare the name with the board position and could reveal information the player should not yet have. Adding decorative praise to a matched card would make repeated navigation more verbose. The existing state words already explain why that card's appearance and action differ.

Face labels come from `faceDesign` in `src/game/board/face-design.ts`. Their lowercase color, fill, shape and marker terms provide a vocabulary a player can remember. “Cyan solid circle, marker top” is reproducible; “bright round one” is an interpretation. The latter might be acceptable as a player's own description in research notes, but it is not a substitute for the generated name in an engineering example.

The result feedback is also available to assistive technology. Writing it as a complete thought matters because a reader may encounter it without visually scanning the cards. Its first clause establishes the event; any following clause supplies the result or the next state. [Screen reader notes](../interface/screen-reader-notes.md) covers the reading journey, and [Announcements policy](../interface/announcements-policy.md) owns delivery details.

## Recovery stays calm and concrete

The browser's two invalid-load messages are “Invalid board code.” and “Invalid snapshot.” They identify the rejected input without guessing how it became invalid. A code might have been mistyped, pasted incompletely or supplied with an unsupported size. A snapshot might be malformed JSON or a structurally inconsistent state. The short message does not pretend to distinguish causes the UI does not expose.

The success status for unfinished progress is more instructional: “Loaded snapshot. Select Resume to continue.” That second sentence matters because cards are not active until the player resumes. Completed progress uses “Loaded completed snapshot.” and has no continuation instruction. A generic “Success” would omit information that explains what the player sees next.

The game keeps failed drafts available for correction. Help can therefore describe correcting the field and selecting the load action again. Correction uses the existing field and load action. Detailed technical causes belong in [Error message style](error-message-style.md), where the browser notices and replay diagnostics are considered separately.

# Numbers style

This page explains how Neon Pairs presents counts, positions, durations and numeric values without confusing display text with saved data.

Numbers cross several boundaries in this game. The status bar shows compact values, accessible card names describe human positions, and snapshots carry machine-readable state. The same quantity can have different representations at those boundaries. The examples below come from `game.ts`, `elapsed-time.ts`, the status component and the version 1 readers; the underlying behavior belongs in [Scoring and moves](../gameplay/scoring-and-moves.md) and [Elapsed time rules](../gameplay/elapsed-time-rules.md).

## Counts in sentences and counts in a display

The current status component separates labels from values using a description list. `StatusLabel.moves` supplies “Moves:” and the adjacent value is `game.moves`. It is a compact display rather than a sentence about the count. Counts of moves read "1 move" and "2 moves", and durations read M:SS, such as 0:07 and 12:30. In prose, a unit makes an otherwise bare number understandable; beside an existing status label, the label already does that work.

This distinction is visible in `src/game/status/GameStatus.tsx`. Moves and best moves are plain numbers. Pairs are a matched count followed by the total. Time passes through `formatElapsed`. A missing best is the word “none”, not a numeric zero. Zero moves describes a real game state; no recorded best describes the absence of a record. Treating those as interchangeable would obscure the difference between starting a game and having completed one before.

The generated completion sentences currently interpolate `${game.moves} moves`. They do not call a general singular/plural helper. A legal completed board needs at least eight moves, so the completion surface does not encounter a one-move finish. The general prose convention above is therefore not evidence that a shared move-count formatter already exists.

The session does handle the singular pair count explicitly. It produces “Pair found. 1 pair matched.” for the first match and uses “pairs” for later nonfinal matches. The code tests `game.matched.length === 2`, because the stored list contains card positions. Counting array entries as if they were pairs would double the reported progress.

## A compact status example

A four-column game with one matched pair, two completed turns and a stored best of twelve moves has these count values:

| Surface | Example | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Moves | `Moves: 2` | Two second-card reveals have resolved turns. |
| Pairs | `Pairs: 1/8` | One pair is matched out of eight pairs. |
| Best | `Best: 12` | The saved record for this size is twelve moves. |
| Best without a record | `Best: none` | This size has no saved result. |

The slash in the pair display expresses progress against a total. It is not a fraction used to calculate a percentage, and the UI does not show a percentage alongside it. A report that says “one of eight pairs” is a readable expansion of the same value. A report that says “one of sixteen pairs” has mixed the card total with the pair total.

## The clock's representation

`formatElapsed(milliseconds)` floors the total seconds, derives total minutes, then pads the seconds component to two digits. Minutes continue growing beyond an hour. The display is an elapsed duration, so there is no time zone, calendar date or time-of-day interpretation to supply.

| Active elapsed milliseconds | Formatted value | What the boundary illustrates |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `0` | `0:00` | An unstarted or just-started clock. |
| `999` | `0:00` | A partial second does not round upward. |
| `1000` | `0:01` | The first complete second. |
| `7000` | `0:07` | Seconds retain a leading zero. |
| `59999` | `0:59` | The minute changes only after its full interval. |
| `60000` | `1:00` | Seconds return to zero at a minute boundary. |
| `750000` | `12:30` | A longer ordinary game duration. |
| `3600000` | `60:00` | Minutes continue past fifty-nine. |
| `359999999` | `5999:59` | The game's elapsed-time ceiling. |

These values describe the formatter's result, without the `Time:` label added by the status bar. The completion banner uses the same formatter. A documentation screenshot may show an earlier rendered tick than an exported snapshot captures, because export synchronizes the active clock before encoding it. That difference does not imply two different elapsed-time formats.

## Active time and serialized milliseconds

The elapsed display omits subsecond detail, while game state retains it during play. `encodeSnapshot` floors `elapsedMs` to a whole millisecond for export. A pending mismatch's `remainingMs` is rounded upward instead. Those two directions serve different fields: flooring elapsed time records completed whole milliseconds; rounding remaining time upward avoids writing a pending interval as zero.

For example, a state with `elapsedMs` equal to `1500.75` exports `1500`. A mismatch with `remainingMs` equal to `0.25` exports `1`. The textarea does not contain the clock's formatted string in place of `elapsedMs`; it contains a numeric JSON field. The display can show only a whole second while the exported state still distinguishes positions within that second.

The usual mismatch begins with `800` active milliseconds remaining. Time while the page is hidden or while an imported unfinished snapshot awaits Resume does not consume that interval. Thus “800 milliseconds after the second reveal” is incomplete if it suggests uninterrupted wall time. “800 active milliseconds” is the precise phrase used when the timing distinction matters.

In engineering prose, the `Ms` suffix on `elapsedMs`, `remainingMs`, `atMs` and `endMs` identifies the unit. It is part of each real field name. Replacing `elapsedMs` with a friendlier invented key in a JSON example would change the format, rather than just improve its wording. [Snapshot format](../sharing/snapshot-format.md) and [Replay format](../sharing/replay-format.md) own the complete schemas.

## Board dimensions, card totals and pair totals

The control options are `4x4`, `6x6`, `8x8`, `10x10`, `12x12`, `14x14` and `16x16`. Their underlying select values are the side lengths. The visible `x` is an ordinary letter in the current labels. Descriptive prose can say “a board with four rows and four columns” when explaining the meaning, while an instruction naming the option uses the actual option text.

| Side length | Cards | Pairs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 4 | 16 | 8 |
| 6 | 36 | 18 |
| 8 | 64 | 32 |
| 10 | 100 | 50 |
| 12 | 144 | 72 |
| 14 | 196 | 98 |
| 16 | 256 | 128 |

The formula is `N * N` cards and half that many pairs. The size is not the number of pairs, and a face ID is not a card's position. Those distinctions matter when a bug report mentions “card 8” without saying whether it means a row-order index, a visible location or an artwork identity. [Board size catalogue](../gameplay/board-size-catalogue.md) covers dimensions; [Pair identity](../gameplay/pair-identity.md) covers what is being matched.

## Human positions and zero-based indices

Deck positions run from zero in row order. Accessible card names use rows and columns starting at one. For a size `N`, the name uses `floor(index / N) + 1` for the row and `(index % N) + 1` for the column. This is a conversion between two coordinate systems, not two different deck orders.

On a `4x4` board, index `0` is row 1, column 1; index `6` is row 2, column 3; and index `15` is row 4, column 4. A replay action's `index: 6` therefore targets the third card in the second row. It does not target a card whose face happens to be 6.

The replay CLI has another human-facing number: an action ordinal in an error. Internally, `readReplay` reports a zero-based action position. `runReplay` adds one when composing “action N” for a person reading stderr. That ordinal identifies the action's location in the list, while the action's `index` identifies a card on the board. An error about action 2 can therefore concern card index 0 without any contradiction.

## Limits are different kinds of numbers

`MOVES_MAX` is `999_999` in TypeScript and `999999` as a plain rendered count. `ELAPSED_MAX_MS` is `359_999_999`. The separators help a source reader scan literals; they are not included in JSON numbers or the current status display. Documentation discussing the constant can show the source spelling, while a literal exported example uses JSON's numeric syntax.

Reaching either gameplay ceiling does not end the game. Moves stop increasing at their cap, and elapsed time stops increasing at its cap, while cards can still be matched and the board can still be completed. “Maximum moves” is consequently different from “a move allowance”. The game does not count down to a loss condition.

Input sizes have a separate distinction. The board-code input has a `maxLength` of 32. The snapshot textarea has a `maxLength` of 65536, and the decoder also checks a UTF-8 byte limit of 65536. Character length in a DOM control and encoded byte length are different measurements, even when their limit has the same numeral. A multibyte character is enough to demonstrate why the second check still matters.

# Comparing tied competition results

This page describes competition result comparison and explains the active-time information available from the current game.

A result comparison uses information from completed play. The game core can tell whether a board is complete and can expose its moves and elapsed time. It does not compare two participants or contain a bracket seed, so the competition decision here sits outside the current single-game transitions.

## Comparison order

Moves are the first useful distinction between two completed attempts, but they can be equal. When both players of a match finish in the same number of moves, the lower active time wins, and if that is also equal the higher seed wins. Seed 1 is the highest seed. The comparison is ordered: an earlier distinction settles the result before a later one is considered.

These example results illustrate the first two levels. The elapsed values are milliseconds in game data.

| Participant | Moves | Active elapsed milliseconds | Result in this example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Ada | 12 | 70200 | Ahead on moves |
| Bo | 13 | 58100 | Faster, but more moves |

| Participant | Moves | Active elapsed milliseconds | Result in this example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Cora | 15 | 65200 | Ahead on active time |
| Dev | 15 | 65900 | Same moves, greater active time |

The examples deliberately separate efficiency from speed. An implementation that adds moves and seconds together, or sorts by time first, would produce a different comparison. There is no weighted combined score in the existing core or in the decision above.

## When every recorded value looks equal

Two equal move counts and equal active times lead to the seed branch described above.

A fixture with two completely equal game results exercises the seed branch, whereas examples with unequal times never reach it. [Competition pairing](competition-pairing.md) supplies the bracket context.

The seed settles the equality case without an extra round of play, shared outcome or random choice. The existing code knows nothing about an opponent or an entrant's seed.

## Active time in the current game

`GameState.elapsedMs` is advanced by `advanceGame` in `src/game/game.ts`. That function does nothing before play has started or after `isWon` becomes true. The first valid reveal sets `started: true`; ignored activations do not create another start event.

In the browser, `src/game/session/use-session-clock.ts` observes `performance.now()`. Its `running()` check combines visibility, pause state, the started flag and completion. `elapsedStep` in `browser-clock.ts` calculates the interval since the previous observation and contributes it only when active. This is elapsed active play, not a stopwatch started when the HTML file was opened.

The clock hook synchronizes before applying a card activation. As a result, the final valid activation is evaluated after accounting for the elapsed interval leading up to it. The source comment on snapshot export also points out that rendered state can trail the clock, which is why export synchronizes before encoding.

The 40ms scheduling constant is an update cadence, not the unit of the stored elapsed value. `performance.now()` can return fractional milliseconds, and the core preserves positive finite deltas. `browser-clock.test.ts` exercises fractional values and compares many observations with one observation over the same overall span.

## Display precision is a separate concern

`formatElapsed` in `src/game/elapsed-time.ts` discards sub-second detail for presentation. It is therefore possible for two visibly identical clock strings to correspond to different `elapsedMs` values. A screenshot of the ordinary status area cannot establish exact equality of active time.

The example with Cora and Dev demonstrates this issue: their stored times differ by 700ms even though a coarser presentation can hide that difference. Reading the rendered text back into a result comparison would throw away information the game already holds.

Snapshot serialization changes precision too, although less dramatically. `encodeSnapshot` floors `elapsedMs` to a whole millisecond. It rounds a pending mismatch's remaining interval upward so that interval remains representable. The game in memory may have fractional time that the snapshot no longer contains.

Current in-memory values, exported values and visible text have different precision, so an implementation review needs to identify which representation a prototype actually compares. Treating these as interchangeable would make exact equality depend on an undocumented conversion.

## Pauses and interruptions

The current browser session excludes hidden-page time and time spent waiting for Resume after an unfinished snapshot import. It does not offer an ordinary manual pause control. Sitting with the visible started board while talking still contributes active elapsed time, even when no cards are activated during that conversation.

A miss also contributes time. The two exposed nonmatching faces remain visible for 800 active milliseconds, during which activation is blocked. That wait is part of the same active timeline as elapsed play. Hiding the page pauses both the elapsed clock and the remaining mismatch interval.

These facts explain some apparent discrepancies in human timing. An observer measuring from the moment the device is handed over will include time before the first reveal. A wall stopwatch will include time while the page is hidden. A person looking only at clicks may overlook the visible thinking intervals between them. Those observations can all differ from `elapsedMs` without demonstrating a clock defect.

[Elapsed time rules](../gameplay/elapsed-time-rules.md), [clock design](../architecture/clock-design.md) and [mismatch interval](../gameplay/mismatch-interval.md) describe the existing mechanisms.

## Completion and boundary values

`isWon` checks whether matched positions cover the deck. Before that condition holds, a board can have many matched pairs and a plausible-looking move count while still being unfinished. A current status reading is not equivalent to a completed result merely because the player has stopped interacting.

The core caps moves at 999999 and elapsed time at 359999999ms. Matching and completion continue at those caps. These limits can increase the number of equal numeric values in artificial boundary fixtures. They do not create an uncapped hidden counter from which a comparison could recover a distinction.

`src/game/move-cap.test.ts` covers completion at the move boundary. The browser and core clock tests cover elapsed behavior separately. Those tests are evidence about single-game values; there is no competition result comparator test in the current source.

## Useful evidence for a disagreement

A disputed outcome can involve several separate questions: whether both attempts completed, which values were captured, how those values were compared and whether the participants understood the result. A screenshot may help with the last question, but it is weak evidence for sub-second equality. A snapshot gives structured game values but applies the integer export precision described above.

A replay can reconstruct card actions on a logical active timeline. In the current core it begins with a code, advances time before each action and advances again to its ending timestamp. It provides no record of the human circumstances around those actions. [Replay format](../sharing/replay-format.md) explains the available evidence without turning it into a competition log.

For a prototype review, the move-first example, the time-second example and an exact-equality example exercise distinct branches. Together they are more informative than many examples where one participant is better on every measure. They also make comparison errors visible before a polished result screen hides them.

# Focus policy

This page records focus behavior in the current game and the policy for a feature that changes the main screen.

Focus tells a keyboard user where input will go next. It is related to game selection but is not stored as part of a turn or snapshot. The current interface deliberately keeps deal-action focus, remembered board focus and card reveal state as distinct things.

## Existing page and future screens

`Game.tsx` currently renders one main area with an h1, deal controls, statistics, instructions, turn output, the Board and reproduction controls. It has no alternate-screen branch or screen-level h2 focus target. Replacing a deal remounts the board within that page; it does not replace the page with a different screen.

A feature that introduces a screen replacement has a different orientation problem from resetting a deck. When a feature replaces what the main area shows, focus moves to that screen's h2, which has tabindex="-1". This gives the new screen a programmatic landing place without adding that heading to ordinary Tab traversal. The current deal and load callbacks can still be understood on their own terms; they are not evidence that such a screen transition already exists.

The policy applies to the feature-level replacement described here. Expanding native details, updating statistics, closing a mismatch or displaying the completed-game paragraph does not currently create a new screen. Those operations retain the page structure and follow the existing behavior below. [Dialog policy](dialog-policy.md) covers a separate interaction with its own opening focus.

## Initial load is quiet

The hook `useBoardFocus(size)` initializes `focused` to zero. Board gives index 0 a tab index of zero and the other card buttons a tab index of minus one. This makes the first card available on entry, but no mount effect calls its focus method.

The browser's current focus therefore remains where it is at initial load. The page does not jump down to the board before a player has found Grid size or New Game. The board help paragraph describes how to enter and operate it. Its region uses `aria-describedby="board-help"` to associate those instructions with the board.

A remembered entry point is often described casually as “focus on the first card.” In this code that wording is incomplete. There is an entry point ready at the first card, while actual focus may be on the document, a deal button or another native control. Keeping those concepts separate prevents accidental mount-time focus stealing.

## Deal actions retain their location

New Game and Restart are native buttons that call the session controller. Neither callback moves focus into the board. After either action, a keyboard user remains on the button they used and can repeat the action or Tab toward the board. The size select uses its native interaction and likewise does not issue a board focus call.

The replacement increments `session.generation`, used as Board's React key. The newly mounted hook begins with a remembered index of zero. Thus the next board entry goes to the first card, even if the previous deal's memory was near its end. Actual action focus and future board entry are updated through different mechanisms.

A valid board-code load also increments generation. BoardCodeForm focuses its Load board ref on successful submission because its input is keyed by generation and will be replaced. That is especially important when the action was Enter in the input. An invalid submission keeps the input node and does not call the button ref, so correction can continue in place.

Clicking the load button starts with focus on that button, and an invalid click leaves it there. The distinction is based on the action's origin and successful input replacement, not on a general rule that all errors move focus into a field. [Error display guide](error-display-guide.md) follows those cases in detail.

## Remembered board focus

Board focus memory is a local hook state containing a card index. The `onFocus` callback updates it whenever a card receives focus. Board renders exactly that index with `tabIndex={0}`. All other cards remain programmatically focusable with `tabIndex={-1}`.

Arrow movement uses the DOM order of the deck and never changes game selection on its own. Tab and Shift+Tab are left to the browser, so the board is one stop in the page sequence rather than a trap. Returning to it finds the last focused card, even if that card is now matched.

Matched positions stay in the navigation geometry. A player does not need to relearn how many arrow presses separate two coordinates after a match. During a mismatch, focus can also move while activation is blocked. The same is true while imported unfinished progress waits for Resume. [Board keyboard navigation](board-keyboard-navigation.md) provides the calculations and edge behavior.

## Resume transfers before removal

Resume is the current exception to retaining focus on the action button. It exists only while `session.paused` is true. Clearing that flag removes the button, so leaving focus there would leave a disappearing target.

In `Game.tsx`, the local `resume()` function first calls `board.current?.focusRemembered()` and then `controller.resume()`. Board's imperative method focuses the remembered card with `preventScroll: true` and then brings it into view. Only after that does the controller clear the paused state and notices.

The ordering is observable. `tests/control-contract.e2e.test.ts` installs a focus listener and confirms that Resume is still present when the card receives focus. A visual assertion after the fact would not establish this timing. The focus-entry test also remembers a far card on a large imported board, scrolls away and confirms that Resume returns to that location with nearest alignment.

The remembered location after import is initially the first card because the import replaced the board. The player can change it while paused. Resume uses that current memory rather than the snapshot's revealed index or a hard-coded first card. A snapshot stores game progress, not the browser's last navigation location.

## Visible focus and scroll clearance

`game.css` defines `:focus-visible` as a `3px` white outline with a `2px` offset. `card.css` gives cards `scroll-margin: 6px`. This combination accommodates the ring when the card is brought to the edge of the scroll area.

The focus hook uses `card.matches(':focus-visible')` before scrolling in `cardFocused`. Keyboard movement can scroll immediately; pointer focus avoids moving a card under a held press. Board scrolls a clicked card after the click completes. The timing is part of reliable focus behavior, not only a visual polish detail.

`useNearestScroll` stores the board's last reported scroll position, restores it and then invokes `scrollIntoView` with nearest alignment. The source records the Chromium-specific reason: Tab or Shift+Tab can center a newly focused card before the handler runs. Starting from the prior view preserves the player's location as much as possible.

The helper leaves the outer page's scrolling to the browser. A review therefore measures both the card inside the board viewport and its visibility inside the window. A ring can be uncut by the board yet still sit partly below the window if the outer document did not move appropriately.

## Focus is not completion feedback

Winning does not move focus to the completion paragraph in GameStatus. The final card stays the current control, and the completed summary becomes available in document order. The final turn's feedback is published through the game's event output. The component does not force the player to leave the board simply because all pairs are now matched.

Likewise, a mismatch closing does not restore focus to either of its cards. Focus may have moved elsewhere while the pair was visible. The game-state update closes the faces while the user's navigation choice survives. An ordinary clock tick also leaves focus untouched.

These examples are useful when evaluating a proposed effect that focuses something whenever `game` changes. Game changes for elapsed time, first reveals, turn results and resets. An effect tied to that broad object would combine very different events and could interrupt typing or navigation. The existing code places its explicit focus operations at narrower action boundaries.

## Review evidence

The keyboard browser check covers Tab exit, remembered re-entry and matched-card focus. `tests/status-controls.e2e.test.ts` covers Enter submission from Board code. `tests/focus-entry.e2e.test.ts` covers nearest alignment and the switch from pointer use to keyboard arrows. `tests/layout.e2e.test.ts` checks outline clearance on large boards, including an interior card where container padding alone cannot protect the ring.

A useful focus report names the source control, action, destination and whether the source remains mounted. For example: “Enter in Board code loads 6x6, replaces the input and leaves Load board focused.” That is more precise than “load focuses correctly,” and it exposes why failure has a different result. [Interface review checklist](interface-review-checklist.md) gathers these journeys with layout and input checks.

For new screen work, the source review begins by locating the actual replacement boundary. For changes within the existing game page, it begins with the current action-specific behavior above. Screen replacement and the established board lifecycle have separate focus behavior.

# Time policy

This page describes how Neon Pairs accounts for active play time and keeps browser timing separate from logical game transitions.

There are three related values to distinguish: a browser observation, the delta between observations and the elapsed milliseconds stored in a game. The browser adapter observes; the clock arithmetic determines a delta; the rules apply that delta. The displayed statistic is derived from stored elapsed time rather than from a second independent stopwatch.

## Where observations enter

`use-session-clock.ts` owns browser observation and scheduling. Its neighbor `browser-clock.ts` accepts observations as arguments and computes a numerical step. Game code reads time only through the session clock. Only files in src/game/session/ may call performance.now, and no game code may use Date. Rule functions therefore receive elapsed amounts directly and can be exercised without a wall clock.

This boundary does not mean every file in the session directory performs an observation. `session.ts` transforms data and delegates logical advancement to `advanceGame`. `browser-clock.ts` creates an observation record from a supplied number. Their placement keeps time-related behavior together while the browser hook contains the actual calls.

The tests have their own environment control. Browser fixtures can install a Playwright clock and test scripts can set the observation that the application sees. Those are verification mechanisms outside the game source, not additional application clocks.

## Conditions for active time

The hook's `running()` predicate reads the latest session ref. It returns true only when the document is considered visible, the session is not paused, the game has started and the game is not won. The rules independently refuse to advance a game that has not started or has already been won.

A first accepted card activation sets `started` to true. The synchronization before that activation treats the preceding wait as inactive. The next active observation can therefore measure from the activation boundary rather than from page load. Repeated activation of the same revealed card is ignored by the rules but synchronization still accounts for time that passed before the attempted action.

An unfinished imported snapshot is paused by `replaceGame`. Its saved elapsed time and mismatch remainder remain game data, while the session prevents further active advancement until Resume. Resume resets the observation baseline and clears pause-related notices. It does not restart the imported game or give a pending mismatch a new full interval.

Completed games stop logical advancement. A completed imported game is already won, so it does not acquire an active timer. Completion through a final match is synchronized before that match, which makes the final stored elapsed time reflect play up to the finishing activation.

## Delta arithmetic

`ActiveClock` stores `observedAt`. `createClock(now)` creates that record. `elapsedStep(clock, now, active)` computes `delta = now - clock.observedAt`; it returns the delta only when active, finite and positive. Otherwise it returns zero. In both cases it returns a new clock whose baseline is `now`.

Advancing the baseline during an inactive observation is essential. Suppose the last active observation was 100ms, the page becomes hidden at 150ms and becomes visible at 5150ms. The hidden-to-visible event synchronizes while the stored visibility flag is still false. That step contributes zero and moves the baseline to 5150ms, so the following active observation excludes the hidden interval.

The arithmetic keeps fractional milliseconds. There is no per-observation integer rounding or tick counter. Several submillisecond positive deltas can add up just as one longer delta would. The tests compare totals with a floating-point tolerance where necessary.

A backward observation or a nonfinite delta produces no advancement. This is defensive handling of supplied values, not a claim that such a sequence is a normal browser clock behavior. The clock still records the supplied observation, so later arithmetic is based on that new baseline. [Clock design](clock-design.md) discusses this small function and the hook separately.

## Scheduling is an opportunity to observe

`CLOCK_INTERVAL_MS` is 40. The hook uses a timeout that reschedules itself. For a mismatch it asks for the smaller of 40 and `remainingMs`; otherwise it uses 40. A scheduled delay is not added directly to the game. When the callback runs, the hook obtains a new observation and computes the actual delta.

This differ…11150 tokens truncated…stays calm and concrete

The browser's two invalid-load messages are “Invalid board code.” and “Invalid snapshot.” They identify the rejected input without guessing how it became invalid. A code might have been mistyped, pasted incompletely or supplied with an unsupported size. A snapshot might be malformed JSON or a structurally inconsistent state. The short message does not pretend to distinguish causes the UI does not expose.

The success status for unfinished progress is more instructional: “Loaded snapshot. Select Resume to continue.” That second sentence matters because cards are not active until the player resumes. Completed progress uses “Loaded completed snapshot.” and has no continuation instruction. A generic “Success” would omit information that explains what the player sees next.

The game keeps failed drafts available for correction. Help can therefore describe correcting the field and selecting the load action again. Correction uses the existing field and load action. Detailed technical causes belong in [Error message style](error-message-style.md), where the browser notices and replay diagnostics are considered separately.

# Numbers style

This page explains how Neon Pairs presents counts, positions, durations and numeric values without confusing display text with saved data.

Numbers cross several boundaries in this game. The status bar shows compact values, accessible card names describe human positions, and snapshots carry machine-readable state. The same quantity can have different representations at those boundaries. The examples below come from `game.ts`, `elapsed-time.ts`, the status component and the version 1 readers; the underlying behavior belongs in [Scoring and moves](../gameplay/scoring-and-moves.md) and [Elapsed time rules](../gameplay/elapsed-time-rules.md).

## Counts in sentences and counts in a display

The current status component separates labels from values using a description list. `StatusLabel.moves` supplies “Moves:” and the adjacent value is `game.moves`. It is a compact display rather than a sentence about the count. Counts of moves read "1 move" and "2 moves", and durations read M:SS, such as 0:07 and 12:30. In prose, a unit makes an otherwise bare number understandable; beside an existing status label, the label already does that work.

This distinction is visible in `src/game/status/GameStatus.tsx`. Moves and best moves are plain numbers. Pairs are a matched count followed by the total. Time passes through `formatElapsed`. A missing best is the word “none”, not a numeric zero. Zero moves describes a real game state; no recorded best describes the absence of a record. Treating those as interchangeable would obscure the difference between starting a game and having completed one before.

The generated completion sentences currently interpolate `${game.moves} moves`. They do not call a general singular/plural helper. A legal completed board needs at least eight moves, so the completion surface does not encounter a one-move finish. The general prose convention above is therefore not evidence that a shared move-count formatter already exists.

The session does handle the singular pair count explicitly. It produces “Pair found. 1 pair matched.” for the first match and uses “pairs” for later nonfinal matches. The code tests `game.matched.length === 2`, because the stored list contains card positions. Counting array entries as if they were pairs would double the reported progress.

## A compact status example

A four-column game with one matched pair, two completed turns and a stored best of twelve moves has these count values:

| Surface | Example | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Moves | `Moves: 2` | Two second-card reveals have resolved turns. |
| Pairs | `Pairs: 1/8` | One pair is matched out of eight pairs. |
| Best | `Best: 12` | The saved record for this size is twelve moves. |
| Best without a record | `Best: none` | This size has no saved result. |

The slash in the pair display expresses progress against a total. It is not a fraction used to calculate a percentage, and the UI does not show a percentage alongside it. A report that says “one of eight pairs” is a readable expansion of the same value. A report that says “one of sixteen pairs” has mixed the card total with the pair total.

## The clock's representation

`formatElapsed(milliseconds)` floors the total seconds, derives total minutes, then pads the seconds component to two digits. Minutes continue growing beyond an hour. The display is an elapsed duration, so there is no time zone, calendar date or time-of-day interpretation to supply.

| Active elapsed milliseconds | Formatted value | What the boundary illustrates |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `0` | `0:00` | An unstarted or just-started clock. |
| `999` | `0:00` | A partial second does not round upward. |
| `1000` | `0:01` | The first complete second. |
| `7000` | `0:07` | Seconds retain a leading zero. |
| `59999` | `0:59` | The minute changes only after its full interval. |
| `60000` | `1:00` | Seconds return to zero at a minute boundary. |
| `750000` | `12:30` | A longer ordinary game duration. |
| `3600000` | `60:00` | Minutes continue past fifty-nine. |
| `359999999` | `5999:59` | The game's elapsed-time ceiling. |

These values describe the formatter's result, without the `Time:` label added by the status bar. The completion banner uses the same formatter. A documentation screenshot may show an earlier rendered tick than an exported snapshot captures, because export synchronizes the active clock before encoding it. That difference does not imply two different elapsed-time formats.

## Active time and serialized milliseconds

The elapsed display omits subsecond detail, while game state retains it during play. `encodeSnapshot` floors `elapsedMs` to a whole millisecond for export. A pending mismatch's `remainingMs` is rounded upward instead. Those two directions serve different fields: flooring elapsed time records completed whole milliseconds; rounding remaining time upward avoids writing a pending interval as zero.

For example, a state with `elapsedMs` equal to `1500.75` exports `1500`. A mismatch with `remainingMs` equal to `0.25` exports `1`. The textarea does not contain the clock's formatted string in place of `elapsedMs`; it contains a numeric JSON field. The display can show only a whole second while the exported state still distinguishes positions within that second.

The usual mismatch begins with `800` active milliseconds remaining. Time while the page is hidden or while an imported unfinished snapshot awaits Resume does not consume that interval. Thus “800 milliseconds after the second reveal” is incomplete if it suggests uninterrupted wall time. “800 active milliseconds” is the precise phrase used when the timing distinction matters.

In engineering prose, the `Ms` suffix on `elapsedMs`, `remainingMs`, `atMs` and `endMs` identifies the unit. It is part of each real field name. Replacing `elapsedMs` with a friendlier invented key in a JSON example would change the format, rather than just improve its wording. [Snapshot format](../sharing/snapshot-format.md) and [Replay format](../sharing/replay-format.md) own the complete schemas.

## Board dimensions, card totals and pair totals

The control options are `4x4`, `6x6`, `8x8`, `10x10`, `12x12`, `14x14` and `16x16`. Their underlying select values are the side lengths. The visible `x` is an ordinary letter in the current labels. Descriptive prose can say “a board with four rows and four columns” when explaining the meaning, while an instruction naming the option uses the actual option text.

| Side length | Cards | Pairs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 4 | 16 | 8 |
| 6 | 36 | 18 |
| 8 | 64 | 32 |
| 10 | 100 | 50 |
| 12 | 144 | 72 |
| 14 | 196 | 98 |
| 16 | 256 | 128 |

The formula is `N * N` cards and half that many pairs. The size is not the number of pairs, and a face ID is not a card's position. Those distinctions matter when a bug report mentions “card 8” without saying whether it means a row-order index, a visible location or an artwork identity. [Board size catalogue](../gameplay/board-size-catalogue.md) covers dimensions; [Pair identity](../gameplay/pair-identity.md) covers what is being matched.

## Human positions and zero-based indices

Deck positions run from zero in row order. Accessible card names use rows and columns starting at one. For a size `N`, the name uses `floor(index / N) + 1` for the row and `(index % N) + 1` for the column. This is a conversion between two coordinate systems, not two different deck orders.

On a `4x4` board, index `0` is row 1, column 1; index `6` is row 2, column 3; and index `15` is row 4, column 4. A replay action's `index: 6` therefore targets the third card in the second row. It does not target a card whose face happens to be 6.

The replay CLI has another human-facing number: an action ordinal in an error. Internally, `readReplay` reports a zero-based action position. `runReplay` adds one when composing “action N” for a person reading stderr. That ordinal identifies the action's location in the list, while the action's `index` identifies a card on the board. An error about action 2 can therefore concern card index 0 without any contradiction.

## Limits are different kinds of numbers

`MOVES_MAX` is `999_999` in TypeScript and `999999` as a plain rendered count. `ELAPSED_MAX_MS` is `359_999_999`. The separators help a source reader scan literals; they are not included in JSON numbers or the current status display. Documentation discussing the constant can show the source spelling, while a literal exported example uses JSON's numeric syntax.

Reaching either gameplay ceiling does not end the game. Moves stop increasing at their cap, and elapsed time stops increasing at its cap, while cards can still be matched and the board can still be completed. “Maximum moves” is consequently different from “a move allowance”. The game does not count down to a loss condition.

Input sizes have a separate distinction. The board-code input has a `maxLength` of 32. The snapshot textarea has a `maxLength` of 65536, and the decoder also checks a UTF-8 byte limit of 65536. Character length in a DOM control and encoded byte length are different measurements, even when their limit has the same numeral. A multibyte character is enough to demonstrate why the second check still matters.

# Comparing tied competition results

This page describes competition result comparison and explains the active-time information available from the current game.

A result comparison uses information from completed play. The game core can tell whether a board is complete and can expose its moves and elapsed time. It does not compare two participants or contain a bracket seed, so the competition decision here sits outside the current single-game transitions.

## Comparison order

Moves are the first useful distinction between two completed attempts, but they can be equal. When both players of a match finish in the same number of moves, the lower active time wins, and if that is also equal the higher seed wins. Seed 1 is the highest seed. The comparison is ordered: an earlier distinction settles the result before a later one is considered.

These example results illustrate the first two levels. The elapsed values are milliseconds in game data.

| Participant | Moves | Active elapsed milliseconds | Result in this example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Ada | 12 | 70200 | Ahead on moves |
| Bo | 13 | 58100 | Faster, but more moves |

| Participant | Moves | Active elapsed milliseconds | Result in this example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Cora | 15 | 65200 | Ahead on active time |
| Dev | 15 | 65900 | Same moves, greater active time |

The examples deliberately separate efficiency from speed. An implementation that adds moves and seconds together, or sorts by time first, would produce a different comparison. There is no weighted combined score in the existing core or in the decision above.

## When every recorded value looks equal

Two equal move counts and equal active times lead to the seed branch described above.

A fixture with two completely equal game results exercises the seed branch, whereas examples with unequal times never reach it. [Competition pairing](competition-pairing.md) supplies the bracket context.

The seed settles the equality case without an extra round of play, shared outcome or random choice. The existing code knows nothing about an opponent or an entrant's seed.

## Active time in the current game

`GameState.elapsedMs` is advanced by `advanceGame` in `src/game/game.ts`. That function does nothing before play has started or after `isWon` becomes true. The first valid reveal sets `started: true`; ignored activations do not create another start event.

In the browser, `src/game/session/use-session-clock.ts` observes `performance.now()`. Its `running()` check combines visibility, pause state, the started flag and completion. `elapsedStep` in `browser-clock.ts` calculates the interval since the previous observation and contributes it only when active. This is elapsed active play, not a stopwatch started when the HTML file was opened.

The clock hook synchronizes before applying a card activation. As a result, the final valid activation is evaluated after accounting for the elapsed interval leading up to it. The source comment on snapshot export also points out that rendered state can trail the clock, which is why export synchronizes before encoding.

The 40ms scheduling constant is an update cadence, not the unit of the stored elapsed value. `performance.now()` can return fractional milliseconds, and the core preserves positive finite deltas. `browser-clock.test.ts` exercises fractional values and compares many observations with one observation over the same overall span.

## Display precision is a separate concern

`formatElapsed` in `src/game/elapsed-time.ts` discards sub-second detail for presentation. It is therefore possible for two visibly identical clock strings to correspond to different `elapsedMs` values. A screenshot of the ordinary status area cannot establish exact equality of active time.

The example with Cora and Dev demonstrates this issue: their stored times differ by 700ms even though a coarser presentation can hide that difference. Reading the rendered text back into a result comparison would throw away information the game already holds.

Snapshot serialization changes precision too, although less dramatically. `encodeSnapshot` floors `elapsedMs` to a whole millisecond. It rounds a pending mismatch's remaining interval upward so that interval remains representable. The game in memory may have fractional time that the snapshot no longer contains.

Current in-memory values, exported values and visible text have different precision, so an implementation review needs to identify which representation a prototype actually compares. Treating these as interchangeable would make exact equality depend on an undocumented conversion.

## Pauses and interruptions

The current browser session excludes hidden-page time and time spent waiting for Resume after an unfinished snapshot import. It does not offer an ordinary manual pause control. Sitting with the visible started board while talking still contributes active elapsed time, even when no cards are activated during that conversation.

A miss also contributes time. The two exposed nonmatching faces remain visible for 800 active milliseconds, during which activation is blocked. That wait is part of the same active timeline as elapsed play. Hiding the page pauses both the elapsed clock and the remaining mismatch interval.

These facts explain some apparent discrepancies in human timing. An observer measuring from the moment the device is handed over will include time before the first reveal. A wall stopwatch will include time while the page is hidden. A person looking only at clicks may overlook the visible thinking intervals between them. Those observations can all differ from `elapsedMs` without demonstrating a clock defect.

[Elapsed time rules](../gameplay/elapsed-time-rules.md), [clock design](../architecture/clock-design.md) and [mismatch interval](../gameplay/mismatch-interval.md) describe the existing mechanisms.

## Completion and boundary values

`isWon` checks whether matched positions cover the deck. Before that condition holds, a board can have many matched pairs and a plausible-looking move count while still being unfinished. A current status reading is not equivalent to a completed result merely because the player has stopped interacting.

The core caps moves at 999999 and elapsed time at 359999999ms. Matching and completion continue at those caps. These limits can increase the number of equal numeric values in artificial boundary fixtures. They do not create an uncapped hidden counter from which a comparison could recover a distinction.

`src/game/move-cap.test.ts` covers completion at the move boundary. The browser and core clock tests cover elapsed behavior separately. Those tests are evidence about single-game values; there is no competition result comparator test in the current source.

## Useful evidence for a disagreement

A disputed outcome can involve several separate questions: whether both attempts completed, which values were captured, how those values were compared and whether the participants understood the result. A screenshot may help with the last question, but it is weak evidence for sub-second equality. A snapshot gives structured game values but applies the integer export precision described above.

A replay can reconstruct card actions on a logical active timeline. In the current core it begins with a code, advances time before each action and advances again to its ending timestamp. It provides no record of the human circumstances around those actions. [Replay format](../sharing/replay-format.md) explains the available evidence without turning it into a competition log.

For a prototype review, the move-first example, the time-second example and an exact-equality example exercise distinct branches. Together they are more informative than many examples where one participant is better on every measure. They also make comparison errors visible before a polished result screen hides them.

# Rules
The rules specification is a game contract that defines turns, scores and session changes in Neon Pairs.

Status: spec version 2.2.

A turn reveals two eligible cards. A match adds one pair, while a miss gives you time to remember the faces before both cards turn back.

## Board

- R01 - Support square boards with side lengths `4`, `6`, `8`, `10`, `12`, `14` and `16`. Every face occurs exactly twice. Positions run from zero in row order.

The deal comes from the board code defined in [Reproducibility](../sharing/reproducibility.md).

## Turn

- R02 - The first valid card activation reveals that card. Activating it again or activating a matched card has no game effect.
- R03 - The next valid activation reveals a different unmatched card. If the two faces match, keep them revealed and add one matched pair immediately.
- R04 - If the faces differ, show both for `800` active milliseconds, then close both together. Ignore all card activation during this interval. Pause the interval while the page is hidden or an imported snapshot awaits Resume.
- R05 - Add one move when the second valid card is revealed. The first reveal and ignored activation add no moves. Matches and misses each cost one move until the count reaches `999999`. At that cap the count stops increasing. Play continues normally, pairs still match and the game still completes. Show the current move count throughout play as `Moves: N`.

For example, revealing two matching cards produces one move and one matched pair. Revealing the same first card twice still leaves one revealed card and zero moves.

## Completion

- R06 - Give one point per matched pair and no other score. Show matched pairs against the board's total pairs throughout play as `Pairs: M/T`, where `M` is matched pairs and `T` is the total. Complete the game when every pair is matched. Show the final moves and elapsed time with a completion banner. Apply the completion motion defined in [Visuals](../visuals/visuals.md).


## Clock

- R07 - Start elapsed time on the first valid reveal. Count active milliseconds while the page is shown. Pause while the page is hidden or an imported snapshot awaits Resume. Stop at completion. Rendering frequency doesn't change the elapsed time. Cap elapsed time at `359999999` milliseconds. At the cap, play continues normally and the clock shows the capped time.

Show the clock throughout play as `Time: m:ss`. Round elapsed seconds down, pad seconds to two digits and let minutes continue past 59. For example, 3600000ms shows `Time: 60:00`.

The mismatch interval and elapsed clock use the same active time. Showing the page again continues the interval from its remaining time.

## Session

- R08 - Start with `4` rows and `4` columns unless a saved supported size exists. Remember the last chosen size after reload. A page load starts a fresh deal. Loading a valid board code or snapshot also saves its size as the last chosen size. A failed load keeps the saved size unchanged.
- R09 - New Game creates a fresh seed at the current size. Restart keeps the current board code. Choosing a different size creates a fresh seed at that size. Each action clears the selection, matched pairs, moves and elapsed time.
- R10 - When play completes a game, keep its moves if they beat the saved best for that size. Keep these records after reload. An equal or worse result keeps the existing best. Starting or restarting a game keeps these records. Show the current size's best move count throughout play and after completion as `Best: N`. Before that size has a record, show `Best: none`.
- R11 - Invalid board codes and snapshots show an error and keep the current game. Invalid saved preferences are ignored. If storage is unavailable, play continues without saving.
- R12 - Starting, restarting, replacing or leaving a game invalidates its pending timer updates. An update from an earlier game or turn can't change the current game.

For example, restarting during a mismatch produces the original hidden deal with zero moves. The earlier mismatch timer can't close a card revealed in the restarted game.

Control behavior is defined in [Input](../interface/input.md). Return to [Neon Pairs](../README.md) for the full specification.

# Input
Input is a set of controls that lets you play Neon Pairs with a pointer, touch or keyboard.

Status: spec version 2.2.

You can reveal a card with a tap, then move to its partner with the arrow keys. Every activation uses the same game action, so changing input methods keeps the same turn.

## Activation

The card controls follow these rules:

- I01 - Render each card as a native button. A primary click, a completed tap, Enter and Space activate the card through the same action.
- I03 - Keep the browser's normal context menu on right-click or long-press. Opening that menu doesn't activate a card.
- I04 - Hover and pointer cancellation leave the game state unchanged.

The game decides whether an activation changes a card. See [Rules](../gameplay/rules.md) for matches, repeated selections, blocked turns and turn timing.

## Keyboard movement

- I05 - Give the board one remembered tab stop. When Tab enters the board, focus that card. Use the first card before any board focus has been remembered.

- I06 - Move focus with these keys. Movement changes focus without activating a card:

| Key | Focus destination |
| --- | --- |
| ArrowLeft | Previous card in the same row |
| ArrowRight | Next card in the same row |
| ArrowUp | Card in the previous row and same column |
| ArrowDown | Card in the next row and same column |

The board handles only these four arrow keys without modifiers, plus Enter and Space. It leaves every other key and modifier combination to the browser and doesn't use them to move focus or activate a card.

- I07 - Stop arrow movement at a board edge. Moving left from the first column keeps focus on the same card.

- I08 - Let native Tab and Shift+Tab leave the board. Moving through the board uses the movement keys instead of adding every card to the page's tab order.

## Focus

The board keeps focus separate from play:

- I09 - Keep matched cards focusable and mark them `aria-disabled="true"`. Their game action follows the matched-card rule in the gameplay document.
- I10 - While a mismatching pair waits to turn back, allow focus movement and block card activation.
- I11 - On initial load, keep the browser's current focus. Loading the game doesn't move focus to the board.
- I12 - After a new deal, Restart or a successful load, reset the board's remembered tab stop to its first card.
- I13 - When a card receives focus, scroll it into view with nearest alignment in the board's scroll area. Give each card a scroll margin of at least 6px, so its complete focus outline stays in view, including mid-board cards.

The session buttons keep their focus as defined in [Controls](controls.md).

## Card names

The button names describe the information available to the player:

- I14 - Name a hidden card by its one-based row, column and closed state. Keep its face SVG and face identifier out of the DOM while it is hidden, including attributes and accessible text.
- I15 - Name a revealed or matched card by its position, face name and state. Use the face names defined in [Visuals](../visuals/visuals.md).

For example, the first hidden button is named "Row 1, column 1, closed". Once revealed, its name includes the face, so a player can remember it without seeing the drawing.

## Announcements

- I16 - Use one polite, atomic live region for turn results and completion. Announce each turn result exactly once. A winning turn has one announcement containing both the match and the win. Consecutive identical results each get their own announcement. Focus movement, clock renders and closing a mismatch don't repeat a result.

Use these turn announcements, where `M` is the matched pair count, `N` is moves and `time` uses R07's display format:

| Event | Announcement |
| --- | --- |
| First match | Pair found. 1 pair matched. |
| Later match | Pair found. M pairs matched. |
| Miss | No match. Cards close after a short pause. |
| Final match | Pair found. All pairs found in N moves and time. |

Send the load statuses in Controls through this same live region once per load event. Keep the visible status beside the reproduction controls.

For example, moving across three cards leaves the current announcement unchanged. Resolving the next pair announces that turn's result.

## Screen reader

- I17 - Support a complete 4x4 keyboard game with a screen reader. Find Grid size and New Game by name, enter the board, expose closed positions and revealed faces by name and state, announce one result per turn and make the win, final moves and time available. Leave the board with Tab and start another game. Deliver automated accessibility-tree evidence for this journey. Record the browser and tool versions in the project README and say whether a screen reader was used. If one was used, record its name and version. The user confirms spoken output during acceptance. Spoken confirmation isn't the developer's deliverable.

The complete game pack starts in [Neon Pairs](../README.md).

# Controls
Controls is a specification that defines the game options and reproduction tools in Neon Pairs.

Status: spec version 2.2.

You can start another deal, repeat the current one or load saved progress. Each control keeps the same label, so you can find the same action after a game changes.

## Deal controls

The main controls are:

- C01 - Label the native size select "Grid size". Give it options `4x4`, `6x6`, `8x8`, `10x10`, `12x12`, `14x14` and `16x16`, with numeric side length `N` as each value. After a successful board-code or snapshot load, select the loaded board's size.
- C02 - Label the fresh-deal button "New Game". It creates a fresh seed and keeps the current size.
- C03 - Label the repeat-deal button "Restart". It starts the same board code again.

Changing size, starting and restarting follow the session rules in [Rules](../gameplay/rules.md).

## Reproduction tools

- C04 - Put reproduction controls inside a native `details` element that starts collapsed. Give its summary the exact text "Reproduce a game".

The controls use the board-code and snapshot formats defined in [Reproducibility](../sharing/reproducibility.md). A board code starts a deal. A snapshot loads progress on a deal.

## Load a board

- C05 - Label the text input "Board code" and limit it to 32 characters. Show the current board code after a new deal, Restart or a successful load. Keep an edited draft when a card action changes the game.

- C06 - Label its button "Load board". Validate the entered code before replacing the current game with that deal's starting state.

For example, loading `np1-4-1` starts its hidden four-column board. Entering that code alone keeps the current game until you select Load board.

## Snapshot tools

- C07 - Label the textarea "Snapshot JSON" and limit it to 65536 characters. The parser also applies the UTF-8 byte limit in the snapshot format.

- C08 - Label the export button "Export snapshot". Fill the textarea with readable version 1 snapshot JSON that you can select and copy manually. Export leaves the game state and clock unchanged. It requires no Clipboard API.

Export `elapsedMs` and a pending mismatch's `remainingMs` as whole milliseconds. A pending mismatch always exports at least 1ms.

- C09 - Label the import button "Load snapshot". Validate the complete draft before replacing the current game. Load unfinished progress paused and show "Loaded snapshot. Select Resume to continue." Load completed progress as completed without pausing and show "Loaded completed snapshot."

- C10 - Show a "Resume" button only while an imported unfinished game is paused. Selecting it clears that pause. Unfinished play continues from the loaded state. While paused, block every card activation and allow board focus movement. On Resume, move focus to the board's remembered tab stop before removing the Resume button. A loaded completed game stays completed and shows no Resume button.

- C11 - On invalid input, keep the current game and the entered draft for correction. Show the exact status for that control:

| Control | Status |
| --- | --- |
| Load board | Invalid board code. |
| Load snapshot | Invalid snapshot. |

- C12 - A loaded completed snapshot keeps the win banner static and plays no celebration. Import doesn't write a best score. Resuming an unfinished snapshot and later winning records a local best under R10.

For example, loading a completed game with fewer moves than the saved best shows that game without replacing the saved record.

## Focus

- C13 - Keep focus on the button used for starting, restarting, loading or exporting. These actions don't move focus to the board. Resume follows C10 because its button disappears. The board's remembered tab stop follows the focus rules in [Input](input.md#focus).

## Replay

- C14 - Keep replay in the developer CLI and game core. V1 has no replay controls in the game UI.

Run `npm run --silent replay -- PATH` to read a replay file. On valid input, print only the final snapshot JSON to stdout and exit 0. On invalid input, print nothing to stdout, write a message to stderr and exit nonzero.

The complete game pack starts in [Neon Pairs](../README.md).

# Visuals
Visuals is a design specification that defines the layout, colors and card artwork for Neon Pairs.

Status: spec version 2.2.

A card face combines a shape, a marker position and a fill. You can identify a pair from those features even when you can't distinguish its color.

## Layout

- V01 - Use native controls and a CSS Grid board of DOM card buttons with inline SVG artwork. Render the game without canvas. Use no component library.
- V02 - Center the content within a maximum width of 1120px and give it 16px padding. Keep the outer page within the viewport width.
- V03 - Limit the board's scroll area to `70dvh`, capped at 768px tall. Give it 6px padding and allow overflow on both axes inside that area.
- V04 - Make each card square and size it from 44px to 88px according to the available board width. Use a 6px grid gap, a 2px card border and an 8px card radius.
- V05 - Fit the default four-column board within a phone viewport. When a larger board reaches the 44px minimum card size, keep that size and scroll inside the board.

For example, a sixteen-column board needs 794px for its cards and gaps, plus 12px for board padding. On a phone, the board scrolls while the outer page stays within the viewport width.

The 44px minimum is the chosen card target size. It doesn't state that the complete game conforms to an accessibility standard.

## Colors

- V06 - Use these colors for the page and controls:

| Token | Color | Use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Page | `#090B14` | Page background |
| Panel | `#141827` | Board scroll area, reproduction panel and non-card button, select, input and textarea backgrounds |
| Back | `#1B2034` | Hidden card background |
| Face | `#111625` | Revealed card background |
| Text | `#F4F6FF` | Main text |
| Secondary | `#B8BDD2` | Help text, status labels and optional supporting text |
| Border | `#757C9A` | Neutral borders |
| Focus | `#FFFFFF` | Focus outline |

- V07 - Use this ordered palette for card artwork:

| Index | Name | Color |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | Cyan | `#63E7FF` |
| 1 | Magenta | `#FF71D6` |
| 2 | Green | `#8BEA7D` |
| 3 | Yellow | `#FFE082` |
| 4 | Orange | `#FFB064` |
| 5 | Violet | `#B49AFF` |
| 6 | Rose | `#FF8296` |
| 7 | Ice | `#D9F3FF` |

## Type and spacing

- V08 - Use the system sans-serif font stack. Set body text to 16px with a 24px line height, the title to 24px and secondary text to 14px. Secondary text means help text, status labels and optional supporting text.

- V09 - Use spacing values of 4px, 6px, 8px, 12px, 16px, 24px and 32px for positive layout gaps, padding and margins you set. Allow zero resets and automatic centering. Reset browser default margins. Native control internals aren't covered. Card borders, radii, focus outlines, font metrics and SVG coordinates use their own stated values.

## Card faces

- V10 - Generate 128 face identities from integer face IDs `0` through `127`. Calculate each face from these ordered values:

| Part | Calculation | Ordered values |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Shape | `id % 8` | Circle, square, triangle, diamond, star, hexagon, plus, chevron |
| Marker | `floor(id / 8) % 8` | Top, top-right, right, bottom-right, bottom, bottom-left, left, top-left |
| Fill | `floor(id / 64)` | Solid, outline |
| Color | Palette at marker index | The eight palette colors above |

- V11 - Treat shape, marker and fill as the face identity. Color repeats the marker distinction and doesn't create a separate identity.

- V12 - Draw each face in an SVG with `viewBox="0 0 100 100"`. Center the main shape within `x=25..75` and `y=25..75`. Draw the marker above the shape as a circle with radius 5, centered 40 units from `(50, 50)` in its marker direction. Give the marker a 3-unit stroke in the Face background color, so it stays separate from the shape. Normalize diagonal directions, giving offsets of about 28.284 units on each axis. Use a 5-unit stroke for an outlined shape. At 44px, all 128 identities must be distinguishable in a grayscale face sheet, including solid and outlined squares with diagonal markers.

Use the face color for the solid shape's fill, the outlined shape's stroke and the marker's fill. An outlined shape has no fill. The marker keeps its Face-background stroke.

- V13 - Name each face with lowercase palette, fill, shape and marker names in the form "{color} {fill} {shape}, marker {position}". For example, face `0` is "cyan solid circle, marker top". Face `64` is "cyan outline circle, marker top".

## Card states

- V14 - Give every hidden card the same back with a neutral diamond. Hidden cards keep their face artwork out of the DOM, as [Input](../interface/input.md#card-names) requires.
- V15 - Show the face artwork on revealed cards. Keep it shown on matched cards and add a Green palette border and check mark. Keep matched cards at full opacity.
- V16 - Show keyboard focus with a 3px white outline offset by 2px. Hover changes only the border to the Text color. Matched cards keep their Green border when hovered.
- V17 - Use a 120ms border-color transition. Under `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce`, turn that transition off.

The gameplay document defines when card states change. See [Rules](../gameplay/rules.md) for turn timing and completion.

## Completion

- V18 - Show a win banner when the game finishes. Give it one 600ms pulse, then keep the banner static. Under `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce`, show the static banner immediately. Use neither flashing nor confetti.

## Large boards

- V19 - At viewport sizes 360x800 and 1280x800 CSS pixels, render all 256 cards of a 16x16 board. Keep the page within the viewport width and keep controls reachable. Keep each card at least 44px square, with scrolling confined to the board when needed. Reach the first and last card by touch scrolling and by keyboard. Scroll focused cards fully into view without clipping their focus outline.

## Browser zoom

- V20 - At a 640x400 CSS-pixel viewport with device scale 2, the equivalent layout of 200% browser zoom from 1280x800, keep controls, status and the win summary readable without overlap. Keep the page within the viewport width. Keep both a 4x4 board and a 16x16 board playable with pointer and keyboard. Allow board scrolling and keep the focused card and its complete focus outline in view. Don't disable pinch zoom.
