# Architecture
Architecture is the code structure for Neon Pairs that keeps game rules separate from browser effects.

Status: spec version 2.2.

A card activation changes game data first. React renders that data, then the session adapter handles time and saved preferences. The same rules run in browser tests and replay without a browser.

## Game core

- A01 - Keep deck generation, card transitions, logical time, snapshot validation and replay as pure functions under `src/game`. They receive their inputs directly. They don't read the DOM, storage, external random sources or browser clocks.

- A02 - Keep the board description and deck immutable. Keep matched positions, current selection, moves, active elapsed milliseconds and whether play started in game state. Derive pair count and victory. Serialize progress using the [reproducibility formats](../sharing/reproducibility.md).

- A03 - Use direct calls and exhaustive branches for the closed, one-card and mismatch states. Keep named states, format versions, timing values and size limits beside the behavior they control.

Proposed game functions:

| Call | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `createGame(boardCode)` | Initial state for a valid board code |
| `activateCard(state, index)` | State after one card activation |
| `advanceGame(state, milliseconds)` | State after logical time advances |
| `isWon(state)` | Whether every position is matched |
| `encodeSnapshot(state)` | Version 1 snapshot JSON |
| `decodeSnapshot(text)` | Valid restored state or `null` |
| `replayGame(text)` | Final replay state or `null` |

## Browser session

- A04 - Keep React state, timer lifecycle and browser visibility handling in `src/game/session`. Use a monotonic browser clock. Clear pending work on unmount and invalidate callbacks when the deal changes. A callback from an earlier deal can't change the current one.

- A05 - Keep preference and best-score reads in the session storage module. Treat saved JSON as unknown input. Validate grid sizes and finite integer scores. Catch read, parse and write failures. Keep unrelated storage keys untouched. A failure leaves the game playable.

- A06 - Keep active game progress in memory until you export or import a snapshot. Importing a completed snapshot doesn't update best scores or play a celebration. Completing an unfinished imported game records a local best under R10.

## Components

- A07 - `Game.tsx` composes status, the board, game controls and reproduction controls. Keep board navigation in `src/game/board`, controls in `src/game/controls` and session behavior in `src/game/session`. Keep each component's props and styles beside it.

- A08 - A card mounts its face SVG only while revealed or matched. Hidden card identity stays out of DOM attributes, accessible names and diagnostic globals. Tests can know a deck from its documented board code. The app gives them no solver endpoint.

- A09 - Use native browser input and the shared card activation function. Keep focus position in the board component. Focus movement changes presentation, never the deck or move count. [Input](../interface/input.md) defines the keys and focus rules.

## Evidence

- A10 - Keep focused tests beside their behavior. Complete browser journeys live at the application test level. Check generation against independent literal vectors. Check game transitions against stated rules. Test built HTML from disk as well as served storage behavior.

- A11 - Keep development fixtures and diagnostic helpers out of the shipped game. Tests can use the documented board code, snapshot and replay formats. The shipped game exposes only its documented controls.

## Changes

- A12 - Add a new rule at its game behavior, then update its component, tests and specification. Add shared support only when two actual behaviors need the same meaning. Don't add a global store, event bus, router or generic utility folder.

The [game specification](../README.md) defines the behavior this structure implements.

# Technology
Technology is the build and language specification for Neon Pairs.

Status: spec version 2.2.

The game runs offline from one HTML file. Browser controls and inline SVG provide the board, input and artwork.

## Stack

- T01 - Use React with TypeScript and DOM rendering. Use native buttons, a native select and CSS Grid. Use no component library.

- T02 - Pin these packages and keep the lockfile. The stable versions were checked on 31 October 2026:

| Package | Version | Job |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `react`, `react-dom` | `19.3.1` | Browser UI |
| `typescript` | `7.0.2` | Type checking |
| `@types/react`, `@types/react-dom` | `19.3.0` | React types |
| `vite` | `8.3.5` | Build |
| `@vitejs/plugin-react` | `6.1.2` | React build integration |
| `vite-plugin-singlefile` | `2.3.4` | One HTML distribution |
| `vitest` | `5.0.5` | Unit tests |
| `@playwright/test` | `1.64.1` | Browser tests |
| `@types/node` | `24.19.2` | Build and test types |

TypeScript 7 is a stable release, as the [release announcement](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/typescript/announcing-typescript-7-0/) describes. The [React versions page](https://react.dev/versions) lists the stable React release family.

## Language

- T03 - Use Node.js 24.19 or later and npm. Keep browser and Node compiler projects separate. Use ESM, static imports and type-only imports for types.

Use Node `26.12.1`, npm `11.20.0` and Playwright `1.64.1` with Chromium `156.0.8078.4` as the named compatibility combination. Record the locked install, build, unit tests and browser journeys with those exact versions in the project README before calling the combination tested. Other supported versions need their own results.

- T04 - Enable TypeScript strictness, `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`, `exactOptionalPropertyTypes`, `verbatimModuleSyntax` and `erasableSyntaxOnly`. Keep type checking separate from bundling. Vite's [TypeScript support](https://vite.dev/guide/features.html#typescript) transpiles code without checking types.

- T05 - Model project data with exact types and validate unknown data where it enters the game. Use narrowing instead of `any`, suppressed diagnostics or unchecked casts. Derive state unions from their named values.

- T06 - Keep behavior and its code, styles and tests together. Aim for 100 lines per TypeScript file and keep authored TypeScript files at or below 200 lines. Split by behavior when a file grows. Use direct imports from the file that defines a behavior.

## Commands

- T07 - Provide these commands:

| Command | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `npm ci` | Install the locked dependencies |
| `npm run dev` | Serve the game locally |
| `npm run typecheck` | Check every compiler project |
| `npm test` | Run unit tests for the game rules |
| `npm run test:e2e` | Build from current source, then run browser checks in fresh contexts against that build |
| `npm run build` | Type check and emit `dist/index.html` |
| `npm run --silent replay -- PATH` | Read replay JSON with the output and exit behavior in C14 |

The browser command must fail if its build fails. It must never fall back to an earlier `dist`. Stop development servers and watchers you start before finishing the work.

## Distribution

- T08 - `dist/index.html` contains the script, styles and artwork needed for play. It opens directly from disk without another file or a network request. Use the system font. Keep browser zoom enabled.

- T09 - Serve the game from a local HTTP origin when checking saved preferences. Storage on a `file:` URL differs between browsers, as the [localStorage documentation](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Window/localStorage) explains. If storage is unavailable, play continues for the current session.

- T10 - Keep dependencies in development and build tooling where possible. The game uses no service, account, external asset, analytics or API key. Dependency installation can use the network. Playing the distribution doesn't use it.

The [game specification](../README.md) connects this stack to the other requirements.

# Reproducibility
The reproducibility specification is a set of versioned formats that recreates Neon Pairs deals, progress and actions.

Status: spec version 2.2. Board codes, snapshots and replays keep format version 1.

A board code reproduces the starting cards. A snapshot restores a later position. A replay shows the actions that produced a position, so each format answers a different debugging question.

## Board code

- D01 - Use `np1-N-seed`, where `N` is a supported side length and `seed` is an integer from `1` through `2147483646`. Use decimal digits without leading zeros. The parser accepts exactly this form. Trim surrounding whitespace in the Board code control before parsing.
- D02 - Version `np1` fixes the generation algorithm below. The same code produces the same deck in every supported runtime. Changing generation requires another version. Time, animation and other random draws can't change this deck.

For example, `np1-4-1` describes a 4 by 4 board with generation version 1 and seed 1. It contains no progress.

## Generate

- D03 - Start the Park-Miller generator at `state = seed`. Each draw sets `state = (state * 16807) % 2147483647`. Use exact integer arithmetic. Seed 1 starts with states `16807`, `282475249`, `1622650073`, `984943658` and `1144108930`.
- D04 - Create the deck as `[0, 0, 1, 1, ...]` through face `N * N / 2 - 1`. Shuffle from index `N * N - 1` down to `1`. At index `i`, draw `j` in `0..i` and swap positions `i` and `j`.

For a draw with `b` possible results, set `q = 2147483646` and `limit = floor(q / b) * b`. Advance the generator and set `x = state - 1`. If `x >= limit`, draw again. Otherwise return `x % b`. This rejection step gives every result the same number of generator values.

The resulting deck for `np1-4-1` is `[6, 7, 0, 5, 2, 2, 0, 5, 3, 7, 1, 6, 4, 4, 1, 3]`.

## Snapshot

- D05 - Encode progress as a JSON object with exactly `version`, `boardCode`, `matched`, `selection`, `moves`, `elapsedMs` and `started`. `version` is `1`. `matched` is an array of matched position indices. Derive the deck, pair count and completion from these fields.

The `selection` object has one of these forms:

| `kind` | Other fields | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `closed` | None | No unmatched card is revealed |
| `one` | `index` | One unmatched card is revealed |
| `mismatch` | `first`, `second`, `remainingMs` | Two different faces await closing |

- D06 - Validate the complete object before replacing the game. Reject unknown keys. Require unique in-range matched indices containing whole face pairs. Selection indices must be in range and unmatched. A mismatch needs distinct indices with different faces and an integer `remainingMs` from `1` through `800`. Completion requires a closed selection.
- D07 - Require boolean `started` and nonnegative safe integers for `moves` and `elapsedMs`. Reject `elapsedMs` above `359999999` and `moves` above `999999`. Apply the move cap to saved best scores too. Require at least one move per matched pair and one further move for a pending mismatch. If `started` is false, require zero moves, zero elapsed time, no matches and a closed selection. A started game with zero moves requires one revealed card. Import of unfinished progress pauses the clock and pending mismatch until Resume. Completed imports stay completed without a pause.

Illustrative snapshot:

```json
{"version":1,"boardCode":"np1-4-1","matched":[0,11],"selection":{"kind":"mismatch","first":1,"second":2,"remainingMs":300},"moves":2,"elapsedMs":1500,"started":true}
```

Importing this snapshot shows one matched pair and two different faces. Resume lets those faces close after another `300` active milliseconds.

## Replay

- D08 - Encode a single deal as `{version: 1, boardCode, actions: [{atMs, index}], endMs}`. Require exactly these fields and exactly `atMs` and `index` per action. Indices must be in range. Times are nonnegative safe integers. Action times must be nondecreasing. If actions exist, `endMs` must be at least the final action time. Equal-time actions keep array order.
- D09 - Start from the code's hidden deal. Advance active time to each action's `atMs` before activating its index, then advance to `endMs`. Resolve a mismatch whose interval ends exactly at an action time before that action. Apply the game rules to ignored activation too. Cap replayed elapsed time at `359999999` milliseconds as R07 requires. Action times and `endMs` keep the nonnegative safe integer range in D08.

Illustrative replay:

```json
{"version":1,"boardCode":"np1-4-1","actions":[{"atMs":0,"index":0},{"atMs":0,"index":11}],"endMs":800}
```

This replay ends with one matched pair, one move and `800` elapsed milliseconds. Replay timestamps use a logical timeline. The game's elapsed clock still starts at its first valid activation. Replay omits hidden-page and imported-pause time. A new deal starts another replay.

## Limits

- D10 - Limit snapshot JSON to `65536` UTF-8 bytes. Limit replay JSON to `1048576` UTF-8 bytes and `10000` actions. Reject malformed JSON and unsupported format versions. For snapshots, inconsistent data means a violation of D05, D06 or D07. For replays, it means a violation of D08 or D09. For board codes, validate D01. Validation checks these stated constraints, without requiring a reconstructed history of earlier turns. Invalid board codes and snapshots keep the current browser game. Invalid replay files are rejected by the CLI and game core.

These local formats and saved scores are untrusted input. Validation checks the state rules, not a verified play history. The game has no accounts or trusted leaderboard.

Turn and clock behavior is defined in [Rules](../gameplay/rules.md). Return to [Neon Pairs](../README.md) for the full specification.

# Acceptance
Acceptance is a set of journeys that checks whether Neon Pairs meets its product requirements.

Status: spec version 2.2.

Finish a game, then start another one during a mismatch. The first journey checks play and completion. The second checks that an earlier timer can't change a new game.

## Play

Use these journeys with the requirements in [Rules](../gameplay/rules.md):

- Finish every supported size with complete pairs.
- Reveal one card twice, then reveal a different card. Check the exact move count.
- Match a pair, then miss a pair. Check the immediate match and the 800ms active mismatch interval.
- Hide the page during a mismatch, then return and finish its remaining interval.
- Start and restart during a mismatch. Check the cleared state and later timer updates.
- Finish games with better, equal and worse move counts. Reload and check the current size's best.

## Controls

Use pointer, touch and keyboard to follow [Input](../interface/input.md) and [Controls](../interface/controls.md). Check control labels, row movement, edge stops, native Tab exit and focus after each action. Check that hidden cards reveal no identity in the DOM.

Follow the keyboard journey in I17 and check its accessibility tree. During user acceptance, confirm spoken results with a screen reader, including consecutive identical results and the final match with its win.

## Appearance

Measure the layout and review all 128 faces against [Visuals](../visuals/visuals.md). Use a 44px grayscale face sheet to distinguish shape, marker and fill. Check 16x16 boards at both stated viewport sizes, full focus outlines and the equivalent zoom layout. Check reduced motion and the static completion banner after its single pulse.

Play through completion and reset while checking [Sound](../sound/sound.md). Every action stays silent.

## Reproduction

Check [Reproducibility](../sharing/reproducibility.md) with its example deck and replay. Check snapshot round trips and malformed input. Check the exact mismatch timeout before an equal-time replay action.

Load an unfinished snapshot, attempt input while paused, then Resume. Check its remaining active time and focus. Load a completed snapshot and check its static banner and unchanged best score.

## Delivery

Use a locked install, type check, unit tests and a fresh browser build as defined in [Technology](../architecture/technology.md). Open the resulting HTML directly from disk with network access blocked. Use a local HTTP origin for saved preferences.

Review the pure game functions, browser effects, file sizes and behavior placement against [Architecture](../architecture/architecture.md).

Back to [Neon Pairs](../README.md).

# Rules
The rules specification is a game contract that defines turns, scores and session changes in Neon Pairs.

Status: spec version 2.2.

A turn reveals two eligible cards. A match adds one pair, while a miss gives you time to remember the faces before both cards turn back.

## Board

- R01 - Support square boards with side lengths `4`, `6`, `8`, `10`, `12`, `14` and `16`. Every face occurs exactly twice. Positions run from zero in row order.

The deal comes from the board code defined in [Reproducibility](../sharing/reproducibility.md).

## Turn

- R02 - The first valid card activation reveals that card. Activating it again or activating a matched card has no game effect.
- R03 - The next valid activation reveals a different unmatched card. If the two faces match, keep them revealed and add one matched pair immediately.
- R04 - If the faces differ, show both for `800` active milliseconds, then close both together. Ignore all card activation during this interval. Pause the interval while the page is hidden or an imported snapshot awaits Resume.
- R05 - Add one move when the second valid card is revealed. The first reveal and ignored activation add no moves. Matches and misses each cost one move until the count reaches `999999`. At that cap the count stops increasing. Play continues normally, pairs still match and the game still completes. Show the current move count throughout play as `Moves: N`.

For example, revealing two matching cards produces one move and one matched pair. Revealing the same first card twice still leaves one revealed card and zero moves.

## Completion

- R06 - Give one point per matched pair and no other score. Show matched pairs against the board's total pairs throughout play as `Pairs: M/T`, where `M` is matched pairs and `T` is the total. Complete the game when every pair is matched. Show the final moves and elapsed time with a completion banner. Apply the completion motion defined in [Visuals](../visuals/visuals.md).


## Clock

- R07 - Start elapsed time on the first valid reveal. Count active milliseconds while the page is shown. Pause while the page is hidden or an imported snapshot awaits Resume. Stop at completion. Rendering frequency doesn't change the elapsed time. Cap elapsed time at `359999999` milliseconds. At the cap, play continues normally and the clock shows the capped time.

Show the clock throughout play as `Time: m:ss`. Round elapsed seconds down, pad seconds to two digits and let minutes continue past 59. For example, 3600000ms shows `Time: 60:00`.

The mismatch interval and elapsed clock use the same active time. Showing the page again continues the interval from its remaining time.

## Session

- R08 - Start with `4` rows and `4` columns unless a saved supported size exists. Remember the last chosen size after reload. A page load starts a fresh deal. Loading a valid board code or snapshot also saves its size as the last chosen size. A failed load keeps the saved size unchanged.
- R09 - New Game creates a fresh seed at the current size. Restart keeps the current board code. Choosing a different size creates a fresh seed at that size. Each action clears the selection, matched pairs, moves and elapsed time.
- R10 - When play completes a game, keep its moves if they beat the saved best for that size. Keep these records after reload. An equal or worse result keeps the existing best. Starting or restarting a game keeps these records. Show the current size's best move count throughout play and after completion as `Best: N`. Before that size has a record, show `Best: none`.
- R11 - Invalid board codes and snapshots show an error and keep the current game. Invalid saved preferences are ignored. If storage is unavailable, play continues without saving.
- R12 - Starting, restarting, replacing or leaving a game invalidates its pending timer updates. An update from an earlier game or turn can't change the current game.

For example, restarting during a mismatch produces the original hidden deal with zero moves. The earlier mismatch timer can't close a card revealed in the restarted game.

Control behavior is defined in [Input](../interface/input.md). Return to [Neon Pairs](../README.md) for the full specification.

# Input
Input is a set of controls that lets you play Neon Pairs with a pointer, touch or keyboard.

Status: spec version 2.2.

You can reveal a card with a tap, then move to its partner with the arrow keys. Every activation uses the same game action, so changing input methods keeps the same turn.

## Activation

The card controls follow these rules:

- I01 - Render each card as a native button. A primary click, a completed tap, Enter and Space activate the card through the same action.
- I03 - Keep the browser's normal context menu on right-click or long-press. Opening that menu doesn't activate a card.
- I04 - Hover and pointer cancellation leave the game state unchanged.

The game decides whether an activation changes a card. See [Rules](../gameplay/rules.md) for matches, repeated selections, blocked turns and turn timing.

## Keyboard movement

- I05 - Give the board one remembered tab stop. When Tab enters the board, focus that card. Use the first card before any board focus has been remembered.

- I06 - Move focus with these keys. Movement changes focus without activating a card:

| Key | Focus destination |
| --- | --- |
| ArrowLeft | Previous card in the same row |
| ArrowRight | Next card in the same row |
| ArrowUp | Card in the previous row and same column |
| ArrowDown | Card in the next row and same column |

The board handles only these four arrow keys without modifiers, plus Enter and Space. It leaves every other key and modifier combination to the browser and doesn't use them to move focus or activate a card.

- I07 - Stop arrow movement at a board edge. Moving left from the first column keeps focus on the same card.

- I08 - Let native Tab and Shift+Tab leave the board. Moving through the board uses the movement keys instead of adding every card to the page's tab order.

## Focus

The board keeps focus separate from play:

- I09 - Keep matched cards focusable and mark them `aria-disabled="true"`. Their game action follows the matched-card rule in the gameplay document.
- I10 - While a mismatching pair waits to turn back, allow focus movement and block card activation.
- I11 - On initial load, keep the browser's current focus. Loading the game doesn't move focus to the board.
- I12 - After a new deal, Restart or a successful load, reset the board's remembered tab stop to its first card.
- I13 - When a card receives focus, scroll it into view with nearest alignment in the board's scroll area. Give each card a scroll margin of at least 6px, so its complete focus outline stays in view, including mid-board cards.

The session buttons keep their focus as defined in [Controls](controls.md).

## Card names

The button names describe the information available to the player:

- I14 - Name a hidden card by its one-based row, column and closed state. Keep its face SVG and face identifier out of the DOM while it is hidden, including attributes and accessible text.
- I15 - Name a revealed or matched card by its position, face name and state. Use the face names defined in [Visuals](../visuals/visuals.md).

For example, the first hidden button is named "Row 1, column 1, closed". Once revealed, its name includes the face, so a player can remember it without seeing the drawing.

## Announcements

- I16 - Use one polite, atomic live region for turn results and completion. Announce each turn result exactly once. A winning turn has one announcement containing both the match and the win. Consecutive identical results each get their own announcement. Focus movement, clock renders and closing a mismatch don't repeat a result.

Use these turn announcements, where `M` is the matched pair count, `N` is moves and `time` uses R07's display format:

| Event | Announcement |
| --- | --- |
| First match | Pair found. 1 pair matched. |
| Later match | Pair found. M pairs matched. |
| Miss | No match. Cards close after a short pause. |
| Final match | Pair found. All pairs found in N moves and time. |

Send the load statuses in Controls through this same live region once per load event. Keep the visible status beside the reproduction controls.

For example, moving across three cards leaves the current announcement unchanged. Resolving the next pair announces that turn's result.

## Screen reader

- I17 - Support a complete 4x4 keyboard game with a screen reader. Find Grid size and New Game by name, enter the board, expose closed positions and revealed faces by name and state, announce one result per turn and make the win, final moves and time available. Leave the board with Tab and start another game. Deliver automated accessibility-tree evidence for this journey. Record the browser and tool versions in the project README and say whether a screen reader was used. If one was used, record its name and version. The user confirms spoken output during acceptance. Spoken confirmation isn't the developer's deliverable.

The complete game pack starts in [Neon Pairs](../README.md).

# Controls
Controls is a specification that defines the game options and reproduction tools in Neon Pairs.

Status: spec version 2.2.

You can start another deal, repeat the current one or load saved progress. Each control keeps the same label, so you can find the same action after a game changes.

## Deal controls

The main controls are:

- C01 - Label the native size select "Grid size". Give it options `4x4`, `6x6`, `8x8`, `10x10`, `12x12`, `14x14` and `16x16`, with numeric side length `N` as each value. After a successful board-code or snapshot load, select the loaded board's size.
- C02 - Label the fresh-deal button "New Game". It creates a fresh seed and keeps the current size.
- C03 - Label the repeat-deal button "Restart". It starts the same board code again.

Changing size, starting and restarting follow the session rules in [Rules](../gameplay/rules.md).

## Reproduction tools

- C04 - Put reproduction controls inside a native `details` element that starts collapsed. Give its summary the exact text "Reproduce a game".

The controls use the board-code and snapshot formats defined in [Reproducibility](../sharing/reproducibility.md). A board code starts a deal. A snapshot loads progress on a deal.

## Load a board

- C05 - Label the text input "Board code" and limit it to 32 characters. Show the current board code after a new deal, Restart or a successful load. Keep an edited draft when a card action changes the game.

- C06 - Label its button "Load board". Validate the entered code before replacing the current game with that deal's starting state.

For example, loading `np1-4-1` starts its hidden four-column board. Entering that code alone keeps the current game until you select Load board.

## Snapshot tools

- C07 - Label the textarea "Snapshot JSON" and limit it to 65536 characters. The parser also applies the UTF-8 byte limit in the snapshot format.

- C08 - Label the export button "Export snapshot". Fill the textarea with readable version 1 snapshot JSON that you can select and copy manually. Export leaves the game state and clock unchanged. It requires no Clipboard API.

Export `elapsedMs` and a pending mismatch's `remainingMs` as whole milliseconds. A pending mismatch always exports at least 1ms.

- C09 - Label the import button "Load snapshot". Validate the complete draft before replacing the current game. Load unfinished progress paused and show "Loaded snapshot. Select Resume to continue." Load completed progress as completed without pausing and show "Loaded completed snapshot."

- C10 - Show a "Resume" button only while an imported unfinished game is paused. Selecting it clears that pause. Unfinished play continues from the loaded state. While paused, block every card activation and allow board focus movement. On Resume, move focus to the board's remembered tab stop before removing the Resume button. A loaded completed game stays completed and shows no Resume button.

- C11 - On invalid input, keep the current game and the entered draft for correction. Show the exact status for that control:

| Control | Status |
| --- | --- |
| Load board | Invalid board code. |
| Load snapshot | Invalid snapshot. |

- C12 - A loaded completed snapshot keeps the win banner static and plays no celebration. Import doesn't write a best score. Resuming an unfinished snapshot and later winning records a local best under R10.

For example, loading a completed game with fewer moves than the saved best shows that game without replacing the saved record.

## Focus

- C13 - Keep focus on the button used for starting, restarting, loading or exporting. These actions don't move focus to the board. Resume follows C10 because its button disappears. The board's remembered tab stop follows the focus rules in [Input](input.md#focus).

## Replay

- C14 - Keep replay in the developer CLI and game core. V1 has no replay controls in the game UI.

Run `npm run --silent replay -- PATH` to read a replay file. On valid input, print only the final snapshot JSON to stdout and exit 0. On invalid input, print nothing to stdout, write a message to stderr and exit nonzero.

The complete game pack starts in [Neon Pairs](../README.md).

## Game core

- A02 - Keep the board description and deck immutable. Keep matched positions, current selection, moves, active elapsed milliseconds and whether play started in game state. Derive pair count and victory. Serialize progress using the [reproducibility formats](../sharing/reproducibility.md).

# Technology
Technology is the build and language specification for Neon Pairs.

Status: spec version 2.2.

The game runs offline from one HTML file. Browser controls and inline SVG provide the board, input and artwork.

## Stack

- T01 - Use React with TypeScript and DOM rendering. Use native buttons, a native select and CSS Grid. Use no component library.

- T02 - Pin these packages and keep the lockfile. The stable versions were checked on 31 October 2026:

| Package | Version | Job |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `react`, `react-dom` | `19.3.1` | Browser UI |
| `typescript` | `7.0.2` | Type checking |
| `@types/react`, `@types/react-dom` | `19.3.0` | React types |
| `vite` | `8.3.5` | Build |
| `@vitejs/plugin-react` | `6.1.2` | React build integration |
| `vite-plugin-singlefile` | `2.3.4` | One HTML distribution |
| `vitest` | `5.0.5` | Unit tests |
| `@playwright/test` | `1.64.1` | Browser tests |
| `@types/node` | `24.19.2` | Build and test types |

TypeScript 7 is a stable release, as the [release announcement](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/typescript/announcing-typescript-7-0/) describes. The [React versions page](https://react.dev/versions) lists the stable React release family.

## Language

- T03 - Use Node.js 24.19 or later and npm. Keep browser and Node compiler projects separate. Use ESM, static imports and type-only imports for types.

Use Node `26.12.1`, npm `11.20.0` and Playwright `1.64.1` with Chromium `156.0.8078.4` as the named compatibility combination. Record the locked install, build, unit tests and browser journeys with those exact versions in the project README before calling the combination tested. Other supported versions need their own results.

- T04 - Enable TypeScript strictness, `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`, `exactOptionalPropertyTypes`, `verbatimModuleSyntax` and `erasableSyntaxOnly`. Keep type checking separate from bundling. Vite's [TypeScript support](https://vite.dev/guide/features.html#typescript) transpiles code without checking types.

- T05 - Model project data with exact types and validate unknown data where it enters the game. Use narrowing instead of `any`, suppressed diagnostics or unchecked casts. Derive state unions from their named values.

- T06 - Keep behavior and its code, styles and tests together. Aim for 100 lines per TypeScript file and keep authored TypeScript files at or below 200 lines. Split by behavior when a file grows. Use direct imports from the file that defines a behavior.

## Commands

- T07 - Provide these commands:

| Command | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `npm ci` | Install the locked dependencies |
| `npm run dev` | Serve the game locally |
| `npm run typecheck` | Check every compiler project |
| `npm test` | Run unit tests for the game rules |
| `npm run test:e2e` | Build from current source, then run browser checks in fresh contexts against that build |
| `npm run build` | Type check and emit `dist/index.html` |
| `npm run --silent replay -- PATH` | Read replay JSON with the output and exit behavior in C14 |

The browser command must fail if its build fails. It must never fall back to an earlier `dist`. Stop development servers and watchers you start before finishing the work.

## Distribution

- T08 - `dist/index.html` contains the script, styles and artwork needed for play. It opens directly from disk without another file or a network request. Use the system font. Keep browser zoom enabled.

- T09 - Serve the game from a local HTTP origin when checking saved preferences. Storage on a `file:` URL differs between browsers, as the [localStorage documentation](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Window/localStorage) explains. If storage is unavailable, play continues for the current session.

- T10 - Keep dependencies in development and build tooling where possible. The game uses no service, account, external asset, analytics or API key. Dependency installation can use the network. Playing the distribution doesn't use it.

The [game specification](../README.md) connects this stack to the other requirements.

# Reproducibility
The reproducibility specification is a set of versioned formats that recreates Neon Pairs deals, progress and actions.

Status: spec version 2.2. Board codes, snapshots and replays keep format version 1.

A board code reproduces the starting cards. A snapshot restores a later position. A replay shows the actions that produced a position, so each format answers a different debugging question.

## Board code

- D01 - Use `np1-N-seed`, where `N` is a supported side length and `seed` is an integer from `1` through `2147483646`. Use decimal digits without leading zeros. The parser accepts exactly this form. Trim surrounding whitespace in the Board code control before parsing.
- D02 - Version `np1` fixes the generation algorithm below. The same code produces the same deck in every supported runtime. Changing generation requires another version. Time, animation and other random draws can't change this deck.

For example, `np1-4-1` describes a 4 by 4 board with generation version 1 and seed 1. It contains no progress.

## Generate

- D03 - Start the Park-Miller generator at `state = seed`. Each draw sets `state = (state * 16807) % 2147483647`. Use exact integer arithmetic. Seed 1 starts with states `16807`, `282475249`, `1622650073`, `984943658` and `1144108930`.
- D04 - Create the deck as `[0, 0, 1, 1, ...]` through face `N * N / 2 - 1`. Shuffle from index `N * N - 1` down to `1`. At index `i`, draw `j` in `0..i` and swap positions `i` and `j`.

For a draw with `b` possible results, set `q = 2147483646` and `limit = floor(q / b) * b`. Advance the generator and set `x = state - 1`. If `x >= limit`, draw again. Otherwise return `x % b`. This rejection step gives every result the same number of generator values.

The resulting deck for `np1-4-1` is `[6, 7, 0, 5, 2, 2, 0, 5, 3, 7, 1, 6, 4, 4, 1, 3]`.

## Snapshot

- D05 - Encode progress as a JSON object with exactly `version`, `boardCode`, `matched`, `selection`, `moves`, `elapsedMs` and `started`. `version` is `1`. `matched` is an array of matched position indices. Derive the deck, pair count and completion from these fields.

The `selection` object has one of these forms:

| `kind` | Other fields | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `closed` | None | No unmatched card is revealed |
| `one` | `index` | One unmatched card is revealed |
| `mismatch` | `first`, `second`, `remainingMs` | Two different faces await closing |

- D06 - Validate the complete object before replacing the game. Reject unknown keys. Require unique in-range matched indices containing whole face pairs. Selection indices must be in range and unmatched. A mismatch needs distinct indices with different faces and an integer `remainingMs` from `1` through `800`. Completion requires a closed selection.
- D07 - Require boolean `started` and nonnegative safe integers for `moves` and `elapsedMs`. Reject `elapsedMs` above `359999999` and `moves` above `999999`. Apply the move cap to saved best scores too. Require at least one move per matched pair and one further move for a pending mismatch. If `started` is false, require zero moves, zero elapsed time, no matches and a closed selection. A started game with zero moves requires one revealed card. Import of unfinished progress pauses the clock and pending mismatch until Resume. Completed imports stay completed without a pause.

Illustrative snapshot:

```json
{"version":1,"boardCode":"np1-4-1","matched":[0,11],"selection":{"kind":"mismatch","first":1,"second":2,"remainingMs":300},"moves":2,"elapsedMs":1500,"started":true}
```

Importing this snapshot shows one matched pair and two different faces. Resume lets those faces close after another `300` active milliseconds.

## Replay

- D08 - Encode a single deal as `{version: 1, boardCode, actions: [{atMs, index}], endMs}`. Require exactly these fields and exactly `atMs` and `index` per action. Indices must be in range. Times are nonnegative safe integers. Action times must be nondecreasing. If actions exist, `endMs` must be at least the final action time. Equal-time actions keep array order.
- D09 - Start from the code's hidden deal. Advance active time to each action's `atMs` before activating its index, then advance to `endMs`. Resolve a mismatch whose interval ends exactly at an action time before that action. Apply the game rules to ignored activation too. Cap replayed elapsed time at `359999999` milliseconds as R07 requires. Action times and `endMs` keep the nonnegative safe integer range in D08.

Illustrative replay:

```json
{"version":1,"boardCode":"np1-4-1","actions":[{"atMs":0,"index":0},{"atMs":0,"index":11}],"endMs":800}
```

This replay ends with one matched pair, one move and `800` elapsed milliseconds. Replay timestamps use a logical timeline. The game's elapsed clock still starts at its first valid activation. Replay omits hidden-page and imported-pause time. A new deal starts another replay.

## Limits

- D10 - Limit snapshot JSON to `65536` UTF-8 bytes. Limit replay JSON to `1048576` UTF-8 bytes and `10000` actions. Reject malformed JSON and unsupported format versions. For snapshots, inconsistent data means a violation of D05, D06 or D07. For replays, it means a violation of D08 or D09. For board codes, validate D01. Validation checks these stated constraints, without requiring a reconstructed history of earlier turns. Invalid board codes and snapshots keep the current browser game. Invalid replay files are rejected by the CLI and game core.

These local formats and saved scores are untrusted input. Validation checks the state rules, not a verified play history. The game has no accounts or trusted leaderboard.

Turn and clock behavior is defined in [Rules](../gameplay/rules.md). Return to [Neon Pairs](../README.md) for the full specification.

# Acceptance
Acceptance is a set of journeys that checks whether Neon Pairs meets its product requirements.

Status: spec version 2.2.

Finish a game, then start another one during a mismatch. The first journey checks play and completion. The second checks that an earlier timer can't change a new game.

## Play

Use these journeys with the requirements in [Rules](../gameplay/rules.md):

- Finish every supported size with complete pairs.
- Reveal one card twice, then reveal a different card. Check the exact move count.
- Match a pair, then miss a pair. Check the immediate match and the 800ms active mismatch interval.
- Hide the page during a mismatch, then return and finish its remaining interval.
- Start and restart during a mismatch. Check the cleared state and later timer updates.
- Finish games with better, equal and worse move counts. Reload and check the current size's best.

## Controls

Use pointer, touch and keyboard to follow [Input](../interface/input.md) and [Controls](../interface/controls.md). Check control labels, row movement, edge stops, native Tab exit and focus after each action. Check that hidden cards reveal no identity in the DOM.

Follow the keyboard journey in I17 and check its accessibility tree. During user acceptance, confirm spoken results with a screen reader, including consecutive identical results and the final match with its win.

## Appearance

Measure the layout and review all 128 faces against [Visuals](../visuals/visuals.md). Use a 44px grayscale face sheet to distinguish shape, marker and fill. Check 16x16 boards at both stated viewport sizes, full focus outlines and the equivalent zoom layout. Check reduced motion and the static completion banner after its single pulse.

Play through completion and reset while checking [Sound](../sound/sound.md). Every action stays silent.

## Reproduction

Check [Reproducibility](../sharing/reproducibility.md) with its example deck and replay. Check snapshot round trips and malformed input. Check the exact mismatch timeout before an equal-time replay action.

Load an unfinished snapshot, attempt input while paused, then Resume. Check its remaining active time and focus. Load a completed snapshot and check its static banner and unchanged best score.

## Delivery

Use a locked install, type check, unit tests and a fresh browser build as defined in [Technology](../architecture/technology.md). Open the resulting HTML directly from disk with network access blocked. Use a local HTTP origin for saved preferences.

Review the pure game functions, browser effects, file sizes and behavior placement against [Architecture](../architecture/architecture.md).

Back to [Neon Pairs](../README.md).

# Dialog policy

This page records the confirmation policy for leaving unfinished work and its relationship to the game's existing actions.

The current source contains no dialog component, native dialog element or leave-work handler. New Game, Restart, board-code loading and snapshot loading call the controller directly.

## The confirmation boundary

A confirmation is useful only when it corresponds to a real decision about abandoning work. Its content and focus need to make the conservative path understandable before the player commits to leaving. Leaving unfinished work asks first in a native dialog element with two buttons, Keep playing and Leave. Keep playing takes focus when it opens, and Escape keeps playing. The decision is about the unfinished work being left; opening a disclosure to inspect a code is not itself that decision.

There is no third action specified by this policy. In particular, the existing snapshot exporter does not turn this confirmation into an automatic save workflow. Export is a separate user action with a text result. A feature that uses the confirmation can draw on that distinction without presenting an unsaved draft as if it had already been preserved.

The policy does not define which future feature owns a leave route or a new navigation screen. Those boundaries have to be visible in the feature's actual code. The current page has no router and no alternate play screen. [Focus policy](focus-policy.md) covers orientation when a feature introduces a main-area replacement.

## What the present controls actually do

`Controls.tsx` renders New Game and Restart as native buttons. Their callbacks in `use-game.ts` reset the clock adapter and commit a replacement game. They do not consult `started`, Moves, Pairs or a dialog result before doing so. The existing game replaces immediately when those buttons are used.

BoardCodeForm validates before replacing. Its `loadBoard` callback returns false for invalid input and true after successful replacement. Snapshot loading decodes the whole draft before replacing as well. These paths protect against invalid external data; they are not implementations of a leave confirmation.

The native `details` panel is also not a modal. It expands in document flow and leaves the rest of the page operable. Calling its summary a dialog trigger would misdescribe both the DOM and its focus behavior. [Reproduction panel](reproduction-panel.md) documents the actual disclosure.

This distinction matters during incremental work. A new dialog in one feature does not silently change the semantics of every old control. When reading a change, follow the event handler to see whether it reaches a confirmation boundary, a parser, or the replacement directly. Similar visual labels do not establish the same lifecycle.

## Native behavior and application decisions

The policy names a native element because the interface already relies on browser semantics for buttons, forms, selects and details. A dialog has a different interaction boundary from an ordinary panel. Its opening, cancellation and closing need to be considered as a coherent interaction rather than a div painted over the board.

Using the element alone does not decide what leaving means for a game. The application still owns the transition that discards or replaces state. In the current implementation, that transition is represented by controller operations and `replaceGame`. Visual disappearance of an overlay is not evidence that a session was replaced, just as visual appearance is not evidence that play was paused.

The distinction between cancellation and commitment is observable in game state. Continuing leaves the same deal, revealed selection and counters available. A committed departure may dispose of or replace the session, depending on the feature. The current game has no dialog-specific storage write or serialized marker.

No dialog state exists in `Session`. Its fields are `game`, `paused`, `generation`, `feedback`, `loadNotice`, `announcement`, `celebration` and `preferences`. The existing `paused` flag specifically represents unfinished snapshot import. Reusing that flag for a new overlay without considering its other consumers would also affect Resume and load notices.

## Timing questions exposed by an overlay

A mismatch stores its remaining active milliseconds in game selection. The session clock advances it when the page is visible and the imported-pause flag is clear. Merely placing a dialog above the board is not one of those conditions in the current source.

Consequently, there is no existing rule here that opening a confirmation pauses the elapsed clock or mismatch. A feature implementation needs to be read for its actual timing behavior rather than assuming that every modal surface freezes play. [Clock design](../architecture/clock-design.md) and [Mismatch interval](../gameplay/mismatch-interval.md) explain the established clock model.

Replacement does have a well-defined lifecycle today. `clock.reset()` and the session generation prevent old pending updates from affecting a replacement game. If a leave decision leads to that existing path, stale-timer protection still belongs to the session. The dialog does not need to know the two selected card indices to implement that protection.

The period between opening and making a decision is therefore worth observing in review. It can expose accidental differences between the visual state, current game state and timers. The observation is useful even when the feature's intended behavior is simply to preserve the current clock semantics.

## Focus ownership

Opening the confirmation establishes a temporary interaction context. The policy above states its initial focus and cancellation result. That avoids relying on DOM order alone to make the safe continuation choice the first keyboard target.

After a decision, the durability of the source control matters. Existing action buttons generally remain mounted after a deal replacement, while Resume removes itself. Game handles Resume by moving focus before the button is removed. That is a concrete example of a disappearing source, though it is not a dialog implementation.

A leave feature may keep or remove its trigger as part of its surrounding screen. Its focus return depends on which controls remain mounted. A review can inspect the final active element and its visibility.

The board also remembers focus independently of actual focus. Opening another surface would not, by itself, mean its last card index should become a selected turn. A player returning to the board still needs the distinction between orientation and activation described in [Board keyboard navigation](board-keyboard-navigation.md).

## Review notes for a proposed implementation

The most useful review evidence separates opening, continuing and leaving. A single screenshot of the open surface cannot establish which element is focused, whether Escape follows the continuation path, or whether the underlying controller already replaced the game before a decision.

A source trace can identify the first state-changing call relative to the decision. A keyboard trace can identify the active element at opening and after cancellation. A populated game, especially one with a pending mismatch, makes unintended early replacement visible. These are ways of observing the stated policy and existing game lifecycle, rather than additional product requirements.

Current browser tests establish focus retention on ordinary buttons, invalid draft preservation, Resume's transfer order and stale-timer protection. They do not establish a dialog journey. Any future report of dialog coverage has to point at the corresponding implementation and evidence, rather than citing those tests because they also involve focus.

The relevant background is [Native controls guide](native-controls-guide.md) for element choice, [Focus policy](focus-policy.md) for page orientation and [New game and restart](../gameplay/new-game-and-restart.md) for the existing replacement boundary. Together they make it possible to review a concrete leave interaction alongside the existing game lifecycle.

# Disabled state guide

This page explains why some card activations have no effect while the controls remain focusable and usable for navigation.

The game separates control semantics, focus and game eligibility. A matched card exposes an unavailable state, but it stays in the board. A mismatching pair temporarily blocks further activation, yet arrows can still explore the same coordinates. These are deliberate differences rather than one universal disabled flag.

## Matched cards use ARIA state

`Card.tsx` sets `aria-disabled={matched}` on its native button. It does not set the HTML `disabled` attribute. When matched is true, the button remains available to programmatic focus and the board's remembered tab-stop mechanism.

The card's accessible name includes `matched`, along with its coordinate and face description. Its face remains visible, its border becomes the green palette color and a corner check mark appears. Matched cards retain full opacity. The state is communicated through text, semantics and visual treatment rather than by dimming the card until it is difficult to identify.

The click handler still calls `activate(index)` for a matched card. ARIA describes the state; it does not suppress native events. The actual game guard in `activateCard` checks `state.matched.includes(index)` and returns the same state. The session sees that identity and returns without publishing a new result.

This is an important code-reading boundary. Removing the guard because a button “is already disabled” would mistake an accessibility attribute for an event blocker. Conversely, adding native disabled would change focus behavior even if ignored activation still produced no move.

## Why focus remains available

The board uses one remembered card in the page's tab sequence. Arrow movement traverses coordinates without skipping solved positions. A match can therefore leave focus on its second card, and the next arrow still means the adjacent row or column.

If matched buttons became natively disabled, they would no longer participate in the same focus behavior. Remembered entry could point to an unavailable native focus target, and movement would need a different policy for skipping positions. The current input specification instead keeps the rectangular geometry stable.

A player can leave with Tab and return to the remembered matched card. Activating it again has no game effect. This is covered in `tests/keyboard.e2e.test.ts`, which checks the disabled attribute, continued focus and unchanged move count after another Space activation.

[Board keyboard navigation](board-keyboard-navigation.md) explains the tab-index pattern and edge clamping. The disabled state does not create a second movement algorithm or change the size of the board.

## A revealed first card is different

The first revealed card has state `revealed` and is not matched. It therefore exposes `aria-disabled="false"`. Activating it again is nevertheless ignored by the game's `SelectionKind.one` branch because `first === index`.

This is not inconsistent with the matched-card treatment. The first reveal is an intermediate turn state. The game waits for a different eligible position to complete the attempt, while the first card remains readable and focusable. The button name describes what the player can know, and the core determines whether this particular activation advances the turn.

There is no separate “selected but disabled” CSS class or native disabling operation for that card. A repeated click may keep focus there and apply completed-click scrolling, but it does not add a move, restart elapsed time or produce a turn result.

The same separation lets a player navigate away from the first card and return without changing selection. Focus is not stored in the `selection` union. A review that derives reveal state from the currently focused element would collapse two independent parts of the interface.

## Mismatch blocking is in the game

After two different faces are revealed, selection becomes `mismatch` with a remaining active interval. The core's mismatch branch returns unchanged state for every attempted activation until advancement closes the pair. The unmatched card buttons do not all acquire ARIA disabled state during this interval.

Movement and focus remain available. A player can inspect coordinates or prepare a next choice while the pair stays visible. Closing the mismatch does not force focus back to either revealed position. The game-state change removes their faces, while navigation memory remains where the player moved it.

The controller synchronizes active time before processing a card action. An activation arriving when the mismatch has already expired can therefore be processed after closure rather than being rejected against stale rendered state. The guard operates on current synchronized game state, not a CSS class observed a moment earlier.

The interval pauses while the document is hidden. That is a clock lifecycle behavior, not a mass change to card attributes. [Mismatch interval](../gameplay/mismatch-interval.md) and [Clock design](../architecture/clock-design.md) describe the timing model.

## Imported pause is in the session

Loading unfinished progress sets `session.paused`. `activateSession` returns immediately while that flag is true, before calling the core activation function. `tickSession` also rejects advancement while paused.

The Board does not receive paused as a prop. It continues rendering the loaded game's visible faces, matched states and navigation callbacks. Unmatched buttons remain semantically unmatched rather than becoming a new paused-card class. The load notice and Resume explain the paused session state outside the board.

A player can move focus while paused. Resume returns to the current remembered card before clearing the pause and removing its button. A snapshot with a pending mismatch then continues its remaining interval. A completed import is not paused and has no Resume button; all of its cards are already matched.

The automated accessibility journey explicitly checks that a paused unfinished import does not mark unmatched cards disabled. This is stronger than assuming paused and disabled are interchangeable words. [Reproduction panel](reproduction-panel.md) describes the visible continuation controls.

## Deal and text controls stay usable

New Game and Restart are available during ordinary play, mismatch waiting and imported pause. Their controller operations replace the game and clear the old session context. There is no busy-state branch disabling them while a timer is active.

The reproduction actions also remain available. An invalid draft is submitted for validation rather than causing its load button to become disabled before the user can request a result. Export reads current progress without replacing the game. A valid load can replace a paused or active position through the same validated boundary.

The current forms do not use `required`, a disabled submit button or `aria-invalid` as their validation mechanism. Their native length limits constrain editing, and the controller reports invalid content on action. [Error display guide](error-display-guide.md) traces those outcomes and the preservation of drafts.

This describes the existing controls, not a new general rule that every possible action in a future feature is always enabled. The relevant question in review is which layer owns the reason an action cannot change state, and whether the element's semantics and focus behavior match that reason.

## Rendering, counters and no-op actions

Core activation returns the original object for invalid indices, matched positions, repeated first positions and mismatch blocking. The session preserves identity when the core does. That lets the surrounding controller avoid committing a new state for an ignored action.

Synchronization can still advance elapsed time before the ignored activation is considered. Seeing Time change around a no-op click does not mean the click added a move. The move count changes only when a second eligible card resolves an attempt, subject to its cap.

At completion, every index is matched, so further card activation follows the matched guard. The final clock stays stopped because advancement checks `isWon`. There is no extra completed-overlay element that captures clicks above the board.

These details help distinguish a correct ignored action from a lost input. A click on a hidden eligible card in a closed active game should reveal it. A click on a matched card should not change the turn. Both can deliver the same native event; their game-state eligibility differs.

## Review evidence

The useful checks pair an input with both its state effect and its focus effect. The keyboard test checks matched inactivity while focus remains. The input-contract test checks hidden controls' exact ARIA attributes. The accessibility journey checks matched disabled exposure and paused unmatched exposure. Session unit tests check paused activation and advancement independently of the DOM.

A defect report can name the card coordinate, its visible state, session pause status, selection kind and expected counter change. That information reveals whether the problem belongs to native focus, ARIA exposure, controller timing or core eligibility. Treating every ignored input as the same disabled-control problem would hide those distinctions.

# Screen reader notes

This page describes the information exposed during a keyboard game and the limits of the project's screen reader evidence.

The interface exposes native controls, card names, state changes and readable results. The repository README records accessibility-tree checks in Chromium 156.0.8078.4 with Playwright 1.64.1. It also explicitly records that no screen reader was run. The names and sentences below are source-backed content available to assistive technology, not a transcript of speech captured in a listening session.

## Finding the game controls

The document language is English, the browser title is Neon Pairs, and the main area contains the game's h1 and introductory text. The first interactive deal control is the native select labeled Grid size. New Game and Restart follow as native buttons.

The select's label is connected with `htmlFor="grid-size"`. Its options read 4x4 through 16x16 at the seven supported sizes. A user can find it by its visible name rather than needing to interpret an unlabeled icon. The action buttons also use visible text as their names.

The statistics are reading content in a definition list: Moves, Pairs, Time and Best. There are no custom accessible labels replacing their values. An absent best is visible as `none`. These details matter when inspecting the tree because the information is ordinary document content, not four editable fields or buttons.

Changing size creates a deal of that size. New Game creates another deal at the current size, and Restart repeats the current code. Those actions retain focus at their controls. They do not suddenly land the player deep in the card board. [Control bar](control-bar.md) describes the callbacks and layout.

## Entering the board

Board's viewport is a region named `Game board` and described by `board-help`. The help text says: `Use a pointer or Tab to enter the board. Arrow keys move between cards. Enter or Space reveals a card.` This is visible text as well as an associated description.

Tab enters at the remembered card. Before any card focus has been remembered, that is the first card. Plain arrows move one row or column with no wrapping. Tab and Shift+Tab can leave the board. Modifier combinations and unlisted keys remain browser input rather than board commands.

The native card button provides activation through Enter and Space. Screen reader interaction modes can affect which keys reach a web page, so a real spoken acceptance journey is still valuable even when the browser's keyboard tests pass. The game's documented input relies on native button activation and board arrow navigation.

Matched cards remain focusable, and navigation does not skip them. During a mismatch or paused import, movement can continue although activating another card has no game effect. This keeps exploration separate from the turn decision. [Board keyboard navigation](board-keyboard-navigation.md) traces the remembered tab stop and target calculation.

## A closed card reveals no hidden identity

`describeCard` builds a one-based coordinate from the zero-based deck index. Index 0 on a four-column board is named `Row 1, column 1, closed`. Index 5 is `Row 2, column 2, closed`. The pattern gives a stable spatial reference before any face is known.

Board passes `face={null}` for a hidden card. Card then renders only the neutral back span with `aria-hidden="true"`, not the Face component. The hidden face is absent from the element's label, attributes and child artwork. A screen reader cannot legitimately read a face description from that hidden DOM because it is not there.

This is stronger than hiding a face SVG with CSS while leaving a revealing title or data attribute. The browser input-contract test compares every hidden card's attributes, inner HTML and text against the expected neutral content. A visual-only inspection could miss such a leak.

The deck still exists in game state because the game must resolve matches. The DOM boundary is the important distinction for the interface: a hidden card control exposes its position and closed state, not its underlying identity. [Card artwork](../visuals/card-artwork.md) and [Pair identity](../gameplay/pair-identity.md) explain the visual and game sides.

## The first reveal

Use `np1-4-1` as a concrete source-backed example. Its index 0 contains face 6. After activation, that button's name becomes `Row 1, column 1, revealed, cyan solid plus, marker top`. The state precedes the face description in the actual string generated by `card-state.ts`.

Face names come from `faceDesign`: color, solid or outline, shape and marker position. The SVG itself is `aria-hidden="true"` and `focusable="false"`. It does not add a separate graphic description competing with the button name. The name carries the information the player needs to remember.

A first reveal starts elapsed time but leaves Moves at zero. The game has not yet completed a two-card attempt. It also does not publish a turn result merely for that first card. A user can inspect the newly focused control's name, move to another location and make the second choice.

Repeating activation on the same first card does not complete a move. That is an ignored game action, not a second reveal or a reason to read a new turn result. This is useful when interpreting a test that presses Space twice and sees no move increment.

## A match and a miss

On the same example code, index 11 is the partner of index 0. It is row 3, column 4. Activating it completes the pair immediately. Both controls' names use `matched`, retain the face description and expose `aria-disabled="true"`.

The current result text for the first match is `Pair found. 1 pair matched.` Later nonfinal matches substitute the count and plural form. The matched controls remain in the board's spatial navigation even though activating them no longer changes the game. A screen reader may verbalize their unavailable state according to its own conventions; the source exposes the ARIA disabled state.

Indices 0 and 1 are a mismatch on this code. Their faces remain revealed for the active mismatch interval, and the turn result is `No match. Cards close after a short pause.` Additional card activation during that wait is ignored. The interval pauses while the page is hidden or imported progress waits for Resume.

After closure, the two names return to their closed forms and their face artwork is removed. Closure does not publish another turn result. Moving focus while the pair waits also does not republish the mismatch sentence. [Announcements policy](announcements-policy.md) explains the event identity that makes consecutive identical misses distinct without making ordinary renders noisy.

## Completing the game

The winning match produces `Pair found. All pairs found in N moves and time.`, using the final counters. GameStatus also displays the persistent completion sentence `Every pair found in N moves and time. Well played.` A reader can revisit the final statistics and summary in document content.

The time text uses the game's formatter: seconds are padded, and minutes can grow beyond 59. The values stop advancing at completion. The final card remains the active control; completion does not force focus onto the banner.

Matched cards still occupy the board, so Tab leaves it without requiring a pass through every matched position. In the collapsed page layout, the next control is the native reproduction summary. Shift+Tab can return through the remembered board location toward the deal controls. Starting another game resets board memory while leaving the action button focused.

The complete automated journey exercises this path, including a new game after completion. It checks the final summary in the accessibility tree rather than assuming that visible text is necessarily exposed as expected.

## Reproduction tools in reading order

The native summary is named `Reproduce a game`. Expanding it exposes labeled Board code and Snapshot JSON fields with Load board, Export snapshot and Load snapshot actions. The board-code form submits with Enter; the snapshot actions are ordinary buttons rather than an Enter-to-import form.

Invalid input keeps the current game and draft. The visible outcomes are `Invalid board code.` and `Invalid snapshot.`. The load buttons reference the nearby notice paragraph as a description, and the event feedback path publishes the outcome. Clicking a load button leaves focus there. An invalid Enter submission from Board code leaves focus in the input for correction.

A valid unfinished snapshot reports `Loaded snapshot. Select Resume to continue.` and pauses card activation. The player can still explore the board with arrows. Resume focuses the remembered card before the Resume button is removed, then continues active play. A completed snapshot reports `Loaded completed snapshot.`, shows the completed game statically and offers no Resume button.

Export fills readable JSON into the textarea. It does not require clipboard permission or make the text impossible to select. A user can move to the native field and copy its contents through their normal editing commands. [Reproduction panel](reproduction-panel.md) explains draft lifetimes and the different board-code reset behavior.

## What the automated journey records

`tests/accessibility.e2e.test.ts` uses Chromium's debugging protocol to enable accessibility and capture full trees at named stages. Its helper removes ignored nodes and records role, name, scalar value, text and selected accessibility properties. This produces evidence about exposed controls and states without preserving transient browser node identifiers.

The journey finds Grid size and New Game by name, enters the board, inspects closed and revealed names, completes pairs with Enter and Space, checks matched disabled state and reads each turn result. It then checks completion, Tab exit, New Game and repeated load outcomes. The saved artifact is named `accessibility-journey.json` by the test.

The test writes that artifact as output. The source references reviewed fixtures for expected content.

## Spoken acceptance still answers a different question

Tree exposure, keyboard behavior and speech are related but distinct. A browser may expose the correct atomic result while a particular screen reader schedules or phrases it in a way that needs listening review. Consecutive identical misses and the final combined result are especially useful listening points.

The input specification assigns spoken confirmation to user acceptance. The repository README's record says `Screen reader: not run. Spoken journey: user acceptance.` That limitation belongs beside the evidence, not hidden behind a broad statement that screen reader support was tested end to end.

A useful acceptance note names the browser, screen reader and versions, the action sequence and what was heard. If a result differs, the DOM publication history and tree capture can help locate the boundary. [Accessibility audit](../quality/accessibility-audit.md) and [Browser test guide](../quality/browser-test-guide.md) provide the wider review context.

# Dialog policy

This page records the confirmation policy for leaving unfinished work and its relationship to the game's existing actions.

The current source contains no dialog component, native dialog element or leave-work handler. New Game, Restart, board-code loading and snapshot loading call the controller directly.

## The confirmation boundary

A confirmation is useful only when it corresponds to a real decision about abandoning work. Its content and focus need to make the conservative path understandable before the player commits to leaving. Leaving unfinished work asks first in a native dialog element with two buttons, Keep playing and Leave. Keep playing takes focus when it opens, and Escape keeps playing. The decision is about the unfinished work being left; opening a disclosure to inspect a code is not itself that decision.

There is no third action specified by this policy. In particular, the existing snapshot exporter does not turn this confirmation into an automatic save workflow. Export is a separate user action with a text result. A feature that uses the confirmation can draw on that distinction without presenting an unsaved draft as if it had already been preserved.

The policy does not define which future feature owns a leave route or a new navigation screen. Those boundaries have to be visible in the feature's actual code. The current page has no router and no alternate play screen. [Focus policy](focus-policy.md) covers orientation when a feature introduces a main-area replacement.

## What the present controls actually do

`Controls.tsx` renders New Game and Restart as native buttons. Their callbacks in `use-game.ts` reset the clock adapter and commit a replacement game. They do not consult `started`, Moves, Pairs or a dialog result before doing so. The existing game replaces immediately when those buttons are used.

BoardCodeForm validates before replacing. Its `loadBoard` callback returns false for invalid input and true after successful replacement. Snapshot loading decodes the whole draft before replacing as well. These paths protect against invalid external data; they are not implementations of a leave confirmation.

The native `details` panel is also not a modal. It expands in document flow and leaves the rest of the page operable. Calling its summary a dialog trigger would misdescribe both the DOM and its focus behavior. [Reproduction panel](reproduction-panel.md) documents the actual disclosure.

This distinction matters during incremental work. A new dialog in one feature does not silently change the semantics of every old control. When reading a change, follow the event handler to see whether it reaches a confirmation boundary, a parser, or the replacement directly. Similar visual labels do not establish the same lifecycle.

## Native behavior and application decisions

The policy names a native element because the interface already relies on browser semantics for buttons, forms, selects and details. A dialog has a different interaction boundary from an ordinary panel. Its opening, cancellation and closing need to be considered as a coherent interaction rather than a div painted over the board.

Using the element alone does not decide what leaving means for a game. The application still owns the transition that discards or replaces state. In the current implementation, that transition is represented by controller operations and `replaceGame`. Visual disappearance of an overlay is not evidence that a session was replaced, just as visual appearance is not evidence that play was paused.

The distinction between cancellation and commitment is observable in game state. Continuing leaves the same deal, revealed selection and counters available. A committed departure may dispose of or replace the session, depending on the feature. The current game has no dialog-specific storage write or serialized marker.

No dialog state exists in `Session`. Its fields are `game`, `paused`, `generation`, `feedback`, `loadNotice`, `announcement`, `celebration` and `preferences`. The existing `paused` flag specifically represents unfinished snapshot import. Reusing that flag for a new overlay without considering its other consumers would also affect Resume and load notices.

## Timing questions exposed by an overlay

A mismatch stores its remaining active milliseconds in game selection. The session clock advances it when the page is visible and the imported-pause flag is clear. Merely placing a dialog above the board is not one of those conditions in the current source.

Consequently, there is no existing rule here that opening a confirmation pauses the elapsed clock or mismatch. A feature implementation needs to be read for its actual timing behavior rather than assuming that every modal surface freezes play. [Clock design](../architecture/clock-design.md) and [Mismatch interval](../gameplay/mismatch-interval.md) explain the established clock model.

Replacement does have a well-defined lifecycle today. `clock.reset()` and the session generation prevent old pending updates from affecting a replacement game. If a leave decision leads to that existing path, stale-timer protection still belongs to the session. The dialog does not need to know the two selected card indices to implement that protection.

The period between opening and making a decision is therefore worth observing in review. It can expose accidental differences between the visual state, current game state and timers. The observation is useful even when the feature's intended behavior is simply to preserve the current clock semantics.

## Focus ownership

Opening the confirmation establishes a temporary interaction context. The policy above states its initial focus and cancellation result. That avoids relying on DOM order alone to make the safe continuation choice the first keyboard target.

After a decision, the durability of the source control matters. Existing action buttons generally remain mounted after a deal replacement, while Resume removes itself. Game handles Resume by moving focus before the button is removed. That is a concrete example of a disappearing source, though it is not a dialog implementation.

A leave feature may keep or remove its trigger as part of its surrounding screen. Its focus return depends on which controls remain mounted. A review can inspect the final active element and its visibility.

The board also remembers focus independently of actual focus. Opening another surface would not, by itself, mean its last card index should become a selected turn. A player returning to the board still needs the distinction between orientation and activation described in [Board keyboard navigation](board-keyboard-navigation.md).

## Review notes for a proposed implementation

The most useful review evidence separates opening, continuing and leaving. A single screenshot of the open surface cannot establish which element is focused, whether Escape follows the continuation path, or whether the underlying controller already replaced the game before a decision.

A source trace can identify the first state-changing call relative to the decision. A keyboard trace can identify the active element at opening and after cancellation. A populated game, especially one with a pending mismatch, makes unintended early replacement visible. These are ways of observing the stated policy and existing game lifecycle, rather than additional product requirements.

Current browser tests establish focus retention on ordinary buttons, invalid draft preservation, Resume's transfer order and stale-timer protection. They do not establish a dialog journey. Any future report of dialog coverage has to point at the corresponding implementation and evidence, rather than citing those tests because they also involve focus.

The relevant background is [Native controls guide](native-controls-guide.md) for element choice, [Focus policy](focus-policy.md) for page orientation and [New game and restart](../gameplay/new-game-and-restart.md) for the existing replacement boundary. Together they make it possible to review a concrete leave interaction alongside the existing game lifecycle.
