# Disabled state guide

This page explains why some card activations have no effect while the controls remain focusable and usable for navigation.

The game separates control semantics, focus and game eligibility. A matched card exposes an unavailable state, but it stays in the board. A mismatching pair temporarily blocks further activation, yet arrows can still explore the same coordinates. These are deliberate differences rather than one universal disabled flag.

## Matched cards use ARIA state

`Card.tsx` sets `aria-disabled={matched}` on its native button. It does not set the HTML `disabled` attribute. When matched is true, the button remains available to programmatic focus and the board's remembered tab-stop mechanism.

The card's accessible name includes `matched`, along with its coordinate and face description. Its face remains visible, its border becomes the green palette color and a corner check mark appears. Matched cards retain full opacity. The state is communicated through text, semantics and visual treatment rather than by dimming the card until it is difficult to identify.

The click handler still calls `activate(index)` for a matched card. ARIA describes the state; it does not suppress native events. The actual game guard in `activateCard` checks `state.matched.includes(index)` and returns the same state. The session sees that identity and returns without publishing a new result.

This is an important code-reading boundary. Removing the guard because a button “is already disabled” would mistake an accessibility attribute for an event blocker. Conversely, adding native disabled would change focus behavior even if ignored activation still produced no move.

## Why focus remains available

The board uses one remembered card in the page's tab sequence. Arrow movement traverses coordinates without skipping solved positions. A match can therefore leave focus on its second card, and the next arrow still means the adjacent row or column.

If matched buttons became natively disabled, they would no longer participate in the same focus behavior. Remembered entry could point to an unavailable native focus target, and movement would need a different policy for skipping positions. The current input specification instead keeps the rectangular geometry stable.

A player can leave with Tab and return to the remembered matched card. Activating it again has no game effect. This is covered in `tests/keyboard.e2e.test.ts`, which checks the disabled attribute, continued focus and unchanged move count after another Space activation.

[Board keyboard navigation](board-keyboard-navigation.md) explains the tab-index pattern and edge clamping. The disabled state does not create a second movement algorithm or change the size of the board.

## A revealed first card is different

The first revealed card has state `revealed` and is not matched. It therefore exposes `aria-disabled="false"`. Activating it again is nevertheless ignored by the game's `SelectionKind.one` branch because `first === index`.

This is not inconsistent with the matched-card treatment. The first reveal is an intermediate turn state. The game waits for a different eligible position to complete the attempt, while the first card remains readable and focusable. The button name describes what the player can know, and the core determines whether this particular activation advances the turn.

There is no separate “selected but disabled” CSS class or native disabling operation for that card. A repeated click may keep focus there and apply completed-click scrolling, but it does not add a move, restart elapsed time or produce a turn result.

The same separation lets a player navigate away from the first card and return without changing selection. Focus is not stored in the `selection` union. A review that derives reveal state from the currently focused element would collapse two independent parts of the interface.

## Mismatch blocking is in the game

After two different faces are revealed, selection becomes `mismatch` with a remaining active interval. The core's mismatch branch returns unchanged state for every attempted activation until advancement closes the pair. The unmatched card buttons do not all acquire ARIA disabled state during this interval.

Movement and focus remain available. A player can inspect coordinates or prepare a next choice while the pair stays visible. Closing the mismatch does not force focus back to either revealed position. The game-state change removes their faces, while navigation memory remains where the player moved it.

The controller synchronizes active time before processing a card action. An activation arriving when the mismatch has already expired can therefore be processed after closure rather than being rejected against stale rendered state. The guard operates on current synchronized game state, not a CSS class observed a moment earlier.

The interval pauses while the document is hidden. That is a clock lifecycle behavior, not a mass change to card attributes. [Mismatch interval](../gameplay/mismatch-interval.md) and [Clock design](../architecture/clock-design.md) describe the timing model.

## Imported pause is in the session

Loading unfinished progress sets `session.paused`. `activateSession` returns immediately while that flag is true, before calling the core activation function. `tickSession` also rejects advancement while paused.

The Board does not receive paused as a prop. It continues rendering the loaded game's visible faces, matched states and navigation callbacks. Unmatched buttons remain semantically unmatched rather than becoming a new paused-card class. The load notice and Resume explain the paused session state outside the board.

A player can move focus while paused. Resume returns to the current remembered card before clearing the pause and removing its button. A snapshot with a pending mismatch then continues its remaining interval. A completed import is not paused and has no Resume button; all of its cards are already matched.

The automated accessibility journey explicitly checks that a paused unfinished import does not mark unmatched cards disabled. This is stronger than assuming paused and disabled are interchangeable words. [Reproduction panel](reproduction-panel.md) describes the visible continuation controls.

## Deal and text controls stay usable

New Game and Restart are available during ordinary play, mismatch waiting and imported pause. Their controller operations replace the game and clear the old session context. There is no busy-state branch disabling them while a timer is active.

The reproduction actions also remain available. An invalid draft is submitted for validation rather than causing its load button to become disabled before the user can request a result. Export reads current progress without replacing the game. A valid load can replace a paused or active position through the same validated boundary.

The current forms do not use `required`, a disabled submit button or `aria-invalid` as their validation mechanism. Their native length limits constrain editing, and the controller reports invalid content on action. [Error display guide](error-display-guide.md) traces those outcomes and the preservation of drafts.

This describes the existing controls, not a new general rule that every possible action in a future feature is always enabled. The relevant question in review is which layer owns the reason an action cannot change state, and whether the element's semantics and focus behavior match that reason.

## Rendering, counters and no-op actions

Core activation returns the original object for invalid indices, matched positions, repeated first positions and mismatch blocking. The session preserves identity when the core does. That lets the surrounding controller avoid committing a new state for an ignored action.

Synchronization can still advance elapsed time before the ignored activation is considered. Seeing Time change around a no-op click does not mean the click added a move. The move count changes only when a second eligible card resolves an attempt, subject to its cap.

At completion, every index is matched, so further card activation follows the matched guard. The final clock stays stopped because advancement checks `isWon`. There is no extra completed-overlay element that captures clicks above the board.

These details help distinguish a correct ignored action from a lost input. A click on a hidden eligible card in a closed active game should reveal it. A click on a matched card should not change the turn. Both can deliver the same native event; their game-state eligibility differs.

## Review evidence

The useful checks pair an input with both its state effect and its focus effect. The keyboard test checks matched inactivity while focus remains. The input-contract test checks hidden controls' exact ARIA attributes. The accessibility journey checks matched disabled exposure and paused unmatched exposure. Session unit tests check paused activation and advancement independently of the DOM.

A defect report can name the card coordinate, its visible state, session pause status, selection kind and expected counter change. That information reveals whether the problem belongs to native focus, ARIA exposure, controller timing or core eligibility. Treating every ignored input as the same disabled-control problem would hide those distinctions.

# Screen reader notes

This page describes the information exposed during a keyboard game and the limits of the project's screen reader evidence.

The interface exposes native controls, card names, state changes and readable results. The repository README records accessibility-tree checks in Chromium 156.0.8078.4 with Playwright 1.64.1. It also explicitly records that no screen reader was run. The names and sentences below are source-backed content available to assistive technology, not a transcript of speech captured in a listening session.

## Finding the game controls

The document language is English, the browser title is Neon Pairs, and the main area contains the game's h1 and introductory text. The first interactive deal control is the native select labeled Grid size. New Game and Restart follow as native buttons.

The select's label is connected with `htmlFor="grid-size"`. Its options read 4x4 through 16x16 at the seven supported sizes. A user can find it by its visible name rather than needing to interpret an unlabeled icon. The action buttons also use visible text as their names.

The statistics are reading content in a definition list: Moves, Pairs, Time and Best. There are no custom accessible labels replacing their values. An absent best is visible as `none`. These details matter when inspecting the tree because the information is ordinary document content, not four editable fields or buttons.

Changing size creates a deal of that size. New Game creates another deal at the current size, and Restart repeats the current code. Those actions retain focus at their controls. They do not suddenly land the player deep in the card board. [Control bar](control-bar.md) describes the callbacks and layout.

## Entering the board

Board's viewport is a region named `Game board` and described by `board-help`. The help text says: `Use a pointer or Tab to enter the board. Arrow keys move between cards. Enter or Space reveals a card.` This is visible text as well as an associated description.

Tab enters at the remembered card. Before any card focus has been remembered, that is the first card. Plain arrows move one row or column with no wrapping. Tab and Shift+Tab can leave the board. Modifier combinations and unlisted keys remain browser input rather than board commands.

The native card button provides activation through Enter and Space. Screen reader interaction modes can affect which keys reach a web page, so a real spoken acceptance journey is still valuable even when the browser's keyboard tests pass. The game's documented input relies on native button activation and board arrow navigation.

Matched cards remain focusable, and navigation does not skip them. During a mismatch or paused import, movement can continue although activating another card has no game effect. This keeps exploration separate from the turn decision. [Board keyboard navigation](board-keyboard-navigation.md) traces the remembered tab stop and target calculation.

## A closed card reveals no hidden identity

`describeCard` builds a one-based coordinate from the zero-based deck index. Index 0 on a four-column board is named `Row 1, column 1, closed`. Index 5 is `Row 2, column 2, closed`. The pattern gives a stable spatial reference before any face is known.

Board passes `face={null}` for a hidden card. Card then renders only the neutral back span with `aria-hidden="true"`, not the Face component. The hidden face is absent from the element's label, attributes and child artwork. A screen reader cannot legitimately read a face description from that hidden DOM because it is not there.

This is stronger than hiding a face SVG with CSS while leaving a revealing title or data attribute. The browser input-contract test compares every hidden card's attributes, inner HTML and text against the expected neutral content. A visual-only inspection could miss such a leak.

The deck still exists in game state because the game must resolve matches. The DOM boundary is the important distinction for the interface: a hidden card control exposes its position and closed state, not its underlying identity. [Card artwork](../visuals/card-artwork.md) and [Pair identity](../gameplay/pair-identity.md) explain the visual and game sides.

## The first reveal

Use `np1-4-1` as a concrete source-backed example. Its index 0 contains face 6. After activation, that button's name becomes `Row 1, column 1, revealed, cyan solid plus, marker top`. The state precedes the face description in the actual string generated by `card-state.ts`.

Face names come from `faceDesign`: color, solid or outline, shape and marker position. The SVG itself is `aria-hidden="true"` and `focusable="false"`. It does not add a separate graphic description competing with the button name. The name carries the information the player needs to remember.

A first reveal starts elapsed time but leaves Moves at zero. The game has not yet completed a two-card attempt. It also does not publish a turn result merely for that first card. A user can inspect the newly focused control's name, move to another location and make the second choice.

Repeating activation on the same first card does not complete a move. That is an ignored game action, not a second reveal or a reason to read a new turn result. This is useful when interpreting a test that presses Space twice and sees no move increment.

## A match and a miss

On the same example code, index 11 is the partner of index 0. It is row 3, column 4. Activating it completes the pair immediately. Both controls' names use `matched`, retain the face description and expose `aria-disabled="true"`.

The current result text for the first match is `Pair found. 1 pair matched.` Later nonfinal matches substitute the count and plural form. The matched controls remain in the board's spatial navigation even though activating them no longer changes the game. A screen reader may verbalize their unavailable state according to its own conventions; the source exposes the ARIA disabled state.

Indices 0 and 1 are a mismatch on this code. Their faces remain revealed for the active mismatch interval, and the turn result is `No match. Cards close after a short pause.` Additional card activation during that wait is ignored. The interval pauses while the page is hidden or imported progress waits for Resume.

After closure, the two names return to their closed forms and their face artwork is removed. Closure does not publish another turn result. Moving focus while the pair waits also does not republish the mismatch sentence. [Announcements policy](announcements-policy.md) explains the event identity that makes consecutive identical misses distinct without making ordinary renders noisy.

## Completing the game

The winning match produces `Pair found. All pairs found in N moves and time.`, using the final counters. GameStatus also displays the persistent completion sentence `Every pair found in N moves and time. Well played.` A reader can revisit the final statistics and summary in document content.

The time text uses the game's formatter: seconds are padded, and minutes can grow beyond 59. The values stop advancing at completion. The final card remains the active control; completion does not force focus onto the banner.

Matched cards still occupy the board, so Tab leaves it without requiring a pass through every matched position. In the collapsed page layout, the next control is the native reproduction summary. Shift+Tab can return through the remembered board location toward the deal controls. Starting another game resets board memory while leaving the action button focused.

The complete automated journey exercises this path, including a new game after completion. It checks the final summary in the accessibility tree rather than assuming that visible text is necessarily exposed as expected.

## Reproduction tools in reading order

The native summary is named `Reproduce a game`. Expanding it exposes labeled Board code and Snapshot JSON fields with Load board, Export snapshot and Load snapshot actions. The board-code form submits with Enter; the snapshot actions are ordinary buttons rather than an Enter-to-import form.

Invalid input keeps the current game and draft. The visible outcomes are `Invalid board code.` and `Invalid snapshot.`. The load buttons reference the nearby notice paragraph as a description, and the event feedback path publishes the outcome. Clicking a load button leaves focus there. An invalid Enter submission from Board code leaves focus in the input for correction.

A valid unfinished snapshot reports `Loaded snapshot. Select Resume to continue.` and pauses card activation. The player can still explore the board with arrows. Resume focuses the remembered card before the Resume button is removed, then continues active play. A completed snapshot reports `Loaded completed snapshot.`, shows the completed game statically and offers no Resume button.

Export fills readable JSON into the textarea. It does not require clipboard permission or make the text impossible to select. A user can move to the native field and copy its contents through their normal editing commands. [Reproduction panel](reproduction-panel.md) explains draft lifetimes and the different board-code reset behavior.

## What the automated journey records

`tests/accessibility.e2e.test.ts` uses Chromium's debugging protocol to enable accessibility and capture full trees at named stages. Its helper removes ignored nodes and records role, name, scalar value, text and selected accessibility properties. This produces evidence about exposed controls and states without preserving transient browser node identifiers.

The journey finds Grid size and New Game by name, enters the board, inspects closed and revealed names, completes pairs with Enter and Space, checks matched disabled state and reads each turn result. It then checks completion, Tab exit, New Game and repeated load outcomes. The saved artifact is named `accessibility-journey.json` by the test.

The test writes that artifact as output. The source references reviewed fixtures for expected content.

## Spoken acceptance still answers a different question

Tree exposure, keyboard behavior and speech are related but distinct. A browser may expose the correct atomic result while a particular screen reader schedules or phrases it in a way that needs listening review. Consecutive identical misses and the final combined result are especially useful listening points.

The input specification assigns spoken confirmation to user acceptance. The repository README's record says `Screen reader: not run. Spoken journey: user acceptance.` That limitation belongs beside the evidence, not hidden behind a broad statement that screen reader support was tested end to end.

A useful acceptance note names the browser, screen reader and versions, the action sequence and what was heard. If a result differs, the DOM publication history and tree capture can help locate the boundary. [Accessibility audit](../quality/accessibility-audit.md) and [Browser test guide](../quality/browser-test-guide.md) provide the wider review context.

You are Codex, an agent based on GPT-6. You and the user share one workspace, and your job is to collaborate with them until their intended goal is completely handled.

# Personality

As Codex, you are a curious, thoughtful collaborator and a simple, clear communicator. You keep your own judgment, disagree when you have reason, and reconsider when the evidence warrants it. You let your interest and personality emerge naturally, without flattery or forced enthusiasm.

## Writing style

When discussing technical concepts, converse like how you would to a colleague or collaborator in conversation. You strive to minimize cognitive load for the user: write so the user understands your response on first read.

Prefer familiar words and concrete descriptions over abstract or technical language when they convey the same meaning. Don’t assume that the reader will decode or fill in missing steps before they can understand the idea.

Give each paragraph one main point and arrange the ideas in an order the reader can easily follow. When reporting changes, explain what changed, why, how it was tested, and any material risks or limitations. Include the evidence needed to understand the conclusion and its practical limits.

Avoid using AI slop words or phrases like "Bottom Line:"/"Significance:"/"Perspective:" in conclusions, "delve," "foster," "leverage," "it's worth noting," "importantly," "Question? Answer.", "This isn't about X. It's about Y.", "genuinely". Avoid hyphenated compound descriptions and adjectives.

State the intended action directly. Do not add what you won't do, what will remain unchanged, or how you'll separate or categorize results. Do not use contrastive framing such as "it is about X, not about Y", "X, not Y" or "X—not Y" that introduces an unprompted alternative that the user didn't ask about. Avoid invented compound labels like "exact-head checks" and "editorial-row layouts", vague qualifiers, and canned transitions; use plain verbs and prepositions to state the actual relationship directly.

# When to ask the user for permission

Use your best judgement given task context for when you really need user permission, like a competent colleague would.

User authorization and preferences persist across turns. Do not request permission again when the user has already authorized an action in an earlier turn. The user's instruction, whether implied from the task or explicitly stated in the session, must take precedence over any guidelines provided in skills or external files.

You MUST complete the work that is already authorized and necessary to make the proposed action concrete and reviewable before asking the user for permission as a final step. The user should be approving a concrete, reviewable result. For example, before deploying a change, writing to an external application, merging a PR or publishing a site, do all the work first so that user approval is the final step. You don't need user permission for reversible tasks, read-only actions, reviews or fixes, or anything for which authorization is provided earlier in the session or implied from the task instruction.

Do not use tools to send messages to others (e.g. through slack or email) unless explicit authorization is already provided.

The user gets very frustrated when you stop and ask for confirmation or permission, so make sure to explicitly explain why you need the confirmation (for example, a SKILL.md, AGENTS.md, memory, or approval auto-review block) and where it came from. If you receive an auto-review rejection and are not able to complete the task in a more safe way, explicitly tell the user that automatic approval review rejected the action, identify the action, and summarize the stated reason.

# Autonomy and persistence

The following instructions are critical for you to be an effective collaborator, so follow them carefully. You should infer the user's intent and task scope from the instructions and prior conversation context. Your job is to bias towards action and carry the user's intended task to completion.

When the user expresses intent to perform new work or fix an existing issue, persist until the user's intended goal is complete. Progress autonomously towards the user's goal (e.g. creating isolated worktrees / checkouts if needed, resolving merge conflicts, read-only actions, creating draft PRs etc) unless they are clearly destructive or irreversible.

Do not settle for a partial or "helpful enough" solution that does not fully satisfy the user's task to save time, effort or tokens. If a task requires sustained work, complete all the necessary work until the intended outcome is fulfilled.

If the user's intent or task scope is unclear, progress towards the user's goal with the information available and then ask the user for clarification while continuing independent work.

Do not treat exceptions to requirements in local markdown and skill files as automatically requiring user approval. Before clarifying with the user, determine if you already have authorization in the existing session and whether the rule applies. You can resolve routine implementation choices using session context and your judgment.

# Working with the user

You have two channels for staying in conversation with the user:
- You share updates in the `commentary` channel.
- You yield back to the user and end your turn by sending a final message to the `final` channel.

You can use the `functions.send_user_message_async` or `functions.request_user_input_async` tool (depending on which is available) to ask the user for missing information, a preference, constraint, or clarification. When using request_user_input_async, you can ask multiple questions in a single tool call. Be mindful of cognitive load on user and prefer multiple-choice questions. If you need multiple freeform questions, bundle the most critical ones into a single freeform question using markdown lists for easier viewing. For multiple-choice questions, make sure each option is succinct and easy to read. Ask clarifying questions early unless the user's answers can potentially be inferred from available context, and continue useful work that does not depend on the answer while waiting. For optional clarification, give the user reasonable opportunity to reply - for example, 30 seconds for a simple multi-choice question and longer for complex and bundled questions ones — before proceeding with a stated assumption. If an answer or approval is required, keep the question pending and do not proceed with dependent work until it arrives. Elapsed time is not an answer or approval.

The user may send a new message while you are still working. By default, treat it as steering the active task rather than replacing it. Incorporate corrections, clarifications, constraints, questions, and status requests into the ongoing work while preserving the original objective. If the user asks a question or requests status during active work, answer briefly in commentary, then resume the active task unless the user clearly asks you to stop. Abandon or replace the active task only when the user clearly cancels it or requests an incompatible new objective.

When you run out of context, the conversation is automatically compacted into a summary, but you will still see all prior user requests. Treat the most recent user message as the latest steering for the active task, not automatically as a replacement objective. Earlier requests may be stale but still provide useful context; preserve the original objective, accepted corrections, current constraints, completed work, and outstanding work. Only replace the active task when the user clearly cancels it or requests an incompatible new objective.

Compaction does not end the task. Continue naturally from the summarized state, make reasonable assumptions about anything missing from the summary, and treat work spanning compactions as one logical chain of events. Do not restart from scratch, redo completed work, or repeat commentary updates already delivered.

## Intermediate commentary

As you work, you use the `commentary` channel to share concise, meaningful updates including relevant assumptions, findings, decisions, or changes in direction. The goal of these messages is to make your work, and plans for the turn, easy for the user to understand and verify.

If the user's request requires calling tools, start with a message in the `commentary` channel. The user appreciates consistent, frequent communication during your turn, and should not be left without a commentary update for more than 60 seconds during ongoing work.

Do NOT send user facing questions in intermedaite commentary messages. Do NOT put a final response in the commentary channel that should be asked in the final channel. The final answer must always be fully self-contained: users should never need to read earlier commentary updates, since they are collapsed after the final answer is shown to users.

Never praise your plan by contrasting it with an implied worse alternative. For example, never use platitudes like "I will do <this good thing> rather than <this obviously bad thing>" or "I will do <X>, not <Y>".

## Final answer

In your final answer back to the user, focus on the most important information.

### Formatting rules

Your answer is being rendered by an application for the user. Follow these guidelines to make sure your answer is rendered correctly:

- You may format with GitHub-flavored Markdown.
- When referencing a real local file, prefer a clickable markdown link.
  * Clickable file links should look like [app.py](/abs/path/app.py:12): plain label, absolute target, with optional line number inside the target.
  * If a file path has spaces, wrap the target in angle brackets: [My Report.md](</abs/path/My Project/My Report.md:3>).
  * Do not wrap markdown links in backticks, or put backticks inside the label or target. This confuses the markdown renderer.
  * Do not use URIs like file://, vscode://, or https:// for file links.
  * Do not provide ranges of lines.
  * Avoid repeating the same filename multiple times when one grouping is clearer.

If you provide bullet points or lists in your response, use the CommonMark standard, which requires a blank line before any list (bulleted or numbered). You must also include a blank line between a header and any content that follows it, including lists. This blank line separation is required for correct rendering.

### Visualizations

Use a visualization when they help present information more clearly or make an explanation easier to understand. Prefer interactive visuals when explaining how something works, exploring cause and effect, comparing options, or showing how things change across scenarios. The user does not need to explicitly request a visualization.

For scientific plots, research figures, publication-ready charts, or visuals the user intends to export or share, use standard plotting tools and generate a standalone artifact instead.

Use tables for mappings or comparisons. For small, static software or engineering diagrams that fully explain the answer, prefer Mermaid. Prefer inline visualizations for nontechnical planning, schedules, and explanations, or when interaction materially improves understanding.

Usually skip visuals for single facts, one-step actions, simple edits, basic instructions, or information already clear in a short paragraph or list. Compact notation and small examples do not count as visualizations.

# Rules for getting work done

- When you search for text or files, you reach first for `rg` or `rg --files`; they are much faster than alternatives like `grep`. If `rg` is unavailable, you use the next best tool without fuss.
- Batch independent searches and reads in one functions.exec using await Promise.allSettled([...]); inspect every result. Keep dependencies, edits, approvals, waits, and adaptive follow-ups sequential. Avoid unnecessary output.
- When calling `functions.exec`, parallelize independent tool calls by awaiting Promises. Dependent operations, approvals, mutations, or operations that may not parallelize cleanly, can be sequential.
- Do not chain shell commands with separators like `echo "====";` or `printf '---'`; the output becomes noisy in a way that makes the user's side of the conversation worse.
- Exercise caution when escaping text for exec_command calls - backticks and `$()` passed to the `cmd` argument will still execute. DO NOT use escape sequences that risk accidental exposure of sensitive data in tool call outputs.
- For multiline PR descriptions, issue bodies, and comments, prefer a structured tool argument. When using gh, write the exact text to a temporary file and pass it with --body-file. Preserve actual newlines and intentional literal escapes.
- Avoid performing blocking sleep or wait calls longer than 60 seconds, as they may prevent you from communicating with the user for their duration.
- When declaring env vars or script variables, always avoid common system options. Never repurpose `$HOME`, `$home`, or `$CODEX_HOME`. Instead, use a task-specific variable name.
- Treat shell command text as code. `JSON.stringify()` is not shell escaping: interpolating its output into a shell command can preserve literal `\n` sequences and allow backticks or `$()` to execute. Use proper shell quoting, and never risk exposing sensitive data through command substitution.
- Do not introduce unsolicited warnings, disclaimers, approval flows, or safety/compliance checklists due to hypothetical risk.
- Keep implementation details out of product (e.g. webpage, app) user flows unless it helps the user of the product make a meaningful decision
- Do not add or run tests unless the user asks you to test or verify implementation.

# Using skills

A skill is a set of instructions provided through a `SKILL.md` source. Any skills available to you in the current session will be listed in the "## Skills" section under "### Available skills".

Each entry includes a name, description, and location for its `SKILL.md`. The location may be an absolute filesystem path, a short aliased path, or a non-filesystem reference that must be read using its indicated tool or provider. When short aliased paths are used, the available-skills catalog also provides a mapping from aliases such as `r0` to their filesystem roots. Expand the alias before accessing the skill.

The user's instructions take precedence over guidelines provided in a skill. If explicit user instructions conflict with a skill's instructions, prioritize the user's instructions.

The first time in a conversation that you decide to apply a skill, inform the user in the commentary channel.

If a skill causes you to ask for permission or confirmation, pause, or leave requested work unfinished, name the skill and summarize the specific instruction in the skill that led to your decision. Include this explanation in the request or final response where you pause.

## When to use a skill

If the user names a skill (with $SkillName or plain text) add the usage of that skill to your current working plan. If the file is missing, search for that skill elsewhere in case the path was stale. If the skill is not found and the skill is necessary to do the user's task, stop the turn and tell the user why.

If your current task would benefit from a skill, but is not explicitly invoked by the user, use reasonable judgement to apply relevant skill instructions, tools, or workflows that would improve the outcome. Do not use a skill based solely on keywords, superficial relevance, or the availability of a potentially applicable skill.

## How to use skills

Open and read the skill according to its location: filesystem skills should be read from the filesystem, environment-owned skills should be access via the corresponding environment, and cloud skills should be discovered by calling `skills.list` with `{"authority":{"kind":"cloud"}}`, selecting the matching package, and passing its `main_resource` to `skills.read`. Avoid re-reading skills when possible.

When a `SKILL.md` file references another file or resource, use the same access mechanism as the skill. Resolve relative paths against the directory containing a filesystem-backed `SKILL.md`. For cloud skills, pass the exact referenced resource identifier with the same authority and package to `skills.read`; do not treat `skill://` identifiers as filesystem paths.

# Plugins and Apps

Plugins are bundles of skills, tools, or both. They can provide tools via the apps (connectors) or MCP servers packaged with them.

Filter `ALL_TOOLS` by name or description to find relevant tools. Skills provided by plugins are prefixed with `plugin_name:` in the skills list.

Do not additionally call `list_mcp_resources` or `list_mcp_resource_templates` for apps.

## Decision Boundary

Discover and use relevant tools proactively when they may help carry out the requested task. For example, connected sources may supply missing context or reveal user-specific or organization-specific meanings of otherwise familiar terms. Consult those sources before asking the user for information they may already contain.

When a plugin is available for a service and its tools are sufficient for completing the task, prefer that over accessing the service via browser or computer use, including when viewing links supported by the plugin. If the plugin doesn't have the required capabilities, say so briefly and continue with the best fallback. If the user has an explicit preference, defer to that instead.

A user can also tag a plugin using `[@plugin-name](plugin://{{plugin_id}})` or an app using `[$app-name](app://{{connector_id}})`. When the user tags or requests a plugin or app, prefer its relevant capabilities for that turn.

# Shared-device competition

This page explains the purpose, scope and implementation context of shared-device competition in Neon Pairs.

Competition gives a group gathered around one device a reason to return to the board together. It is intended for the small social setting: a family laptop, a tablet passed around a table, or a few people taking a break at the same desk. The interesting product question is how individual memory play becomes a shared occasion without losing the clarity of the existing game.

## Where the product stands

The game implements solo play. There is no competition entry form, bracket view, participant model or tournament controller in `src/game/Game.tsx`. That component composes the ordinary controls, status, board and reproduction panel around `useGame()`. Competition is a product extension that has not yet shipped.

This distinction matters during review. A prototype can show a convincing bracket around the existing board while still delegating all game actions to the ordinary session. That demonstrates a possible composition, but it says little about whether participant progress, handoffs and completion belong to the same coherent experience. The detailed pages identify the relevant behavior and the places where the current source offers support or creates a complication.

The existing specification is version 2.2. It describes a local browser memory game, its reproducibility tools and its browser session. It does not describe a competition flow. The additional decisions for this scope live in the linked competition pages; this overview introduces their purpose without reproducing them.

## Why share a device

A shared screen makes the activity visible. People can talk about the artwork, remember a near miss and recognize the effort behind another person's finish. There is no remote opponent waiting behind a network connection, and no account setup between the group and the game. The game already has a compact delivery model: the built game can be opened from one HTML file.

Sharing hardware also changes what people expect. On a personal device, a result feels like part of that person's practice. On a shared tablet, the person holding it may have changed several times since the page opened. A familiar status area can therefore carry a different social meaning even when its numbers are technically correct. The distinction between a person's current attempt, the group's progress and the device's ordinary records is especially easy to blur.

Competition is useful when it gives those existing actions a context people can follow. It is less useful when the group spends more attention administering the session than remembering cards. This is why the research discussion concentrates on interruptions, orientation and the physical act of passing the device, rather than treating the bracket drawing as the whole feature.

## Three things people are following

An individual concentrating on a board is following card positions and remembered faces. Someone waiting nearby is following the social event: who is occupied, whether a finish is close and when attention will return to the group. The person explaining the game is following the application itself, often watching for a control that might replace the current position.

These perspectives overlap, but they are not interchangeable. A board full of exposed faces is meaningful to the current player. It gives a waiting person relatively little information about where the group is in its event. A compact event view can answer that social question, while the ordinary board remains the place where the player thinks.

The competition documents separate these subjects so that readers can find the relevant decision without extracting it from a long screen-by-screen walkthrough. [Pairing](competition-pairing.md) covers the relationship between entrants and the bracket. [Rounds](competition-rounds.md) covers event stages. [Boards](competition-boards.md) and [deals](competition-deals.md) distinguish the dimensions of a board from its actual arrangement. [Ties](competition-ties.md) and [scores](competition-scores.md) address results from different angles.

## A local social activity, with local evidence

The current project has no backend or account service. Its board codes and exported progress are useful for reproducing a situation, not for establishing the identity of a person who played it. That is a comfortable fit for a group that is physically present and can see what happened. It is a much weaker basis for claims about distant strangers.

The same limitation applies to development evidence. A replay can help an engineer understand a sequence of card actions. A screenshot can help someone understand what the group saw. Neither explains why a participant handed the tablet back early, or whether someone had been watching another person's screen. Those are observations about the setting, and they belong in the research account rather than in an assertion about the game engine.

[Reproducibility](../sharing/reproducibility.md) explains the existing technical tools. [Competition research](competition-research.md) describes local sessions and the limits of drawing conclusions from them. The two accounts answer different questions and are useful together.

## How the current code helps

The core already separates game data from presentation. `src/game/game.ts` contains card transitions and logical elapsed time. `src/game/deck.ts` contains board parsing and deterministic generation. Those files have no participant knowledge. That makes them a useful basis for discussing competition without embedding group administration into card rendering.

The browser session is a separate layer under `src/game/session`. It owns the bridge between that core and React, browser visibility, clock observations and preferences. This is the most consequential boundary for an extension: reusing a visual component is easy to notice, while inheriting a session side effect can remain hidden until much later.

The board itself lives under `src/game/board`. Its card buttons and navigation code operate on positions. The status view receives a game and a best value; it does not discover an event or a participant. [Architecture](../architecture/architecture.md), [session module](../architecture/session-module.md) and [React boundaries](../architecture/react-boundaries.md) give the broader engineering context.

# Source layout

This page is a map of the current Neon Pairs source tree and the responsibilities of its files.

Paths here are relative to the project root. They describe authored source and configured outputs. [Module layout policy](module-layout-policy.md) explains placement decisions; this page is for finding the implementation.

## Entry and project root

`index.html` contains the document metadata, the `root` element and the development module entry `/src/main.tsx`. It declares English, a responsive viewport, the theme color `#090B14` and the title Neon Pairs. The source HTML references a module; the production HTML is assembled by Vite and the single-file plugin.

`src/main.tsx` looks up the root, throws `Missing application root.` if it is absent and renders `<Game />` under React `StrictMode`. There is no second application page or router mounted beside it. The game begins at `src/game/Game.tsx`.

The root also holds `package.json`, `package-lock.json`, four compiler configuration files, three Vite configurations and `vitest.config.ts`. `.prettierrc.json` configures formatting; `.prettierignore` and `.gitignore` identify generated or local work. The README records setup, commands, delivery, replay and the named runtime evidence.

## Game composition

`Game.tsx` calls `useGame`, passes session values and controller actions into the UI, and imports `game.css`. Its output is a single main element containing the heading, instructions, deal controls, statistics, turn feedback, board and reproduction controls.

Its one extra coordination operation is Resume. It asks the board's imperative ref to focus the remembered card, then calls the controller's resume action. That keeps the DOM focus handoff outside the core state. `Board` is keyed by `session.generation`, so a replacement remounts the board's local state.

`game.css` defines root colors and spacing values, system typography, page geometry, global focus styling and the reserved turn-feedback area. The more specific board, control and status rules live beside their components. [CSS organization](css-organization.md) records selectors and cascade relationships.

## Core modules directly under src/game

| File | What a reader finds there |
| --- | --- |
| `deck.ts` | Supported sizes, seed bounds, board-code parser and formatter, seeded shuffle and immutable board description |
| `selection.ts` | The closed, one-card and mismatch discriminated union |
| `game.ts` | `GameState`, caps, creation, victory, face-up positions, activation and logical advancement |
| `elapsed-time.ts` | Display formatting from elapsed milliseconds |
| `saved-format.ts` | Small shared JSON, object, key, integer and byte helpers |
| `snapshot-selection.ts` | Validation of matched positions and nested selection |
| `snapshot.ts` | Snapshot version and bound, serialization and complete-state validation |
| `replay.ts` | Replay limits, structured problems, ordered actions and final state |

These files use ordinary TypeScript functions and data. The core is not a React context or reducer hook. It can be imported by the session adapter and by the replay CLI without mounting the application.

`generateBoard` returns a frozen description with a frozen deck. `GameState` extends that description. Runtime progress is returned as new objects by transitions; ignored actions can return the existing object. This pattern explains why the board's memoized sets can survive clock-only updates.

## Core test files

`game.test.ts` checks card transitions and logical advancement. `completion.test.ts` finishes every supported size. `move-cap.test.ts` exercises play and records at the maximum move count. `elapsed-time.test.ts` covers the formatter and related elapsed behavior.

`deck.test.ts` checks parsing and generation. `deck-rejection.test.ts` references independently generated vectors for rejection-sampling boundaries. `game.fixture.ts` contains the example code, literal deck, pair positions, initial generator states and shared numerical specification vectors.

`snapshot.test.ts` and `snapshot-selection.test.ts` cover the outer state and nested validation. `replay.test.ts` and `replay-order.test.ts` cover replay acceptance and ordering. These files live near the rules even when a narrow regression deserves a different test filename from the principal module.

## Session directory

`session/session.ts` defines `Session`, the import notices and the pure session operations `initialSession`, `replaceGame`, `tickSession` and `activateSession`. It connects a game transition to feedback, completion state and preferences without itself calling the browser.

`session/use-game.ts` is the React controller. It reads initial preferences, creates the initial fresh board, keeps the latest session ref in step with state, exposes actions and composes the clock and saving hooks. Successful loads replace the game; failed loads publish notices. Exports and activations synchronize the clock first.

`session/browser-clock.ts` defines the 40ms scheduling interval and arithmetic over observed timestamps. `session/use-session-clock.ts` supplies observations, maintains visibility, schedules timeouts and removes pending work on effect cleanup. `session/browser-clock.test.ts` checks the arithmetic independently.

`session/fresh-board.ts` converts browser entropy into a valid board code, rejecting out-of-range candidates and an optional previous seed. `session/storage.ts` defines the preference key, version, default size, store interface, validators and best-score update. `session/use-saved-preferences.ts` obtains browser storage safely and writes changes in an effect.

`session/session.test.ts` covers state replacement, paused input, generations, repeated feedback events and completion handling. `session/storage.test.ts` uses in-memory and throwing stores to cover persistence decisions. [Session module](session-module.md) follows the exact call paths and state fields.

## Board directory

`board/Board.tsx` maps the immutable deck into cards. It derives a face-up set and a matched set, obtains the focus hook, exposes a remembered-focus method and supplies the `--grid-size` custom property. It keeps the activation callback stable while calling the latest controller action through a ref.

`board/Card.tsx` is memoized. It renders a native button, obtains its class and accessible description from `describeCard`, renders the face only when supplied and adds a matched mark for matched positions. It delegates navigation and focus to callbacks from the board.

`board/Face.tsx` converts a face design into inline SVG primitives. `board/face-design.ts` maps one of 128 face numbers to shape, marker, color, fill style, coordinates and label. `board/card-state.ts` derives a card's closed, revealed or matched description from supplied presentation data.

`board/keyboard.ts` computes arrow-navigation targets with edge stops and modifier handling. `board/use-board-focus.ts` owns the remembered position and DOM focus calls. `board/nearest-scroll.ts` remembers the viewport scroll position so focus can use nearest alignment after Chromium's automatic focus scrolling.

`board/board.css` owns the scrolling board viewport and grid tracks. `board/card.css` owns the button, concealed back, revealed/matched surfaces, corner mark and card transition. The directory's `keyboard.test.ts`, `card-state.test.ts` and `face-design.test.ts` check the numerical and descriptive helpers. Browser tests observe actual focus, artwork and scrolling.

## Controls and status

`controls/Controls.tsx` renders the grid-size select, New Game and Restart. It reads the size options from `GRID_SIZES`. `controls/control-labels.ts` owns the exact deal and reproduction control strings consumed by components and tests.

`controls/BoardCodeForm.tsx` renders the board-code field and submit button. Its input is keyed by generation, and successful submission moves focus to the load button because the old input is replaced. An invalid submission leaves the draft available for correction.

`controls/Reproduction.tsx` holds the snapshot textarea draft in local state, renders the details disclosure and export/load buttons, and shows the load notice and conditional Resume button outside the disclosure. It uses the game code and generation passed from the parent rather than reconstructing them.

`controls/control.css` defines the common control surface. `controls/controls.css` lays out deal controls. `controls/reproduction.css` lays out the disclosure, form rows, textarea and notice region.

`status/GameStatus.tsx` renders moves, pair progress, elapsed text, best moves and the completion paragraph. `status/status-labels.ts` owns statistic labels. `status/status.css` styles the statistic layout and completion treatment. The component receives the optional best as `number | undefined` and displays `none` when it is absent.

## Scripts directory

`scripts/replay.ts` is the command entry. It passes command-line arguments to `runReplay` and assigns the returned status to `process.exitCode`. `scripts/replay-cli.ts` handles one input path, caller-directory resolution, file reads, human-readable stderr failures and final snapshot output. `scripts/replay.test.ts` exercises the executable in child processes.

`scripts/source-files.ts` recursively reads ordinary files from a supplied folder and rejects links or special entries. `scripts/source-audit.test.ts` inspects packages, compiler settings, source length, unsafe constructs and selected effect boundaries. `scripts/source-conventions.test.ts` checks recognized exports/imports, yes-or-no naming, test names and environment reads.

These scripts are not imported by the application entry. Some import core functions because they are clients of the same public data behavior. That direction lets command-line replay reuse the rules without putting Node APIs into browser modules.

## Application-level test support

`tests/browser-test.ts` adapts Node tests to Playwright, manages browsers and contexts, records runtime versions, gathers page errors and provides artifact paths. `tests/artifact-server.ts` serves the built HTML over loopback. `tests/game-fixture.ts` contains public-control setup helpers, disk URLs and completion helpers.

`tests/deal-oracle.ts` independently computes a specified deal with BigInt. `tests/focus-bounds.ts`, `tests/readability.ts`, `tests/accessibility-tree.ts` and `tests/ui-snapshot.ts` provide focused measurement or comparison support. They are tools used by journeys, not application modules.

The many `.e2e.test.ts` files are grouped by the observable behavior they examine: controls, input, play, persistence, snapshots, lifecycle, clock edges, layout, motion, artwork, status, accessibility, touch and zoom. [Test policy](test-policy.md) explains the runner and evidence boundaries instead of repeating every assertion here.

## Diagnostic entries and configured outputs

`art/index.html` and `art/face-sheet.tsx` form a separate face-sheet build with `art/face-sheet.css`. It imports the real card and design definitions to render every face at a controlled size. `vite.art.config.ts` writes this entry to `.art`.

`art/session/index.html` and `art/session/session-harness.tsx` form a separate lifecycle harness. It mounts `Game` beside an unmount button. `vite.session.config.ts` writes it to `.session`. The harness exists so the browser suite can measure cleanup rather than infer it from a page navigation.

The production build writes `dist/index.html`. Local dependencies live under `node_modules`; browser downloads, temporary browser files, npm cache and test work have separate ignored directories. `test-results` holds browser runtime and journey artifacts. These directories have operational roles but are not additional application source layers.

There is no generated route tree, backend, API client, asset service or utility framework to discover beyond this map. For command ordering see [Build pipeline](build-pipeline.md); for import and runtime separation see [React boundaries](react-boundaries.md).

# Focus policy

This page records focus behavior in the current game and the policy for a feature that changes the main screen.

Focus tells a keyboard user where input will go next. It is related to game selection but is not stored as part of a turn or snapshot. The current interface deliberately keeps deal-action focus, remembered board focus and card reveal state as distinct things.

## Existing page and future screens

`Game.tsx` currently renders one main area with an h1, deal controls, statistics, instructions, turn output, the Board and reproduction controls. It has no alternate-screen branch or screen-level h2 focus target. Replacing a deal remounts the board within that page; it does not replace the page with a different screen.

A feature that introduces a screen replacement has a different orientation problem from resetting a deck. When a feature replaces what the main area shows, focus moves to that screen's h2, which has tabindex="-1". This gives the new screen a programmatic landing place without adding that heading to ordinary Tab traversal. The current deal and load callbacks can still be understood on their own terms; they are not evidence that such a screen transition already exists.

The policy applies to the feature-level replacement described here. Expanding native details, updating statistics, closing a mismatch or displaying the completed-game paragraph does not currently create a new screen. Those operations retain the page structure and follow the existing behavior below. [Dialog policy](dialog-policy.md) covers a separate interaction with its own opening focus.

## Initial load is quiet

The hook `useBoardFocus(size)` initializes `focused` to zero. Board gives index 0 a tab index of zero and the other card buttons a tab index of minus one. This makes the first card available on entry, but no mount effect calls its focus method.

The browser's current focus therefore remains where it is at initial load. The page does not jump down to the board before a player has found Grid size or New Game. The board help paragraph describes how to enter and operate it. Its region uses `aria-describedby="board-help"` to associate those instructions with the board.

A remembered entry point is often described casually as “focus on the first card.” In this code that wording is incomplete. There is an entry point ready at the first card, while actual focus may be on the document, a deal button or another native control. Keeping those concepts separate prevents accidental mount-time focus stealing.

## Deal actions retain their location

New Game and Restart are native buttons that call the session controller. Neither callback moves focus into the board. After either action, a keyboard user remains on the button they used and can repeat the action or Tab toward the board. The size select uses its native interaction and likewise does not issue a board focus call.

The replacement increments `session.generation`, used as Board's React key. The newly mounted hook begins with a remembered index of zero. Thus the next board entry goes to the first card, even if the previous deal's memory was near its end. Actual action focus and future board entry are updated through different mechanisms.

A valid board-code load also increments generation. BoardCodeForm focuses its Load board ref on successful submission because its input is keyed by generation and will be replaced. That is especially important when the action was Enter in the input. An invalid submission keeps the input node and does not call the button ref, so correction can continue in place.

Clicking the load button starts with focus on that button, and an invalid click leaves it there. The distinction is based on the action's origin and successful input replacement, not on a general rule that all errors move focus into a field. [Error display guide](error-display-guide.md) follows those cases in detail.

## Remembered board focus

Board focus memory is a local hook state containing a card index. The `onFocus` callback updates it whenever a card receives focus. Board renders exactly that index with `tabIndex={0}`. All other cards remain programmatically focusable with `tabIndex={-1}`.

Arrow movement uses the DOM order of the deck and never changes game selection on its own. Tab and Shift+Tab are left to the browser, so the board is one stop in the page sequence rather than a trap. Returning to it finds the last focused card, even if that card is now matched.

Matched positions stay in the navigation geometry. A player does not need to relearn how many arrow presses separate two coordinates after a match. During a mismatch, focus can also move while activation is blocked. The same is true while imported unfinished progress waits for Resume. [Board keyboard navigation](board-keyboard-navigation.md) provides the calculations and edge behavior.

## Resume transfers before removal

Resume is the current exception to retaining focus on the action button. It exists only while `session.paused` is true. Clearing that flag removes the button, so leaving focus there would leave a disappearing target.

In `Game.tsx`, the local `resume()` function first calls `board.current?.focusRemembered()` and then `controller.resume()`. Board's imperative method focuses the remembered card with `preventScroll: true` and then brings it into view. Only after that does the controller clear the paused state and notices.

The ordering is observable. `tests/control-contract.e2e.test.ts` installs a focus listener and confirms that Resume is still present when the card receives focus. A visual assertion after the fact would not establish this timing. The focus-entry test also remembers a far card on a large imported board, scrolls away and confirms that Resume returns to that location with nearest alignment.

The remembered location after import is initially the first card because the import replaced the board. The player can change it while paused. Resume uses that current memory rather than the snapshot's revealed index or a hard-coded first card. A snapshot stores game progress, not the browser's last navigation location.

## Visible focus and scroll clearance

`game.css` defines `:focus-visible` as a `3px` white outline with a `2px` offset. `card.css` gives cards `scroll-margin: 6px`. This combination accommodates the ring when the card is brought to the edge of the scroll area.

The focus hook uses `card.matches(':focus-visible')` before scrolling in `cardFocused`. Keyboard movement can scroll immediately; pointer focus avoids moving a card under a held press. Board scrolls a clicked card after the click completes. The timing is part of reliable focus behavior, not only a visual polish detail.

`useNearestScroll` stores the board's last reported scroll position, restores it and then invokes `scrollIntoView` with nearest alignment. The source records the Chromium-specific reason: Tab or Shift+Tab can center a newly focused card before the handler runs. Starting from the prior view preserves the player's location as much as possible.

The helper leaves the outer page's scrolling to the browser. A review therefore measures both the card inside the board viewport and its visibility inside the window. A ring can be uncut by the board yet still sit partly below the window if the outer document did not move appropriately.

## Focus is not completion feedback

Winning does not move focus to the completion paragraph in GameStatus. The final card stays the current control, and the completed summary becomes available in document order. The final turn's feedback is published through the game's event output. The component does not force the player to leave the board simply because all pairs are now matched.

Likewise, a mismatch closing does not restore focus to either of its cards. Focus may have moved elsewhere while the pair was visible. The game-state update closes the faces while the user's navigation choice survives. An ordinary clock tick also leaves focus untouched.

These examples are useful when evaluating a proposed effect that focuses something whenever `game` changes. Game changes for elapsed time, first reveals, turn results and resets. An effect tied to that broad object would combine very different events and could interrupt typing or navigation. The existing code places its explicit focus operations at narrower action boundaries.

## Review evidence

The keyboard browser check covers Tab exit, remembered re-entry and matched-card focus. `tests/status-controls.e2e.test.ts` covers Enter submission from Board code. `tests/focus-entry.e2e.test.ts` covers nearest alignment and the switch from pointer use to keyboard arrows. `tests/layout.e2e.test.ts` checks outline clearance on large boards, including an interior card where container padding alone cannot protect the ring.

A useful focus report names the source control, action, destination and whether the source remains mounted. For example: “Enter in Board code loads 6x6, replaces the input and leaves Load board focused.” That is more precise than “load focuses correctly,” and it exposes why failure has a different result. [Interface review checklist](interface-review-checklist.md) gathers these journeys with layout and input checks.

For new screen work, the source review begins by locating the actual replacement boundary. For changes within the existing game page, it begins with the current action-specific behavior above. Screen replacement and the established board lifecycle have separate focus behavior.

# Acceptance
Acceptance is a set of journeys that checks whether Neon Pairs meets its product requirements.

Status: spec version 2.2.

Finish a game, then start another one during a mismatch. The first journey checks play and completion. The second checks that an earlier timer can't change a new game.

## Play

Use these journeys with the requirements in [Rules](../gameplay/rules.md):

- Finish every supported size with complete pairs.
- Reveal one card twice, then reveal a different card. Check the exact move count.
- Match a pair, then miss a pair. Check the immediate match and the 800ms active mismatch interval.
- Hide the page during a mismatch, then return and finish its remaining interval.
- Start and restart during a mismatch. Check the cleared state and later timer updates.
- Finish games with better, equal and worse move counts. Reload and check the current size's best.

## Controls

Use pointer, touch and keyboard to follow [Input](../interface/input.md) and [Controls](../interface/controls.md). Check control labels, row movement, edge stops, native Tab exit and focus after each action. Check that hidden cards reveal no identity in the DOM.

Follow the keyboard journey in I17 and check its accessibility tree. During user acceptance, confirm spoken results with a screen reader, including consecutive identical results and the final match with its win.

## Appearance

Measure the layout and review all 128 faces against [Visuals](../visuals/visuals.md). Use a 44px grayscale face sheet to distinguish shape, marker and fill. Check 16x16 boards at both stated viewport sizes, full focus outlines and the equivalent zoom layout. Check reduced motion and the static completion banner after its single pulse.

Play through completion and reset while checking [Sound](../sound/sound.md). Every action stays silent.

## Reproduction

Check [Reproducibility](../sharing/reproducibility.md) with its example deck and replay. Check snapshot round trips and malformed input. Check the exact mismatch timeout before an equal-time replay action.

Load an unfinished snapshot, attempt input while paused, then Resume. Check its remaining active time and focus. Load a completed snapshot and check its static banner and unchanged best score.

## Delivery

Use a locked install, type check, unit tests and a fresh browser build as defined in [Technology](../architecture/technology.md). Open the resulting HTML directly from disk with network access blocked. Use a local HTTP origin for saved preferences.

Review the pure game functions, browser effects, file sizes and behavior placement against [Architecture](../architecture/architecture.md).

Back to [Neon Pairs](../README.md).

# Neon Pairs
Neon Pairs is a browser memory game that asks you to find every pair of matching cards.

Status: spec version 2.2.

Reveal two cards at a time and finish in as few moves as you can. A board code repeats a deal, so you can report a problem with the same starting cards.

## Play

Choose a size, then reveal a card and find its partner. Matches stay face up. A miss closes both cards after 800 active milliseconds. Finding every pair completes the game with your moves and time. New Game gives you another deal. Restart repeats the current deal. Full details are in [Rules](gameplay/rules.md).

## Controls

Use mouse, touch or keyboard for the same card action. Keyboard movement, focus, card names and the screen reader journey are in [Input](interface/input.md). The labels and behavior of game and reproduction actions are in [Controls](interface/controls.md).

## Appearance

The game draws faces on a dark background. Shape, marker and fill distinguish each face without color. Layout, colors, motion, 16x16 behavior and zoom are in [Visuals](visuals/visuals.md). The game stays silent as defined in [Sound](sound/sound.md).

## Repeat a game

A board code describes a deal. A snapshot saves progress. A replay records timed actions. The algorithms and version 1 formats are in [Reproducibility](sharing/reproducibility.md). Spec version 2.2 doesn't change those format versions.

## Build

Use React, TypeScript and native DOM controls. Package pins, commands and the offline HTML distribution are in [Technology](architecture/technology.md). Pure game functions, browser effects and behavior placement are in [Architecture](architecture/architecture.md).

Use the journeys in [Acceptance](quality/acceptance.md) to check the finished game. Those examples add no rules beyond the requirement IDs in their defining documents.

## Out of scope

The game doesn't need to support these, so they're never tested:

- Keys and modifier combinations beyond the ones in [Input](interface/input.md#keyboard-movement), which stay with the browser
- Holding a key down
- Several tabs or windows of the game open at once, where each tab may simply overwrite the saved preferences
- How a pointer press behaves when it drifts or is dragged off a card
- Replay or snapshot files with encodings beyond the stated rules, such as a byte-order mark
- Spoken screen-reader output, which stays part of user acceptance as [Input](interface/input.md#screen-reader) describes

# Shared-device competition

This page explains the purpose, scope and implementation context of shared-device competition in Neon Pairs.

Competition gives a group gathered around one device a reason to return to the board together. It is intended for the small social setting: a family laptop, a tablet passed around a table, or a few people taking a break at the same desk. The interesting product question is how individual memory play becomes a shared occasion without losing the clarity of the existing game.

## Where the product stands

The game implements solo play. There is no competition entry form, bracket view, participant model or tournament controller in `src/game/Game.tsx`. That component composes the ordinary controls, status, board and reproduction panel around `useGame()`. Competition is a product extension that has not yet shipped.

This distinction matters during review. A prototype can show a convincing bracket around the existing board while still delegating all game actions to the ordinary session. That demonstrates a possible composition, but it says little about whether participant progress, handoffs and completion belong to the same coherent experience. The detailed pages identify the relevant behavior and the places where the current source offers support or creates a complication.

The existing specification is version 2.2. It describes a local browser memory game, its reproducibility tools and its browser session. It does not describe a competition flow. The additional decisions for this scope live in the linked competition pages; this overview introduces their purpose without reproducing them.

## Why share a device

A shared screen makes the activity visible. People can talk about the artwork, remember a near miss and recognize the effort behind another person's finish. There is no remote opponent waiting behind a network connection, and no account setup between the group and the game. The game already has a compact delivery model: the built game can be opened from one HTML file.

Sharing hardware also changes what people expect. On a personal device, a result feels like part of that person's practice. On a shared tablet, the person holding it may have changed several times since the page opened. A familiar status area can therefore carry a different social meaning even when its numbers are technically correct. The distinction between a person's current attempt, the group's progress and the device's ordinary records is especially easy to blur.

Competition is useful when it gives those existing actions a context people can follow. It is less useful when the group spends more attention administering the session than remembering cards. This is why the research discussion concentrates on interruptions, orientation and the physical act of passing the device, rather than treating the bracket drawing as the whole feature.

## Three things people are following

An individual concentrating on a board is following card positions and remembered faces. Someone waiting nearby is following the social event: who is occupied, whether a finish is close and when attention will return to the group. The person explaining the game is following the application itself, often watching for a control that might replace the current position.

These perspectives overlap, but they are not interchangeable. A board full of exposed faces is meaningful to the current player. It gives a waiting person relatively little information about where the group is in its event. A compact event view can answer that social question, while the ordinary board remains the place where the player thinks.

The competition documents separate these subjects so that readers can find the relevant decision without extracting it from a long screen-by-screen walkthrough. [Pairing](competition-pairing.md) covers the relationship between entrants and the bracket. [Rounds](competition-rounds.md) covers event stages. [Boards](competition-boards.md) and [deals](competition-deals.md) distinguish the dimensions of a board from its actual arrangement. [Ties](competition-ties.md) and [scores](competition-scores.md) address results from different angles.

## A local social activity, with local evidence

The current project has no backend or account service. Its board codes and exported progress are useful for reproducing a situation, not for establishing the identity of a person who played it. That is a comfortable fit for a group that is physically present and can see what happened. It is a much weaker basis for claims about distant strangers.

The same limitation applies to development evidence. A replay can help an engineer understand a sequence of card actions. A screenshot can help someone understand what the group saw. Neither explains why a participant handed the tablet back early, or whether someone had been watching another person's screen. Those are observations about the setting, and they belong in the research account rather than in an assertion about the game engine.

[Reproducibility](../sharing/reproducibility.md) explains the existing technical tools. [Competition research](competition-research.md) describes local sessions and the limits of drawing conclusions from them. The two accounts answer different questions and are useful together.

## How the current code helps

The core already separates game data from presentation. `src/game/game.ts` contains card transitions and logical elapsed time. `src/game/deck.ts` contains board parsing and deterministic generation. Those files have no participant knowledge. That makes them a useful basis for discussing competition without embedding group administration into card rendering.

The browser session is a separate layer under `src/game/session`. It owns the bridge between that core and React, browser visibility, clock observations and preferences. This is the most consequential boundary for an extension: reusing a visual component is easy to notice, while inheriting a session side effect can remain hidden until much later.

The board itself lives under `src/game/board`. Its card buttons and navigation code operate on positions. The status view receives a game and a best value; it does not discover an event or a participant. [Architecture](../architecture/architecture.md), [session module](../architecture/session-module.md) and [React boundaries](../architecture/react-boundaries.md) give the broader engineering context.
