# Dialog policy

This page records the confirmation policy for leaving unfinished work and its relationship to the game's existing actions.

The current source contains no dialog component, native dialog element or leave-work handler. New Game, Restart, board-code loading and snapshot loading call the controller directly.

## The confirmation boundary

A confirmation is useful only when it corresponds to a real decision about abandoning work. Its content and focus need to make the conservative path understandable before the player commits to leaving. Leaving unfinished work asks first in a native dialog element with two buttons, Keep playing and Leave. Keep playing takes focus when it opens, and Escape keeps playing. The decision is about the unfinished work being left; opening a disclosure to inspect a code is not itself that decision.

There is no third action specified by this policy. In particular, the existing snapshot exporter does not turn this confirmation into an automatic save workflow. Export is a separate user action with a text result. A feature that uses the confirmation can draw on that distinction without presenting an unsaved draft as if it had already been preserved.

The policy does not define which future feature owns a leave route or a new navigation screen. Those boundaries have to be visible in the feature's actual code. The current page has no router and no alternate play screen. [Focus policy](focus-policy.md) covers orientation when a feature introduces a main-area replacement.

## What the present controls actually do

`Controls.tsx` renders New Game and Restart as native buttons. Their callbacks in `use-game.ts` reset the clock adapter and commit a replacement game. They do not consult `started`, Moves, Pairs or a dialog result before doing so. The existing game replaces immediately when those buttons are used.

BoardCodeForm validates before replacing. Its `loadBoard` callback returns false for invalid input and true after successful replacement. Snapshot loading decodes the whole draft before replacing as well. These paths protect against invalid external data; they are not implementations of a leave confirmation.

The native `details` panel is also not a modal. It expands in document flow and leaves the rest of the page operable. Calling its summary a dialog trigger would misdescribe both the DOM and its focus behavior. [Reproduction panel](reproduction-panel.md) documents the actual disclosure.

This distinction matters during incremental work. A new dialog in one feature does not silently change the semantics of every old control. When reading a change, follow the event handler to see whether it reaches a confirmation boundary, a parser, or the replacement directly. Similar visual labels do not establish the same lifecycle.

## Native behavior and application decisions

The policy names a native element because the interface already relies on browser semantics for buttons, forms, selects and details. A dialog has a different interaction boundary from an ordinary panel. Its opening, cancellation and closing need to be considered as a coherent interaction rather than a div painted over the board.

Using the element alone does not decide what leaving means for a game. The application still owns the transition that discards or replaces state. In the current implementation, that transition is represented by controller operations and `replaceGame`. Visual disappearance of an overlay is not evidence that a session was replaced, just as visual appearance is not evidence that play was paused.

The distinction between cancellation and commitment is observable in game state. Continuing leaves the same deal, revealed selection and counters available. A committed departure may dispose of or replace the session, depending on the feature. The current game has no dialog-specific storage write or serialized marker.

No dialog state exists in `Session`. Its fields are `game`, `paused`, `generation`, `feedback`, `loadNotice`, `announcement`, `celebration` and `preferences`. The existing `paused` flag specifically represents unfinished snapshot import. Reusing that flag for a new overlay without considering its other consumers would also affect Resume and load notices.

## Timing questions exposed by an overlay

# React boundaries

This page explains where React participates in Neon Pairs and where ordinary data functions remain independent of rendering.

React mounts the application, holds the session for presentation, owns local UI state and manages browser-effect lifetimes. The game rules are callable outside React. That separation lets the browser UI and replay CLI share behavior without teaching the core about components, effects or DOM events.

## The mounted tree

`src/main.tsx` calls `createRoot` after checking the `root` element and renders `Game` inside `StrictMode`. `Game.tsx` composes deal controls, status, feedback, board and reproduction controls. It calls `useGame` once to obtain the current session and actions.

The component tree is intentionally direct. There is no React context carrying a global game store and no router coordinating separate screens. `Controls` receives size and two actions. `GameStatus` receives a game, an optional best and a celebration flag. `Board` receives the game and activation action. `Reproduction` receives current code context, exchange actions and pause-related presentation.

These props describe the existing contracts. A component can render data it does not own without gaining responsibility for deciding a turn. The core still computes matches, move counts, elapsed advancement and victory.

## The data-only side

`deck.ts`, `game.ts`, `selection.ts`, `elapsed-time.ts`, `saved-format.ts`, `snapshot.ts`, `snapshot-selection.ts` and `replay.ts` do not import React. They accept values and return values. `session/session.ts` is also a data transformation module, although it lives beside hooks that import React.

The board has data-only helpers too. `keyboard.ts` computes a target from keys and coordinates. `card-state.ts` computes a state description. `face-design.ts` maps an integer identity to design values. These helpers can be tested without rendering `Board` or building a synthetic browser tree.

This is the meaningful interpretation of the React boundary: importing a rule in a CLI does not start an effect or require a mounted component. It is not a claim that every file ending in `.ts` is independent of React. `use-board-focus.ts`, `nearest-scroll.ts` and the session hooks are TypeScript modules with hooks and browser behavior.

## React imports in application code

| Module | React mechanisms used |
| --- | --- |
| `main.tsx` | `StrictMode`; root rendering through React DOM |
| `Game.tsx` | Ref for the board's focus interface |
| `Board.tsx` | Memoized derivations, refs, stable callback, layout effect and imperative handle |
| `Card.tsx` | `memo` and a keyboard event type |
| `use-board-focus.ts` | Local state, refs and callbacks |
| `nearest-scroll.ts` | Ref, effect and callback |
| `BoardCodeForm.tsx` | Ref for the successful-load focus target |
| `Reproduction.tsx` | Local snapshot draft state |
| `use-game.ts` | Session state and current-value ref |
| `use-session-clock.ts` | Clock/visibility refs and timer effect |
| `use-saved-preferences.ts` | Persistence effect |

`Controls`, `GameStatus` and `Face` contain JSX without importing a React runtime object. The compiler uses `jsx: react-jsx`, so those files do not need the older `import React` pattern. JSX participation and explicit hook imports are related but different observations.

The diagnostic entries also use React DOM. The face sheet renders real cards, while the session harness mounts and unmounts the real game. Their entrypoints are outside `src` and built separately, so they do not become extra runtime controls in the distributed game.

## One action path for activation

`Card` renders a native button and invokes its supplied activation callback from `onClick`. Native keyboard activation and ordinary pointer activation therefore reach the same controller action. The keydown handler delegates navigation; it does not implement another matching algorithm.

The controller synchronizes active time and calls `activateSession`, which calls `activateCard`. Components receive the resulting state and render it. A class such as `matched` is an outcome of the data, not the authoritative record of a matched pair. Reading CSS classes back into the core would reverse that relationship.

Matched buttons use `aria-disabled`, keeping them in the board's focus model. The rule function still rejects activating matched positions. During a mismatch, the session does not mark every other button disabled; the core rejects new activations while that selection is pending. Semantic presentation and transition legality are both visible, with legality centralized in the rules.

## Latest values without another store

`useGame` keeps React state for rendering and a ref for immediate event-time access. `commit` updates the ref before setting React state. A clock synchronization can therefore commit a new game, and the immediately following activation can consume that new game in the same task.

The board has a similar but narrower pattern for callback identity. `Game` supplies a new activation function as it renders. `Board` stores that function in `latestActivate`, updates the ref in a layout effect and passes a stable `useCallback` wrapper to cards. Memoized cards see a stable function prop while it calls the latest controller closure.

These refs do not bypass the rules. They keep the correct data/action visible across render scheduling. The data transition still returns a new immutable description, and React still receives the committed session. [Session module](session-module.md) explains why the current ref matters for export and activation boundaries.

## Render cost on a large board

A 16 by 16 board has 256 cards. Active time can update on the 40ms observation cadence, but most ticks do not change any card's appearance. `advanceGame` retains the deck and matched array and, outside a mismatch change, retains the selection object. `Board` memoizes face-up and matched sets from those references.

`Card` is wrapped in `memo`. Its props are primitive presentation values and stable callbacks. On an elapsed-only update, face, matched, tabIndex, size and handlers stay equal, so the cards do not all need to rerender. The parent can still update the statistic.

A pending mismatch changes selection as its remainder decreases, so the face-up set can be recomputed. The resulting card props can nevertheless remain equal until the selection actually closes. This distinction explains why immutable reference stability is useful even though the board's parent renders more often than its cards.

Memoization is not a substitute for correct state ownership. Mutating the matched array in place could keep its reference stable while changing its meaning, causing derived sets to miss an update. The transition code returns a new matched array when a pair is found, matching the assumptions of the board's memoization.

## Concealed identity is a prop boundary

`Board` knows the immutable deck, but it passes `face={null}` for every position outside the derived face-up set. `Card` then renders only a decorative back. It does not mount `Face` and hide it with CSS. Its accessible description omits face design when the supplied face is null.

When revealed or matched, a card gets the face number and renders inline SVG. `Face` marks the SVG as decorative, while the button's label describes the visible design. The board can therefore hold authoritative identity without exposing concealed identity through every child element.

This behavior is also why tests use documented board codes rather than a diagnostic global. A test can reconstruct a deal independently and activate matching positions through the public interface. There is no application solver endpoint that a production user or test needs to query.

## Local focus and DOM work

`useBoardFocus` holds a focused index initialized to zero and refs to the viewport and grid. Arrow handling calls `navigationTarget`; a non-null result prevents the browser default and focuses the target button with `preventScroll: true`. Focus events update the remembered index.

`useNearestScroll` listens to the board viewport's scroll events and remembers the reported position. For keyboard focus it restores that position before calling `scrollIntoView` with nearest alignment. This accounts for Chromium's automatic centering on focus. A click scrolls after activation so the pressed card is not moved under a held pointer before release.

These browser operations belong with the board presentation, not `GameState`. A replay contains positions and logical times, not a scroll offset. A snapshot can load into a differently sized viewport. Keeping focus and scrolling local preserves that independence.

## Replacement and imperative focus

`Game` gives `Board` a ref typed as `BoardFocus`. The board exposes only `focusRemembered()` through `useImperativeHandle`. The parent does not receive the whole grid DOM or a collection of card nodes.

Resume uses that limited operation, then calls the controller's resume action. A replacement instead increments generation and changes the board key, remounting its local focus state. `BoardCodeForm` keys its uncontrolled input by that same generation, so successful loading replaces the old draft with the current code.

A generation is consequently a lifecycle boundary shared by adapters and components. It is not a reason to put DOM state in the session core. The rule functions remain unaware of keyed mounts, refs or focus methods.

## Effects and cleanup

Browser effects pair setup with cleanup: the clock removes its listener and timeout, and nearest scrolling removes its viewport listener. The separate session harness lets tests unmount the real game and measure that cleanup. [Clock design](clock-design.md) details the active flag, generation checks and scheduling lifetime.

## Keeping a change on the right side

An incorrect pair count starts in the game state and derivation, not in JSX text. An incorrect load-pause state starts in session replacement, not a disabled style. An incorrect arrow stop starts in the numerical navigation helper, while an incorrect scroll alignment starts in the DOM hook. The boundary narrows where an explanation should begin.

The architecture specification permits shared support when two actual behaviors need the same meaning. It does not introduce a generic hooks or utilities layer merely because several files use React. Current direct imports keep ownership legible, and the module policy describes feature placement. Together they make small components useful without making rendering the owner of the game rules.

# Dialog policy

This page records the confirmation policy for leaving unfinished work and its relationship to the game's existing actions.

The current source contains no dialog component, native dialog element or leave-work handler. New Game, Restart, board-code loading and snapshot loading call the controller directly.

## The confirmation boundary

A confirmation is useful only when it corresponds to a real decision about abandoning work. Its content and focus need to make the conservative path understandable before the player commits to leaving. Leaving unfinished work asks first in a native dialog element with two buttons, Keep playing and Leave. Keep playing takes focus when it opens, and Escape keeps playing. The decision is about the unfinished work being left; opening a disclosure to inspect a code is not itself that decision.

There is no third action specified by this policy. In particular, the existing snapshot exporter does not turn this confirmation into an automatic save workflow. Export is a separate user action with a text result. A feature that uses the confirmation can draw on that distinction without presenting an unsaved draft as if it had already been preserved.

The policy does not define which future feature owns a leave route or a new navigation screen. Those boundaries have to be visible in the feature's actual code. The current page has no router and no alternate play screen. [Focus policy](focus-policy.md) covers orientation when a feature introduces a main-area replacement.

`Controls.tsx` renders New Game and Restart as native buttons. Their callbacks in `use-game.ts` reset the clock adapter and commit a replacement game. They do not consult `started`, Moves, Pairs or a dialog result before doing so. The existing game replaces immediately when those buttons are used.

BoardCodeForm validates before replacing. Its `loadBoard` callback returns false for invalid input and true after successful replacement. Snapshot loading decodes the whole draft before replacing as well. These paths protect against invalid external data; they are not implementations of a leave confirmation.

The native `details` panel is also not a modal. It expands in document flow and leaves the rest of the page operable. Calling its summary a dialog trigger would misdescribe both the DOM and its focus behavior. [Reproduction panel](reproduction-panel.md) documents the actual disclosure.

# React boundaries

This page explains where React participates in Neon Pairs and where ordinary data functions remain independent of rendering.

React mounts the application, holds the session for presentation, owns local UI state and manages browser-effect lifetimes. The game rules are callable outside React. That separation lets the browser UI and replay CLI share behavior without teaching the core about components, effects or DOM events.

## The mounted tree

`src/main.tsx` calls `createRoot` after checking the `root` element and renders `Game` inside `StrictMode`. `Game.tsx` owns the solo or Tournament screen choice. Its solo branch uses `useGame`; its Tournament branch uses the separate tournament controller.

The component tree is intentionally direct. There is no React context carrying a global game store and no router coordinating the two screens. `Controls` receives size and actions. `GameStatus` receives a solo game, an optional best and a celebration flag. `Board` receives the current screen's game and activation action. `Reproduction` receives solo code context, exchange actions and pause-related presentation.

These props describe the existing contracts. A component can render data it does not own without gaining responsibility for deciding a turn. The core still computes matches, move counts, elapsed advancement and victory.

## The data-only side

`deck.ts`, `game.ts`, `selection.ts`, `elapsed-time.ts`, `saved-format.ts`, `snapshot.ts`, `snapshot-selection.ts` and `replay.ts` do not import React. They accept values and return values. `session/session.ts` is also a data transformation module, although it lives beside hooks that import React.

The board has data-only helpers too. `keyboard.ts` computes a target from keys and coordinates. `card-state.ts` computes a state description. `face-design.ts` maps an integer identity to design values. These helpers can be tested without rendering `Board` or building a synthetic browser tree.

This is the meaningful interpretation of the React boundary: importing a rule in a CLI does not start an effect or require a mounted component. It is not a claim that every file ending in `.ts` is independent of React. `use-board-focus.ts`, `nearest-scroll.ts` and the session hooks are TypeScript modules with hooks and browser behavior.

## React imports in application code

| Module | React mechanisms used |
| --- | --- |
| `main.tsx` | `StrictMode`; root rendering through React DOM |
| `Game.tsx` | Ref for the board's focus interface |
| `Board.tsx` | Memoized derivations, refs, stable callback, layout effect and imperative handle |
| `Card.tsx` | `memo` and a keyboard event type |
| `use-board-focus.ts` | Local state, refs and callbacks |
| `nearest-scroll.ts` | Ref, effect and callback |
| `BoardCodeForm.tsx` | Ref for the successful-load focus target |
| `Reproduction.tsx` | Local snapshot draft state |
| `use-game.ts` | Session state and current-value ref |
| `use-session-clock.ts` | Clock/visibility refs and timer effect |
| `use-tournament.ts` | Tournament state, history and current-value ref |
| `use-tournament-clock.ts` | Tournament clock/visibility refs and timer effect |
| `use-saved-preferences.ts` | Persistence effect |

`Controls`, `GameStatus` and `Face` contain JSX without importing a React runtime object. The compiler uses `jsx: react-jsx`, so those files do not need the older `import React` pattern. JSX participation and explicit hook imports are related but different observations.

The diagnostic entries also use React DOM. The face sheet renders real cards, while the session harness mounts and unmounts the real game. Their entrypoints are outside `src` and built separately, so they do not become extra runtime controls in the distributed game.

## One action path for activation

`Card` renders a native button and invokes its supplied activation callback from `onClick`. Native keyboard activation and ordinary pointer activation therefore reach the same controller action. The keydown handler delegates navigation; it does not implement another matching algorithm.

In solo play the controller synchronizes active time and calls `activateSession`, which calls `activateCard`. Tournament play synchronizes its own clock and calls the separate tournament transition, which then uses `activateCard`. Components receive the resulting state and render it. A class such as `matched` is an outcome of the data, not the authoritative record of a matched pair. Reading CSS classes back into the core would reverse that relationship.

Matched buttons use `aria-disabled`, keeping them in the board's focus model. The rule function still rejects activating matched positions. During a mismatch, the session does not mark every other button disabled; the core rejects new activations while that selection is pending. Semantic presentation and transition legality are both visible, with legality centralized in the rules.

A completed valid snapshot is not an error merely because its result exceeds the local stored best. It loads as completed with a completion notice and static banner. An unfinished valid snapshot loads paused with an instruction to resume. The notice area carries both success and failure outcomes, so `.load-notice` is a more accurate name than a field-specific error class.

## Existing visual and semantic treatment

The notice paragraph uses the surrounding document styles and the load-status layout. The current fields do not receive `aria-invalid`, an error border class or an inline replacement label on failure. Those absences are part of the existing markup, not evidence that validation did not run.

The paragraph can wrap and has `min-width: 0` in its flex row. Resume can wrap alongside it on a constrained viewport. There is no absolute positioning that places a message over the field. [Form layout guide](form-layout-guide.md) explains how the notice row relates to the grid inside the disclosure.

Name-related errors do not exist in the current component tree. Their policies are in [Name length policy](name-length-policy.md) and [Duplicate names policy](duplicate-names-policy.md). The load forms use their own messages and have no shared name-error component.

## Evidence for preservation and retry

`tests/control-contract.e2e.test.ts` populates progress, submits both invalid drafts and compares exported state before and after. It also advances the browser clock to show that the preserved game is still running. That distinguishes failure preservation from an accidental reset or pause.

`tests/status-controls.e2e.test.ts` submits a valid code with Enter, then an invalid code, checking both focus and the unchanged card count. `tests/controls.e2e.test.ts` checks exact notices, retained drafts and action focus. Repeated invalid submissions are covered in the announcement and accessibility journeys.

A useful defect report includes the draft, action origin, notice text and a before/after state observation. For example, an invalid snapshot followed by an unchanged exported selection is evidence of preservation. A notice alone cannot prove it, and a preserved game alone cannot prove that the user was told what happened. Reviewing both gives the error path its full meaning.

open-forge:
  description: Name-length acceptance, Unicode counting units and boundary examples.
  tags:
    - Forms
    - Names
    - Unicode

# Name length policy

This page defines how the name-length check is interpreted and separates it from native text-field limits.

The current game has no person-name field or name validator. Its existing text limits belong to Board code and Snapshot JSON. They are useful examples of browser entry constraints, but neither is an implementation of the name policy on this page.

## The checked value

The length check concerns the accepted name representation, after the processing described in [Text entry policy](text-entry-policy.md). Counting the raw draft instead can produce a different result from counting the value that the feature will store and display. A name has 2 to 20 Unicode code points after normalization. Anything else blocks the action and shows "Use 2 to 20 characters." This check therefore belongs at the point where a draft would become an accepted name, rather than being inferred from the field's apparent width.

The message is the user-facing explanation of this failure. The numerical bounds are inclusive: the endpoints pass, and values outside them fail. The policy does not define an exception for a one-character name, a separate limit for a family name or an alternate bound for another script.

A failure blocks the action that is trying to accept the name. It is not a request to silently cut the entered value to fit. Truncating a longer string would accept a different name and would conceal which action failed. The policy specifies feedback and blocking rather than a repair that guesses the user's intended spelling.

## Code points, code units and visible text

JavaScript string `.length` counts UTF-16 code units. That is not always the number required here. Many characters outside the Basic Multilingual Plane occupy two code units but one Unicode code point. For example, `A😀` has three code units and two code points.

A user-perceived symbol can also contain several code points. An emoji sequence joined with a zero-width joiner may look like one symbol while contributing multiple points. A base letter plus a combining mark can be another example, depending on whether canonical composition produces a single point in the accepted form.

The policy chooses code points, not rendered glyph count or grapheme cluster count. A font can draw two code points as one ligature, and an input method can produce a composed-looking sequence. Neither observation changes which unit the check uses. Reviewing only a screenshot cannot establish that the correct unit was counted.

In JavaScript, iterating a string by code point is different from indexing its individual UTF-16 units. `Array.from(value).length` or a spread-based count illustrates that distinction for well-formed text. This is an explanatory example, not a requirement to allocate an array in a particular implementation. The source has no name helper.

## Boundary examples

The examples below assume that the value shown is already in its accepted representation. They illustrate the count, not an additional character allowlist.

| Value | Code-point count | Length result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Empty string | 0 | Fails |
| `A` | 1 | Fails |
| `Al` | 2 | Passes |
| `A😀` | 2 | Passes |
| Twenty ASCII letters | 20 | Passes |
| Twenty-one ASCII letters | 21 | Fails |
| Twenty supplementary-plane symbols | 20 | Passes |

The supplementary-plane example can expose a validator that accidentally uses `.length`: it sees forty code units instead. The opposite mistake is counting a joined visual sequence as one merely because it occupies one displayed cell. A correct boundary check is about the string's code points after representation processing.

“Passes” here means that the length condition is satisfied. It does not imply that an action with other applicable checks is guaranteed to succeed. The [Duplicate names policy](duplicate-names-policy.md) addresses a separate group-level condition without changing the unit used by this check.

## The order is observable

A raw draft may have surrounding or repeated spacing that will not be retained in its accepted form. Counting before the representation step can reject a value that would fit after processing, or accept a value whose later transformations were not what the length helper expected. The policy's ordering avoids having the stored name disagree with the checked name.

A reviewer can follow one candidate from field submission to accepted model and then display. The decisive value is the same one used for the count. An implementation that checks one temporary string but saves a different raw draft has two representations and cannot establish the stated condition simply by having a correctly named length function.

There is no instruction here to run the full action after every individual keystroke. Composition and editing are part of the input experience. The check governs acceptance, while timing of draft feedback is not otherwise specified by the current code or this policy.

## Scope of current evidence

There is no name-length test in the repository. Keyboard and reproduction checks establish native field labels, draft preservation and load outcomes. They do not verify the name count merely because they type strings into controls.

When this policy is implemented, its evidence can name the processed candidate and observed outcome at the boundary. That is enough to distinguish a counting defect from a display problem or another group-level validation failure. The policy stays narrow: one accepted value, one counting unit, one inclusive interval and the stated blocking message.

# Duplicate names policy

This page explains the group-level name comparison policy and the distinctions a reviewer needs when checking it.

The current source has no name list or group editor. A board code identifies a deal, a card label identifies a position and face state, and a local best is indexed by board size. None of those is a collection of person-entered names. The policy below belongs to a feature that introduces such a collection.

## Comparison boundary

The group being edited supplies the comparison scope; the draft alone cannot establish whether it repeats an existing entry. The candidate's accepted representation comes from [Text entry policy](text-entry-policy.md). Names in one group compare without regard to case, after normalization. A repeat blocks the action and shows "Each name must be different." This lets the same visible spelling with different capitalization be recognized as a repeat without requiring that all displayed names be rewritten in one case.

The scope is one group. Neon Pairs has no global name registry across devices, browser origins or unrelated groups. A local comparison can answer whether an entry repeats within the group being acted on without implying that the person owns a unique account name.

The check concerns names, rather than board positions or face identities. Two cards intentionally share a face, and a replay can intentionally activate the same position more than once. Those repetitions follow their own game rules. A generic “remove duplicates everywhere” helper would not express this policy's subject or scope.

## Display value and comparison value

Case-insensitive comparison does not by itself prescribe changing a name's displayed capitalization. `Mira` and `mira` can compare as the same candidate while the accepted display spelling remains the one chosen by the person who entered it. Showing a lowercased comparison key as the name would conflate two purposes.

A useful implementation trace therefore distinguishes the value displayed, the value accepted into the group and whatever representation is used to compare it. The comparison representation is an internal tool. It is not a new user-visible identifier, a format field or a replacement for the accepted name.

The policy does not specify locale selection or a particular Unicode case-folding API. That matters for names whose case behavior differs across languages or scripts. Name normalization retains diacritics and does not transliterate names. Examples with ordinary Latin letters illustrate the unambiguous case while case behavior across Unicode varies.

The representation step is also not a license to treat all visually similar strings as equal. Latin and Cyrillic lookalikes, differing accents and compatibility characters can resemble one another without being the same processed string. Visual similarity would be a broader identity rule than the policy states.

## Small examples

| Existing accepted name | Candidate | What the example demonstrates |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Mira` | `Mira` | A direct repeat |
| `Mira` | `mira` | Capitalization does not distinguish the names |
| `Mira` | `MIRA` | The comparison is not limited to the first letter |
| `Ada Lovelace` | The same name after representation processing | The comparison uses accepted name text |

# Name length policy

This page defines how the name-length check is interpreted and separates it from native text-field limits.

The current game has no person-name field or name validator. Its existing text limits belong to Board code and Snapshot JSON. They are useful examples of browser entry constraints, but neither is an implementation of the name policy on this page.

## The checked value

The length check concerns the accepted name representation, after the processing described in [Text entry policy](text-entry-policy.md). Counting the raw draft instead can produce a different result from counting the value that the feature will store and display. A name has 2 to 20 Unicode code points after normalization. Anything else blocks the action and shows "Use 2 to 20 characters." This check therefore belongs at the point where a draft would become an accepted name, rather than being inferred from the field's apparent width.

The message is the user-facing explanation of this failure. The numerical bounds are inclusive: the endpoints pass, and values outside them fail. The policy does not define an exception for a one-character name, a separate limit for a family name or an alternate bound for another script.

A failure blocks the action that is trying to accept the name. It is not a request to silently cut the entered value to fit. Truncating a longer string would accept a different name and would conceal which action failed. The policy specifies feedback and blocking rather than a repair that guesses the user's intended spelling.

## Code points, code units and visible text

JavaScript string `.length` counts UTF-16 code units. That is not always the number required here. Many characters outside the Basic Multilingual Plane occupy two code units but one Unicode code point. For example, `A😀` has three code units and two code points.

A user-perceived symbol can also contain several code points. An emoji sequence joined with a zero-width joiner may look like one symbol while contributing multiple points. A base letter plus a combining mark can be another example, depending on whether canonical composition produces a single point in the accepted form.

The policy chooses code points, not rendered glyph count or grapheme cluster count. A font can draw two code points as one ligature, and an input method can produce a composed-looking sequence. Neither observation changes which unit the check uses. Reviewing only a screenshot cannot establish that the correct unit was counted.

In JavaScript, iterating a string by code point is different from indexing its individual UTF-16 units. `Array.from(value).length` or a spread-based count illustrates that distinction for well-formed text. This is an explanatory example, not a requirement to allocate an array in a particular implementation. The source has no name helper.

## Boundary examples

The examples below assume that the value shown is already in its accepted representation. They illustrate the count, not an additional character allowlist.

| Value | Code-point count | Length result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Empty string | 0 | Fails |
| `A` | 1 | Fails |
| `Al` | 2 | Passes |
| `A😀` | 2 | Passes |
| Twenty ASCII letters | 20 | Passes |
| Twenty-one ASCII letters | 21 | Fails |
| Twenty supplementary-plane symbols | 20 | Passes |

The supplementary-plane example can expose a validator that accidentally uses `.length`: it sees forty code units instead. The opposite mistake is counting a joined visual sequence as one merely because it occupies one displayed cell. A correct boundary check is about the string's code points after representation processing.

“Passes” here means that the length condition is satisfied. It does not imply that an action with other applicable checks is guaranteed to succeed. The [Duplicate names policy](duplicate-names-policy.md) addresses a separate group-level condition without changing the unit used by this check.

## The order is observable

A raw draft may have surrounding or repeated spacing that will not be retained in its accepted form. Counting before the representation step can reject a value that would fit after processing, or accept a value whose later transformations were not what the length helper expected. The policy's ordering avoids having the stored name disagree with the checked name.

A reviewer can follow one candidate from field submission to accepted model and then display. The decisive value is the same one used for the count. An implementation that checks one temporary string but saves a different raw draft has two representations and cannot establish the stated condition simply by having a correctly named length function.

There is no instruction here to run the full action after every individual keystroke. Composition and editing are part of the input experience. The check governs acceptance, while timing of draft feedback is not otherwise specified by the current code or this policy.

## Scope of current evidence

There is no name-length test in the repository. Keyboard and reproduction checks establish native field labels, draft preservation and load outcomes. They do not verify the name count merely because they type strings into controls.

When this policy is implemented, its evidence can name the processed candidate and observed outcome at the boundary. That is enough to distinguish a counting defect from a display problem or another group-level validation failure. The policy stays narrow: one accepted value, one counting unit, one inclusive interval and the stated blocking message.

# Duplicate names policy

This page explains the group-level name comparison policy and the distinctions a reviewer needs when checking it.

The current source has no name list or group editor. A board code identifies a deal, a card label identifies a position and face state, and a local best is indexed by board size. None of those is a collection of person-entered names. The policy below belongs to a feature that introduces such a collection.

## Comparison boundary

The group being edited supplies the comparison scope; the draft alone cannot establish whether it repeats an existing entry. The candidate's accepted representation comes from [Text entry policy](text-entry-policy.md). Names in one group compare without regard to case, after normalization. A repeat blocks the action and shows "Each name must be different." This lets the same visible spelling with different capitalization be recognized as a repeat without requiring that all displayed names be rewritten in one case.

The scope is one group. Neon Pairs has no global name registry across devices, browser origins or unrelated groups. A local comparison can answer whether an entry repeats within the group being acted on without implying that the person owns a unique account name.

The check concerns names, rather than board positions or face identities. Two cards intentionally share a face, and a replay can intentionally activate the same position more than once. Those repetitions follow their own game rules. A generic “remove duplicates everywhere” helper would not express this policy's subject or scope.

Case-insensitive comparison does not by itself prescribe changing a name's displayed capitalization. `Mira` and `mira` can compare as the same candidate while the accepted display spelling remains the one chosen by the person who entered it. Showing a lowercased comparison key as the name would conflate two purposes.

A useful implementation trace therefore distinguishes the value displayed, the value accepted into the group and whatever representation is used to compare it. The comparison representation is an internal tool. It is not a new user-visible identifier, a format field or a replacement for the accepted name.

The policy does not specify locale selection or a particular Unicode case-folding API. That matters for names whose case behavior differs across languages or scripts. Name normalization retains diacritics and does not transliterate names. Examples with ordinary Latin letters illustrate the unambiguous case while case behavior across Unicode varies.

The representation step is also not a license to treat all visually similar strings as equal. Latin and Cyrillic lookalikes, differing accents and compatibility characters can resemble one another without being the same processed string. Visual similarity would be a broader identity rule than the policy states.

--- 2 ---
A completed valid snapshot is not an error merely because its result exceeds the local stored best. It loads as completed with a completion notice and static banner. An unfinished valid snapshot loads paused with an instruction to resume. The notice area carries both success and failure outcomes, so `.load-notice` is a more accurate name than a field-specific error class.

## Existing visual and semantic treatment

The notice paragraph uses the surrounding document styles and the load-status layout. The current fields do not receive `aria-invalid`, an error border class or an inline replacement label on failure. Those absences are part of the existing markup, not evidence that validation did not run.

The paragraph can wrap and has `min-width: 0` in its flex row. Resume can wrap alongside it on a constrained viewport. There is no absolute positioning that places a message over the field. [Form layout guide](form-layout-guide.md) explains how the notice row relates to the grid inside the disclosure.

Name-related errors do not exist in the current component tree. Their policies are in [Name length policy](name-length-policy.md) and [Duplicate names policy](duplicate-names-policy.md). The load forms use their own messages and have no shared name-error component.

## Evidence for preservation and retry

`tests/control-contract.e2e.test.ts` populates progress, submits both invalid drafts and compares exported state before and after. It also advances the browser clock to show that the preserved game is still running. That distinguishes failure preservation from an accidental reset or pause.

`tests/status-controls.e2e.test.ts` submits a valid code with Enter, then an invalid code, checking both focus and the unchanged card count. `tests/controls.e2e.test.ts` checks exact notices, retained drafts and action focus. Repeated invalid submissions are covered in the announcement and accessibility journeys.

A useful defect report includes the draft, action origin, notice text and a before/after state observation. For example, an invalid snapshot followed by an unchanged exported selection is evidence of preservation. A notice alone cannot prove it, and a preserved game alone cannot prove that the user was told what happened. Reviewing both gives the error path its full meaning.

# Text entry policy

This page records the treatment of person-entered names and distinguishes it from the game's existing code and JSON fields.

Neon Pairs currently asks for a board code and snapshot text, not a player name. There is no name field, group-name store or name rendering component in the source. The name policy below applies when such input is introduced; it does not describe a transformation already applied to the reproduction textarea.

## One name representation

A name can arrive with incidental spaces from typing, pasting or an input method. Keeping several representations of that same entered name would make later display and comparison harder to reason about. Every name a person types is stored and shown after trimming both ends, collapsing each run of inner whitespace to one space and normalizing to NFC. The stored value and visible value therefore describe the same processed name rather than exposing the original draft in one view and a different spelling in another.

The policy is about a person's name. It does not turn all user input into name text, and it does not change the board-code grammar or snapshot serialization. The current fields demonstrate why that distinction matters: significant punctuation and structural whitespace belong to their own formats.

For names, the other checks are documented separately in [Name length policy](name-length-policy.md) and [Duplicate names policy](duplicate-names-policy.md). This page explains representation and input boundaries without duplicating their conditions or error messages.

## Examples of representation

The following examples use quotes only to make surrounding whitespace visible. The quotes are not part of the entered name.

| Entered draft | Displayed and stored form | What changed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `  Mira  ` | `Mira` | Space around the name is removed |
| `Ada   Lovelace` | `Ada Lovelace` | An interior run becomes one separating space |
| `Jean Luc` | `Jean Luc` | Ordinary spacing stays ordinary |
| `Cafe` followed by a combining acute on the e | `Café` | Canonically equivalent text gets a composed representation where available |
| `O'Neil` | `O'Neil` | The apostrophe is retained |

The last example matters because representation cleanup is not an instruction to remove meaningful punctuation or rewrite a person's preferred spelling. The policy does not transliterate scripts, strip accents or convert names to ASCII. Those would be additional transformations beyond what is stated.

NFC addresses canonical equivalence in Unicode text. It is not the compatibility normalization form. Text that merely looks similar is not necessarily canonically equivalent, and this policy does not define visual resemblance as identity. That boundary prevents a representation step from quietly becoming a broad name-matching heuristic.

A name can also contain multiple words. Collapsing a whitespace run does not merge words together; it leaves a separating space. Treating the policy as “delete all whitespace” would change `Ada Lovelace` into a different string and would not implement the stated behavior.

## Drafts and accepted values

A draft is what someone is still editing. A stored value is what an action has accepted. # Interface review checklist

This page is a review route through the existing controls, input behavior and related interface policies.

A useful review follows a few populated journeys and checks source at the transitions. An empty board screenshot cannot show preserved drafts, matched-card focus or a stale timer after Restart. The checks below are grounded in the current source and specifications; links identify the separate policies for feature surfaces that do not exist yet.

## Establish what changed

Start with the actual component and its callback. A control can retain its appearance while changing submission, focus or session behavior. A CSS-only change can also alter the hit area or clipping without touching an event handler.

- Identify whether the change affects `Controls`, `Reproduction`, `BoardCodeForm`, `GameStatus`, `Board`, `Card` or the focus hook.
- Follow callbacks into `use-game.ts` and `session.ts` when the change replaces a game, accepts input or publishes feedback.
- Compare element types, ids, label associations, explicit button types and source order as well as class names.
- Check mobile selectors that depend on direct children before accepting a wrapper-only refactor as behaviorally neutral.

The current page has no name editor, dialog or result table. A change introducing one has more scope than styling an existing control. Its relevant policy is linked below, and its current behavior has to be established from its own implementation.

## Deal controls

Use [Control bar](control-bar.md) and the Controls specification as the reference for these observations.

- Grid size is a labeled native select with the seven supported choices, and its selected value agrees with the current game after either successful load type.
- New Game keeps the current size and creates a fresh deal; Restart repeats the current board code.
- Both actions reset selection, pairs, moves and elapsed time, and leave their action button focused.
- Replacing a game during a mismatch does not let an old timer change the replacement.
- The board's next native entry starts at its first card after a replacement, rather than retaining an index from the old deal.

A code comparison can distinguish New Game from Restart even when the two visible decks happen to share some positions. A move-count comparison alone cannot establish that distinction. For size changes, check both card count and the controlled select value.

The current buttons act immediately. A reviewer should not claim existing confirmation coverage from the presence of a leave policy elsewhere. [Dialog policy](dialog-policy.md) records that separate feature boundary.

## Text tools and errors

The useful draft is one that differs from the currently displayed code, and the useful game state has some progress. [Reproduction panel](reproduction-panel.md) and [Error display guide](error-display-guide.md) provide the source trace.

- The native disclosure starts collapsed and is named Reproduce a game.
- Board code and Snapshot JSON retain visible, correctly associated labels and their existing native limits.
- Editing Board code, then playing a card, keeps the edited draft.
- Invalid board-code and snapshot submissions preserve the current game and the entered text, and show their exact existing load outcomes.
- Successful Board code submission refreshes the field from the accepted code and updates the selected size.
- Export fills selectable, readable JSON without replacing or pausing play.

Try Enter from Board code as well as clicking Load board. Success focuses Load board because the input is replaced. Failure from the input keeps editing focus there. A click-origin failure keeps focus on the clicked action. The distinction can be lost in a test that only inspects the final board.

The snapshot textarea is multiline and has its own local state. Enter is not an implicit import action. Its draft is not automatically rewritten on every turn or deal replacement. The visible notice sits outside the disclosure, so closing it does not hide an unfinished import's way to continue.

## Import and Resume

A valid unfinished snapshot and a valid completed snapshot exercise different paths. The current specification gives concrete examples and constraints in [Snapshot format](../sharing/snapshot-format.md).

- Unfinished progress loads paused, including an imported position that has not started its clock yet.
- Card activation is blocked while paused, but focus movement still works.
- Resume focuses the board's remembered card before its own button is removed.
- A pending mismatch continues its remaining active interval after Resume.
- Completed progress loads completed, with static completion output and no Resume button.
- Import is not treated as a newly achieved play completion for best-record updates.

A far remembered card on a large board makes the Resume check meaningful. Scroll the board away from that card before resuming and inspect both focus and nearest visibility. Merely finding any focused button afterward would not establish that the remembered destination survived.

## Board movement and activation

Use [Board keyboard navigation](board-keyboard-navigation.md), [Pointer and touch](pointer-and-touch.md) and [Disabled state guide](disabled-state-guide.md) together.

- Tab enters the remembered card and can leave the board again; reverse traversal is native too.
- Plain arrows move one row or column, stop at edges and do not reveal cards.
- Modifier combinations and unlisted keys retain browser behavior.
- Enter, Space, primary click and completed tap reach the shared card action.
- Hover, touch scrolling, pointer cancellation and context-menu interaction do not choose a card.
- Matched cards stay focusable and expose their matched state while activation leaves the turn unchanged.
- Repeated activation of the first revealed card does not add a move.

# Error display guide

This page explains how failed board-code and snapshot loads are reported without replacing the current game.

The current UI has two validation outcomes that are errors: `Invalid board code.` and `Invalid snapshot.`. They describe the attempted load, not a broken game. The player can correct the draft and retry while the current deal remains available.

## The visible location

Reproduction renders a paragraph with `id="load-notice"` and class `load-notice` inside `.load-status`. That container follows the native details element. It is adjacent to the reproduction tools but outside their collapsible body.

Both Load board and Load snapshot carry `aria-describedby="load-notice"`. Their visible names remain the action labels; the description associates the nearby outcome with those actions. The field labels stay Board code and Snapshot JSON rather than being replaced with an error sentence.

Because the paragraph is outside details, it remains in document flow when the panel is closed. A person does not have to reopen the JSON field merely to see the most recent load notice or Resume. The `.load-status` flex row wraps, has a `12px` gap and a `56px` minimum height; its paragraph can grow and shrink within the available width.

The same load outcome is also published through the game's feedback path. [Announcements policy](announcements-policy.md) describes that event handling. The local paragraph's role here is visible context beside the load tools, not a second independent validation system.

## Who decides that a load failed

BoardCodeForm reads its draft through FormData and calls the `loadBoard` prop. The controller in `use-game.ts` trims surrounding whitespace and checks `parseBoardCode`. Failure calls `notice(SessionNotice.invalidBoard)` and returns false before clock reset or replacement.

Reproduction passes the complete snapshot draft to `loadSnapshot`. The controller calls `decodeSnapshot`. Failure calls `notice(SessionNotice.invalidSnapshot)` and returns false, again before resetting or replacing the game. The textarea component does not try to validate JSON structure itself.

`SessionNotice` in `session.ts` owns the literal messages. The shared `notice` helper sets both `feedback` and `loadNotice` and advances announcement identity. The exact words therefore come from the session boundary that knows the operation failed, rather than being duplicated in each field's change handler.

This ordering is important. If a load reset the timer before parsing, even an invalid draft could alter play. If it replaced the game before reporting failure, the notice would not describe the preservation behavior promised by the controls specification. The current callbacks validate first.

## What a failure preserves

A failed board-code load leaves the input's DOM node intact because generation does not change. Its edited value remains available. A failed snapshot load leaves Reproduction's local string state intact. Neither failure clears the draft to make the panel look clean.

The game object, board size, matched positions, selection, moves and elapsed state are not replaced by the error path. The existing game can continue to advance active time. An invalid input is not an imported pause, and it does not freeze a pending mismatch merely because a notice appeared.

Focus memory also survives because Board is not remounted. A player who last visited a far card can return there after correcting a form. The current saved size is unchanged by a failed load; successful replacement is what updates that preference.

The load notice is a session field separate from the game. Adding it can produce a render without changing card state. This is why comparing the complete session object for identity is different from asserting that gameplay was replaced. [Game state model](../gameplay/game-state-model.md) and [Session module](../architecture/session-module.md) explain those boundaries.

## Focus depends on how submission began

A click on Load board ordinarily leaves focus on the button. If the code is invalid, BoardCodeForm does not issue another focus call. A keyboard Enter submission from inside Board code leaves focus in the field on failure, so the user can continue editing.

On successful Enter submission, the input is about to be replaced because it is keyed by generation. BoardCodeForm explicitly focuses its Load board ref when the callback returns true. That is a success-path focus correction, not an error-summary jump.

Load snapshot is a `type="button"` action. Its handler passes local text to the controller and does not move focus elsewhere on failure or success. The snapshot textarea stays mounted. Export likewise keeps its action focus and fills the field rather than focusing or selecting it automatically.

These cases show why “errors focus the field” would be an inaccurate description of this interface. The source preserves the user's current interaction where it can. [Focus policy](focus-policy.md) covers the complete set of current focus transfers.

## Notices are outcomes, not sticky field annotations

`loadNotice` is one session string used for the latest published load outcome. It is not an error object keyed separately by field. The UI does not render two simultaneous field-specific error paragraphs or an error list above the panel.

After an invalid Board code attempt followed by an invalid snapshot attempt, the visible notice is the snapshot message. The Board code draft can still be invalid; the notice records the most recent action rather than continuously describing all field values.

Editing the snapshot string changes local state but does not itself clear the controller's notice. Editing Board code is native uncontrolled editing and likewise does not call a notice-clearing function. The outcome can remain visible while the user works on a correction.

Export replaces textarea text but does not explicitly clear `loadNotice`. Card turns update feedback without rewriting the load notice. New Game, Restart and a successful board-code replacement clear both through `replaceGame(..., false)`. Successful snapshot loading replaces the notice with its load outcome, and Resume clears it when continuing play.

This lifecycle explains a report that an old load message is still visible after editing. The message is action feedback, not a live validator attached to every keystroke. Adding an on-change clearing behavior would be a change to this lifecycle, not a fix to a missing CSS state.

## Format validity is more than native limits

Board code has a 32-character entry cap, but many shorter strings are invalid. An unsupported size, zero seed, leading zeros or malformed separators fail the parser even when the input is well below its native maximum. The loader's surrounding trim is a deliberate adapter step, not broad syntax repair.

Snapshot JSON has a 65536-character textarea limit and a UTF-8 byte bound in the decoder. Malformed JSON is only one failure kind. Unsupported versions, unknown properties, inconsistent matched positions, invalid selections and out-of-range counters can also produce the same UI error.

The UI intentionally gives the short outcome rather than exposing the decoder's internal reasoning. There is no implemented per-property error report or highlighted JSON line number. [Import safety policy](../sharing/import-safety-policy.md) and [Snapshot format](../sharing/snapshot-format.md) are the useful debugging references for engineers handling a rejected draft.

A completed valid snapshot is not an error merely because its result exceeds the local stored best. It loads as completed with a completion notice and static banner. An unfinished valid snapshot loads paused with an instruction to resume. The notice area carries both success and failure outcomes, so `.load-notice` is a more accurate name than a field-specific error class.

## Existing visual and semantic treatment

The notice paragraph uses the surrounding document styles and the load-status layout. The current fields do not receive `aria-invalid`, an error border class or an inline replacement label on failure. Those absences are part of the existing markup, not evidence that validation did not run.

The paragraph can wrap and has `min-width: 0` in its flex row. Resume can wrap alongside it on a constrained viewport. There is no absolute positioning that places a message over the field. [Form layout guide](form-layout-guide.md) explains how the notice row relates to the grid inside the disclosure.

Name-related errors do not exist in the current component tree. Their policies are in [Name length policy](name-length-policy.md) and [Duplicate names policy](duplicate-names-policy.md). The load forms use their own messages and have no shared name-error component.

## Evidence for preservation and retry

`tests/control-contract.e2e.test.ts` populates progress, submits both invalid drafts and compares exported state before and after. It also advances the browser clock to show that the preserved game is still running. That distinguishes failure preservation from an accidental reset or pause.

`tests/status-controls.e2e.test.ts` submits a valid code with Enter, then an invalid code, checking both focus and the unchanged card count. `tests/controls.e2e.test.ts` checks exact notices, retained drafts and action focus. Repeated invalid submissions are covered in the announcement and accessibility journeys.

A useful defect report includes the draft, action origin, notice text and a before/after state observation. For example, an invalid snapshot followed by an unchanged exported selection is evidence of preservation. A notice alone cannot prove it, and a preserved game alone cannot prove that the user was told what happened. Reviewing both gives the error path its full meaning.

A code comparison can distinguish New Game from Restart even when the two visible decks happen to share some positions. A move-count comparison alone cannot establish that distinction. For size changes, check both card count and the controlled select value.

The current buttons act immediately. A reviewer should not claim existing confirmation coverage from the presence of a leave policy elsewhere. [Dialog policy](dialog-policy.md) records that separate feature boundary.

## Text tools and errors

The useful draft is one that differs from the currently displayed code, and the useful game state has some progress. [Reproduction panel](reproduction-panel.md) and [Error display guide](error-display-guide.md) provide the source trace.

- The native disclosure starts collapsed and is named Reproduce a game.
- Board code and Snapshot JSON retain visible, correctly associated labels and their existing native limits.
- Editing Board code, then playing a card, keeps the edited draft.
- Invalid board-code and snapshot submissions preserve the current game and the entered text, and show their exact existing load outcomes.
- Successful Board code submission refreshes the field from the accepted code and updates the selected size.
- Export fills selectable, readable JSON without replacing or pausing play.

Try Enter from Board code as well as clicking Load board. Success focuses Load board because the input is replaced. Failure from the input keeps editing focus there. A click-origin failure keeps focus on the clicked action. The distinction can be lost in a test that only inspects the final board.

The snapshot textarea is multiline and has its own local state. Enter is not an implicit import action. Its draft is not automatically rewritten on every turn or deal replacement. The visible notice sits outside the disclosure, so closing it does not hide an unfinished import's way to continue.

## Import and Resume

A valid unfinished snapshot and a valid completed snapshot exercise different paths. The current specification gives concrete examples and constraints in [Snapshot format](../sharing/snapshot-format.md).

- Unfinished progress loads paused, including an imported position that has not started its clock yet.
- Card activation is blocked while paused, but focus movement still works.
- Resume focuses the board's remembered card before its own button is removed.
- A pending mismatch continues its remaining active interval after Resume.
- Completed progress loads completed, with static completion output and no Resume button.
- Import is not treated as a newly achieved play completion for best-record updates.

A far remembered card on a large board makes the Resume check meaningful. Scroll the board away from that card before resuming and inspect both focus and nearest visibility. Merely finding any focused button afterward would not establish that the remembered destination survived.

## Board movement and activation

Use [Board keyboard navigation](board-keyboard-navigation.md), [Pointer and touch](pointer-and-touch.md) and [Disabled state guide](disabled-state-guide.md) together.

- Tab enters the remembered card and can leave the board again; reverse traversal is native too.
- Plain arrows move one row or column, stop at edges and do not reveal cards.
- Modifier combinations and unlisted keys retain browser behavior.
- Enter, Space, primary click and completed tap reach the shared card action.
- Hover, touch scrolling, pointer cancellation and context-menu interaction do not choose a card.
- Matched cards stay focusable and expose their matched state while activation leaves the turn unchanged.
- Repeated activation of the first revealed card does not add a move.

# Error display guide

This page explains how failed board-code and snapshot loads are reported without replacing the current game.

The current UI has two validation outcomes that are errors: `Invalid board code.` and `Invalid snapshot.`. They describe the attempted load, not a broken game. The player can correct the draft and retry while the current deal remains available.

## The visible location

Reproduction renders a paragraph with `id="load-notice"` and class `load-notice` inside `.load-status`. That container follows the native details element. It is adjacent to the reproduction tools but outside their collapsible body.

Both Load board and Load snapshot carry `aria-describedby="load-notice"`. Their visible names remain the action labels; the description associates the nearby outcome with those actions. The field labels stay Board code and Snapshot JSON rather than being replaced with an error sentence.

Because the paragraph is outside details, it remains in document flow when the panel is closed. A person does not have to reopen the JSON field merely to see the most recent load notice or Resume. The `.load-status` flex row wraps, has a `12px` gap and a `56px` minimum height; its paragraph can grow and shrink within the available width.

The same load outcome is also published through the game's feedback path. [Announcements policy](announcements-policy.md) describes that event handling. The local paragraph's role here is visible context beside the load tools, not a second independent validation system.

## Who decides that a load failed

BoardCodeForm reads its draft through FormData and calls the `loadBoard` prop. The controller in `use-game.ts` trims surrounding whitespace and checks `parseBoardCode`. Failure calls `notice(SessionNotice.invalidBoard)` and returns false before clock reset or replacement.

Reproduction passes the complete snapshot draft to `loadSnapshot`. The controller calls `decodeSnapshot`. Failure calls `notice(SessionNotice.invalidSnapshot)` and returns false, again before resetting or replacing the game. The textarea component does not try to validate JSON structure itself.

`SessionNotice` in `session.ts` owns the literal messages. The shared `notice` helper sets both `feedback` and `loadNotice` and advances announcement identity. The exact words therefore come from the session boundary that knows the operation failed, rather than being duplicated in each field's change handler.

This ordering is important. If a load reset the timer before parsing, even an invalid draft could alter play. If it replaced the game before reporting failure, the notice would not describe the preservation behavior promised by the controls specification. The current callbacks validate first.

## What a failure preserves

A failed board-code load leaves the input's DOM node intact because generation does not change. Its edited value remains available. A failed snapshot load leaves Reproduction's local string state intact. Neither failure clears the draft to make the panel look clean.

The game object, board size, matched positions, selection, moves and elapsed state are not replaced by the error path. The existing game can continue to advance active time. An invalid input is not an imported pause, and it does not freeze a pending mismatch merely because a notice appeared.

Focus memory also survives because Board is not remounted. A player who last visited a far card can return there after correcting a form. The current saved size is unchanged by a failed load; successful replacement is what updates that preference.

The load notice is a session field separate from the game. Adding it can produce a render without changing card state. This is why comparing the complete session object for identity is different from asserting that gameplay was replaced. [Game state model](../gameplay/game-state-model.md) and [Session module](../architecture/session-module.md) explain those boundaries.

## Focus depends on how submission began

A click on Load board ordinarily leaves focus on the button. If the code is invalid, BoardCodeForm does not issue another focus call. A keyboard Enter submission from inside Board code leaves focus in the field on failure, so the user can continue editing.

On successful Enter submission, the input is about to be replaced because it is keyed by generation. BoardCodeForm explicitly focuses its Load board ref when the callback returns true. That is a success-path focus correction, not an error-summary jump.

Load snapshot is a `type="button"` action. Its handler passes local text to the controller and does not move focus elsewhere on failure or success. The snapshot textarea stays mounted. Export likewise keeps its action focus and fills the field rather than focusing or selecting it automatically.

These cases show why “errors focus the field” would be an inaccurate description of this interface. The source preserves the user's current interaction where it can. [Focus policy](focus-policy.md) covers the complete set of current focus transfers.

## Notices are outcomes, not sticky field annotations

`loadNotice` is one session string used for the latest published load outcome. It is not an error object keyed separately by field. The UI does not render two simultaneous field-specific error paragraphs or an error list above the panel.

After an invalid Board code attempt followed by an invalid snapshot attempt, the visible notice is the snapshot message. The Board code draft can still be invalid; the notice records the most recent action rather than continuously describing all field values.

Editing the snapshot string changes local state but does not itself clear the controller's notice. Editing Board code is native uncontrolled editing and likewise does not call a notice-clearing function. The outcome can remain visible while the user works on a correction.

Export replaces textarea text but does not explicitly clear `loadNotice`. Card turns update feedback without rewriting the load notice. New Game, Restart and a successful board-code replacement clear both through `replaceGame(..., false)`. Successful snapshot loading replaces the notice with its load outcome, and Resume clears it when continuing play.

This lifecycle explains a report that an old load message is still visible after editing. The message is action feedback, not a live validator attached to every keystroke. Adding an on-change clearing behavior would be a change to this lifecycle, not a fix to a missing CSS state.

## Format validity is more than native limits

Board code has a 32-character entry cap, but many shorter strings are invalid. An unsupported size, zero seed, leading zeros or malformed separators fail the parser even when the input is well below its native maximum. The loader's surrounding trim is a deliberate adapter step, not broad syntax repair.

Snapshot JSON has a 65536-character textarea limit and a UTF-8 byte bound in the decoder. Malformed JSON is only one failure kind. Unsupported versions, unknown properties, inconsistent matched positions, invalid selections and out-of-range counters can also produce the same UI error.

The UI intentionally gives the short outcome rather than exposing the decoder's internal reasoning. There is no implemented per-property error report or highlighted JSON line number. [Import safety policy](../sharing/import-safety-policy.md) and [Snapshot format](../sharing/snapshot-format.md) are the useful debugging references for engineers handling a rejected draft.

A completed valid snapshot is not an error merely because its result exceeds the local stored best. It loads as completed with a completion notice and static banner. An unfinished valid snapshot loads paused with an instruction to resume. The notice area carries both success and failure outcomes, so `.load-notice` is a more accurate name than a field-specific error class.

## Existing visual and semantic treatment

The notice paragraph uses the surrounding document styles and the load-status layout. The current fields do not receive `aria-invalid`, an error border class or an inline replacement label on failure. Those absences are part of the existing markup, not evidence that validation did not run.

The paragraph can wrap and has `min-width: 0` in its flex row. Resume can wrap alongside it on a constrained viewport. There is no absolute positioning that places a message over the field. [Form layout guide](form-layout-guide.md) explains how the notice row relates to the grid inside the disclosure.

Name-related errors do not exist in the current component tree. Their policies are in [Name length policy](name-length-policy.md) and [Duplicate names policy](duplicate-names-policy.md). The load forms use their own messages and have no shared name-error component.

## Evidence for preservation and retry

`tests/control-contract.e2e.test.ts` populates progress, submits both invalid drafts and compares exported state before and after. It also advances the browser clock to show that the preserved game is still running. That distinguishes failure preservation from an accidental reset or pause.

`tests/status-controls.e2e.test.ts` submits a valid code with Enter, then an invalid code, checking both focus and the unchanged card count. `tests/controls.e2e.test.ts` checks exact notices, retained drafts and action focus. Repeated invalid submissions are covered in the announcement and accessibility journeys.

A useful defect report includes the draft, action origin, notice text and a before/after state observation. For example, an invalid snapshot followed by an unchanged exported selection is evidence of preservation. A notice alone cannot prove it, and a preserved game alone cannot prove that the user was told what happened. Reviewing both gives the error path its full meaning.
