# Tables policy

This page records the markup policy for ordered result data and explains why the current game statistics use a different structure.

There is no result table in the current UI. `GameStatus.tsx` displays four properties of a single game in a definition list. Reproduction controls use forms, and the board is a CSS grid of buttons. None of those structures is evidence that ordered records have already been implemented.

## Policy for result data

When the content represents records with comparable columns, its relationships need to survive reading beyond the visual arrangement. CSS alone can align text while leaving those relationships absent from the document structure. Ranked or bracket data is a table element with a caption and th scope="col" header cells. The caption identifies the collection being read, while the column headers connect each record's values to their meaning.

This is a content-specific policy. It does not make the game board a data table because it has rows and columns, and it does not require converting every compact summary to tabular markup. The distinction begins with what the content means: interactive card coordinates, a property's value and a record in an ordered result collection are different things.

No such result feature is present in `Game.tsx`. The policy applies when result data is introduced. [Native controls guide](native-controls-guide.md) discusses the broader preference for native semantics without adding another result format.

## Why the statistics are a definition list

GameStatus renders Moves, Pairs, Time and Best as four `dt`/`dd` groups inside a `dl`. Each term names a property of the same current game. There are no peer result rows and no column whose meaning changes with the row being read.

The layout happens to use flex and can wrap. At a wide width, those groups may look like cells in a horizontal strip. At a narrow width, they can flow to multiple lines. Neither visual arrangement changes the definition-list relationship. Replacing the wrapper with a table solely to preserve one desktop arrangement would confuse layout with content structure.

The Best value is one saved move count selected by current size. It does not present a list of people or a comparison across many records. `session.preferences.bestMoves[String(game.size)]` chooses the value before it reaches GameStatus. A single local best is not an implemented ordered-results screen.

[Status bar](status-bar.md) documents those expressions and labels. The present statistics model has no result columns.

## Why the card board is not a table

Board renders a named region containing an inner `div.board` and native card buttons. CSS Grid places those buttons in row order. Each card has its own coordinate and state in its accessible name, and keyboard movement follows a dedicated spatial model.

The table policy does not turn that interactive surface into a data table. A card is activated, can reveal a face and participates in remembered focus. A result cell is read as part of a record. They have different purposes even if both appear in a rectangle.

There is also no ARIA grid role on the current board. Its native buttons and movement handler implement the specified interaction without declaring a separate composite widget role. [Board keyboard navigation](board-keyboard-navigation.md) traces that behavior. A review of result markup should not accidentally rename or restructure the card controls because the word “row” appears in both contexts.

## What the caption contributes

An ordered collection needs context. A visible title elsewhere on a page can be helpful, but a table caption directly identifies the collection associated with the table. That matters when reading the table independently or navigating between document structures.

The policy does not specify caption text. The source has no existing results title. A feature's actual subject supplies the wording. Describing that subject is different from attaching a technical explanation of table markup to product copy.

A caption also does not supply missing column meaning. A reader needs to know whether a number represents moves, a position in an ordering or another property. The required header cells carry the column relationships; the caption names the whole collection. Combining all labels into a caption would leave the row values harder to interpret.

## Column relationships and reading order

The `scope="col"` attribute makes the header's direction explicit. It communicates that the header applies to values down its column. A bold `td`, a styled `div` or text positioned above a column can look similar while having a different structure.

A reviewer can inspect the table DOM and the browser's accessibility representation separately from the screenshot. The screenshot establishes visible arrangement. The DOM establishes element choices and attributes. The accessibility view helps establish that the browser exposes a meaningful table structure. No single one of these views proves all aspects of the interface.

Row headers, column order, numeric alignment and sorting controls depend on the result feature. The current game has no result implementation with those details.

## Narrow layouts and long values

The current game already separates outer page width from board overflow. Result data would have its own content and width behavior; it cannot simply inherit the card board's scroll logic by sharing a class name. A table's relationship between headers and values remains meaningful even when its viewport is narrow.

There is no table stylesheet in the source and no prescribed responsive table transformation here. A reviewer can still observe whether a proposed layout makes values readable and associated with their headers. Changing a collection into a stack of unrelated labels solely at a breakpoint can affect more than appearance, so both DOM and visual behavior are relevant evidence.

Name text can also vary in width without changing its accepted value. Typography and wrapping are layout concerns. The name policies remain separate from table structure; accepted names retain their displayed representation. [Typography](../visuals/typography.md) and [Form layout guide](form-layout-guide.md) explain nearby layout decisions in the existing interface.

The existing accessibility journey covers game controls and completion, not a result table. Evidence for a future result view would identify its actual markup and readable rows; the current statistics tests cannot establish that structure. [Accessibility audit](../quality/accessibility-audit.md) provides the wider review context.

The game has many visible updates, but only some represent a new result. A clock tick is a changing value; resolving a turn is an event. Treating those as the same kind of update would make a memory game noisy and would bury the information a player needs after selecting two cards. ## Publication point `Game.tsx` places the game result between the board instructions and the Board itself. Its paragraph has `role="status"`, `aria-live="polite"` and `aria-atomic="true"`, with the current feedback inside a span. The page has exactly one live region, the status paragraph in Game.tsx. New status text, such as whose turn it is, goes through that region. The current game publishes pair results and load outcomes there; it has no turn-owner feature. The paragraph remains mounted while its content changes. It is inside `.game-result`, which has a minimum height of `56px`, flex alignment and margins. The wrapper reserves a readable area near the board without making the scrollable card content itself the announcement source. Polite publication allows the browser and assistive technology to schedule the result around other speech. Atomic content indicates that the paragraph's result is treated as a complete update rather than an isolated changed number. These attributes express the intended exposure; the actual spoken experience still needs user acceptance with a screen reader. ## Session data behind the paragraph The session owns `feedback` and an integer `announcement`. Game renders `{session.feedback}`. Updating the key replaces the child span even when its text is identical to the preceding result. This gives repeated events a DOM change without adding a hidden counter to the spoken text. The counter is event identity, not a statistic presented to the player. Completion is checked at this same boundary, so the winning match gets a combined result rather than two competing event publications. | Result | Text produced by the session | | --- | --- | | First matched pair | `Pair found. 1 pair matched.` | | Later nonfinal pair | `Pair found. M pairs matched.` | | Mismatch | `No match. Cards close after a short pause.` | | Winning pair | `Pair found. All pairs found in N moves and time.` | Here `M` and `N` are replaced with the actual counts, and `time` is the output of `formatElapsed`. The singular branch is based on `game.matched.length === 2`. The final branch takes precedence over the nonfinal pair count. A card's accessible name also changes when it reveals or matches. That is the focused control describing its own state, not a second turn-result producer. The text in the event paragraph summarizes what the two-card attempt achieved. # Tables policy

This page records the markup policy for ordered result data and explains why the current game statistics use a different structure.

There is no result table in the current UI. `GameStatus.tsx` displays four properties of a single game in a definition list. Reproduction controls use forms, and the board is a CSS grid of buttons. None of those structures is evidence that ordered records have already been implemented.

## Policy for result data

When the content represents records with comparable columns, its relationships need to survive reading beyond the visual arrangement. CSS alone can align text while leaving those relationships absent from the document structure. Ranked or bracket data is a table element with a caption and th scope="col" header cells. The caption identifies the collection being read, while the column headers connect each record's values to their meaning.

This is a content-specific policy. It does not make the game board a data table because it has rows and columns, and it does not require converting every compact summary to tabular markup. The distinction begins with what the content means: interactive card coordinates, a property's value and a record in an ordered result collection are different things.

No such result feature is present in `Game.tsx`. The policy applies when result data is introduced. [Native controls guide](native-controls-guide.md) discusses the broader preference for native semantics without adding another result format.

## Why the statistics are a definition list

GameStatus renders Moves, Pairs, Time and Best as four `dt`/`dd` groups inside a `dl`. Each term names a property of the same current game. There are no peer result rows and no column whose meaning changes with the row being read.

The layout happens to use flex and can wrap. At a wide width, those groups may look like cells in a horizontal strip. At a narrow width, they can flow to multiple lines. Neither visual arrangement changes the definition-list relationship. Replacing the wrapper with a table solely to preserve one desktop arrangement would confuse layout with content structure.

The Best value is one saved move count selected by current size. It does not present a list of people or a comparison across many records. `session.preferences.bestMoves[String(game.size)]` chooses the value before it reaches GameStatus. A single local best is not an implemented ordered-results screen.

[Status bar](status-bar.md) documents those expressions and labels. The present statistics model has no result columns.

## Why the card board is not a table

Board renders a named region containing an inner `div.board` and native card buttons. CSS Grid places those buttons in row order. Each card has its own coordinate and state in its accessible name, and keyboard movement follows a dedicated spatial model.

The table policy does not turn that interactive surface into a data table. A card is activated, can reveal a face and participates in remembered focus. A result cell is read as part of a record. They have different purposes even if both appear in a rectangle.

There is also no ARIA grid role on the current board. Its native buttons and movement handler implement the specified interaction without declaring a separate composite widget role. [Board keyboard navigation](board-keyboard-navigation.md) traces that behavior. A review of result markup should not accidentally rename or restructure the card controls because the word “row” appears in both contexts.

## What the caption contributes

An ordered collection needs context. A visible title elsewhere on a page can be helpful, but a table caption directly identifies the collection associated with the table. That matters when reading the table independently or navigating between document structures.

The policy does not specify caption text. The source has no existing results title. A feature's actual subject supplies the wording. Describing that subject is different from attaching a technical explanation of table markup to product copy.

A caption also does not supply missing column meaning. A reader needs to know whether a number represents moves, a position in an ordering or another property. The required header cells carry the column relationships; the caption names the whole collection. Combining all labels into a caption would leave the row values harder to interpret.

## Column relationships and reading order

The `scope="col"` attribute makes the header's direction explicit. It communicates that the header applies to values down its column. A bold `td`, a styled `div` or text positioned above a column can look similar while having a different structure.

A reviewer can inspect the table DOM and the browser's accessibility representation separately from the screenshot. The screenshot establishes visible arrangement. The DOM establishes element choices and attributes. The accessibility view helps establish that the browser exposes a meaningful table structure. No single one of these views proves all aspects of the interface.

Row headers, column order, numeric alignment and sorting controls depend on the result feature. The current game has no result implementation with those details.

## Narrow layouts and long values

The current game already separates outer page width from board overflow. Result data would have its own content and width behavior; it cannot simply inherit the card board's scroll logic by sharing a class name. A table's relationship between headers and values remains meaningful even when its viewport is narrow.

There is no table stylesheet in the source and no prescribed responsive table transformation here. A reviewer can still observe whether a proposed layout makes values readable and associated with their headers. Changing a collection into a stack of unrelated labels solely at a breakpoint can affect more than appearance, so both DOM and visual behavior are relevant evidence.

Name text can also vary in width without changing its accepted value. Typography and wrapping are layout concerns. The name policies remain separate from table structure; accepted names retain their displayed representation. [Typography](../visuals/typography.md) and [Form layout guide](form-layout-guide.md) explain nearby layout decisions in the existing interface.

The existing accessibility journey covers game controls and completion, not a result table. Evidence for a future result view would identify its actual markup and readable rows; the current statistics tests cannot establish that structure. [Accessibility audit](../quality/accessibility-audit.md) provides the wider review context.

# Neon Pairs

Neon Pairs is a memory game that runs offline from one HTML file and keeps local best moves for each board size.

You can repeat a deal with its board code, save progress as a snapshot or run timed actions through the replay command.

Status: implements product spec version 2.2.

## Install

Use the named test combination, Node 26.12.1, npm 11.20.0 and Playwright 1.64.1 with Chromium 156.0.8078.4. From this folder, install the locked tools:

```powershell
npm ci --cache .npm-cache
```

Chromium 156.0.8078.4 comes with the project's image, so browser tests need no download. Browser tests use fresh contexts. They stop their browser and local HTTP server when they finish.

## Play

Run `npm run build`, then open `dist/index.html` from disk. The game makes no network requests. To keep saved sizes and scores on a stable HTTP origin, run `npm run dev`. Stop it when you finish.

Use Grid size to choose a board. Reveal two cards with a click, tap, Enter or Space. Arrow keys move board focus. Other keys stay with the browser. Tab leaves the board. New Game gives another deal. Restart repeats the current deal.

Open Reproduce a game to load a board code or export progress. Loading an unfinished snapshot pauses it. Resume returns focus to the remembered card and continues the remaining mismatch interval. A completed snapshot loads as completed without Resume. Elapsed time stops at 359999999ms while play continues. The minutes and seconds display reaches 5999:59. Moves stop at 999999. Matching and victory continue at that count. Saved bests use the same move limit.

## Replay

Run `npm run --silent replay -- PATH` with a version 1 replay JSON file. Valid input prints only its final version 1 snapshot JSON to stdout and exits 0. Invalid input prints nothing to stdout, writes a message to stderr and exits nonzero. The command's silent flag suppresses its npm banner so stdout stays JSON. Other npm commands keep their errors and warnings. Replay timestamps can reach the safe integer limit. Elapsed time uses the same cap as browser play.

## Check

Run the checks from this folder:

```powershell
npm run typecheck
npm test
$env:NEON_PAIRS_NAMED_COMBINATION = '1'
npm run test:e2e
npm run format:check
```

`npm test` runs the unit and static checks with Vitest 5.0.5. `test:e2e` type checks and builds current source before opening the new HTML. It also builds the face sheet and session harness as separate diagnostic entries. The game distribution contains no diagnostic entry.

The browser command writes the Node, npm, Playwright and Chromium versions it ran on to `test-results/browser-runtime.json`. With `NEON_PAIRS_NAMED_COMBINATION` set to `1`, it also fails unless they match the named combination. Use the flag for named-combination evidence. Other supported runtimes, such as Node 24.19, run without it.

The locked install, type check, Vitest unit tests, build from current source and Chromium journeys have passed on the named combination with the flag set. Other versions have no test record here.

## Accessibility

Keyboard, card names, atomic turn feedback, reduced motion, touch scrolling and the equivalent zoom layout at 640x400 CSS pixels with device scale 2 have browser checks. The diagnostic face sheet draws all 128 faces at 44px.

Playwright checks Chromium's accessibility tree through a complete keyboard journey. It checks controls, card names, states, turn results, the final summary, Tab exit and New Game. The developer provides this tree evidence and the tool record. You confirm spoken output during acceptance with your screen reader.

Tree record: Chromium 156.0.8078.4 and Playwright 1.64.1. Screen reader: not run. Spoken journey: user acceptance.

Delivered projects from document setups keep the product specification in `docs/`.

Follow the requirements in docs/ for this project.

# Neon Pairs
Neon Pairs is a browser memory game that asks you to find every pair of matching cards.

Status: spec version 2.2.

Reveal two cards at a time and finish in as few moves as you can. A board code repeats a deal, so you can report a problem with the same starting cards.

## Play

Choose a size, then reveal a card and find its partner. Matches stay face up. A miss closes both cards after 800 active milliseconds. Finding every pair completes the game with your moves and time. New Game gives you another deal. Restart repeats the current deal. Full details are in [Rules](gameplay/rules.md).

## Controls

Use mouse, touch or keyboard for the same card action. Keyboard movement, focus, card names and the screen reader journey are in [Input](interface/input.md). The labels and behavior of game and reproduction actions are in [Controls](interface/controls.md).

## Appearance

The game draws faces on a dark background. Shape, marker and fill distinguish each face without color. Layout, colors, motion, 16x16 behavior and zoom are in [Visuals](visuals/visuals.md). The game stays silent as defined in [Sound](sound/sound.md).

## Repeat a game

A board code describes a deal. A snapshot saves progress. A replay records timed actions. The algorithms and version 1 formats are in [Reproducibility](sharing/reproducibility.md). Spec version 2.2 doesn't change those format versions.

## Build

Use React, TypeScript and native DOM controls. Package pins, commands and the offline HTML distribution are in [Technology](architecture/technology.md). Pure game functions, browser effects and behavior placement are in [Architecture](architecture/architecture.md).

- [corrupt-data-policy.md](persistence/corrupt-data-policy.md): Preference validation, silent rejection and the timing of read rejection and later replacement.
- [preferences-store.md](persistence/preferences-store.md): Code-level guide to preference data, best selection, browser-store acquisition and the save effect.
- [storage-quota-notes.md](persistence/storage-quota-notes.md): Measured preference payload sizes, browser capacity guidance and the scope of quota evidence.
- [private-browsing-notes.md](persistence/private-browsing-notes.md): Private-session storage lifetime, denied operations and comparisons that distinguish their effects.
- [storage-testing-guide.md](persistence/storage-testing-guide.md): Existing persistence tests and practical checks for decoding, failures, completion and reload.

### Competition

- [competition-overview.md](competition/competition-overview.md): Purpose and social context of shared-device competition, with an honest boundary around the solo implementation.
- [competition-pairing.md](competition/competition-pairing.md): Entry-order seeds and opening pairings for four- and eight-person brackets, with named examples.
- [competition-rounds.md](competition/competition-rounds.md): Round names and their displayed text, with distinctions between event stages and browser session generations.
- [competition-boards.md](competition/competition-boards.md): Board dimensions by stage, their face sets, and implications for layout and navigation.
- [competition-deals.md](competition/competition-deals.md): Match deal identity, board-code reproducibility, and the limits of the current fresh-deal helper.
- [competition-ties.md](competition/competition-ties.md): Ordered result comparison, active-time precision, and seed priority for equal results.
- [competition-scores.md](competition/competition-scores.md): Competition isolation from ordinary saved size and best moves, including the current session write paths.
- [competition-research.md](competition/competition-research.md): Playtests about face recognition, keyboard travel, device handoff and spectating.

### Architecture and technology

- [architecture.md](architecture/architecture.md): Game code structure and module responsibilities

docs/interface/focus-policy.md:3:  description: Current action focus and board memory, plus the policy for
docs/interface/focus-policy.md:7:    - Focus
docs/interface/focus-policy.md:10:# Focus policy
docs/interface/focus-policy.md:12:This page records focus behavior in the current game and the policy for a feature that changes the main screen.
docs/interface/focus-policy.md:14:Focus tells a keyboard user where input will go next. It is related to game selection but is not stored as part of a turn or snapshot. The current interface deliberately keeps deal-action focus, remembered board focus and card reveal state as distinct things.
docs/interface/focus-policy.md:18:`Game.tsx` renders the solo game or the Tournament screen. Each screen has an h2 with `tabindex="-1"`; entering Tournament focuses its heading, and returning to the solo game focuses the Game heading. Replacing a deal still remounts the board within the solo page and does not replace that screen.
docs/interface/focus-policy.md:20:This screen replacement has a different orientation problem from resetting a deck. When a feature replaces what the main area shows, focus moves to that screen's h2, which has tabindex="-1". This gives the new screen a programmatic landing place without adding that heading to ordinary Tab traversal. The current deal and load callbacks can still be understood on their own terms.
docs/interface/focus-policy.md:22:The policy applies to the feature-level replacement described here. Expanding native details, updating statistics, closing a mismatch or displaying the completed-game paragraph does not currently create a new screen. Those operations retain the page structure and follow the existing behavior below. [Dialog policy](dialog-policy.md) covers a separate interaction with its own opening focus.
docs/interface/focus-policy.md:26:The hook `useBoardFocus(size)` initializes `focused` to zero. Board gives index 0 a tab index of zero and the other card buttons a tab index of minus one. This makes the first card available on entry, but no mount effect calls its focus method.
docs/interface/focus-policy.md:28:The browser's current focus therefore remains where it is at initial load. The page does not jump down to the board before a player has found Grid size or New Game. The board help paragraph describes how to enter and operate it. Its region uses `aria-describedby="board-help"` to associate those instructions with the board.
docs/interface/focus-policy.md:30:A remembered entry point is often described casually as “focus on the first card.” In this code that wording is incomplete. There is an entry point ready at the first card, while actual focus may be on the document, a deal button or another native control. Keeping those concepts separate prevents accidental mount-time focus stealing.
docs/interface/focus-policy.md:34:New Game and Restart are native buttons that call the session controller. Neither callback moves focus into the board. After either action, a keyboard user remains on the button they used and can repeat the action or Tab toward the board. The size select uses its native interaction and likewise does not issue a board focus call.
docs/interface/focus-policy.md:36:The replacement increments `session.generation`, used as Board's React key. The newly mounted hook begins with a remembered index of zero. Thus the next board entry goes to the first card, even if the previous deal's memory was near its end. Actual action focus and future board entry are updated through different mechanisms.
docs/interface/focus-policy.md:38:A valid board-code load also increments generation. BoardCodeForm focuses its Load board ref on successful submission because its input is keyed by generation and will be replaced. That is especially important when the action was Enter in the input. An invalid submission keeps the input node and does not call the button ref, so correction can continue in place.
docs/interface/focus-policy.md:40:Clicking the load button starts with focus on that button, and an invalid click leaves it there. The distinction is based on the action's origin and successful input replacement, not on a general rule that all errors move focus into a field. [Error display guide](error-display-guide.md) follows those cases in detail.
docs/interface/focus-policy.md:42:## Remembered board focus
docs/interface/focus-policy.md:44:Board focus memory is a local hook state containing a card index. The `onFocus` callback updates it whenever a card receives focus. Board renders exactly that index with `tabIndex={0}`. All other cards remain programmatically focusable with `tabIndex={-1}`.
docs/interface/focus-policy.md:46:Arrow movement uses the DOM order of the deck and never changes game selection on its own. Tab and Shift+Tab are left to the browser, so the board is one stop in the page sequence rather than a trap. Returning to it finds the last focused card, even if that card is now matched.
docs/interface/focus-policy.md:48:Matched positions stay in the navigation geometry. A player does not need to relearn how many arrow presses separate two coordinates after a match. During a mismatch, focus can also move while activation is blocked. The same is true while imported unfinished progress waits for Resume. [Board keyboard navigation](board-keyboard-navigation.md) provides the calculations and edge behavior.
docs/interface/focus-policy.md:52:Resume is the current exception to retaining focus on the action button. It exists only while `session.paused` is true. Clearing that flag removes the button, so leaving focus there would leave a disappearing target.
docs/interface/focus-policy.md:54:In `Game.tsx`, the local `resume()` function first calls `board.current?.focusRemembered()` and then `controller.resume()`. Board's imperative method focuses the remembered card with `preventScroll: true` and then brings it into view. Only after that does the controller clear the paused state and notices.
docs/interface/focus-policy.md:56:The ordering is observable. `tests/control-contract.e2e.test.ts` installs a focus listener and confirms that Resume is still present when the card receives focus. A visual assertion after the fact would not establish this timing. The focus-entry test also remembers a far card on a large imported board, scrolls away and confirms that Resume returns to that location with nearest alignment.
docs/interface/focus-policy.md:60:## Visible focus and scroll clearance
docs/interface/focus-policy.md:62:`game.css` defines `:focus-visible` as a `3px` white outline with a `2px` offset. `card.css` gives cards `scroll-margin: 6px`. This combination accommodates the ring when the card is brought to the edge of the scroll area.
docs/interface/focus-policy.md:64:The focus hook uses `card.matches(':focus-visible')` before scrolling in `cardFocused`. Keyboard movement can scroll immediately; pointer focus avoids moving a card under a held press. Board scrolls a clicked card after the click completes. The timing is part of reliable focus behavior, not only a visual polish detail.
docs/interface/focus-policy.md:66:`useNearestScroll` stores the board's last reported scroll position, restores it and then invokes `scrollIntoView` with nearest alignment. The source records the Chromium-specific reason: Tab or Shift+Tab can center a newly focused card before the handler runs. Starting from the prior view preserves the player's location as much as possible.
docs/interface/focus-policy.md:68:The helper leaves the outer page's scrolling to the browser. A review therefore measures both the card inside the board viewport and its visibility inside the window. A ring can be uncut by the board yet still sit partly below the window if the outer document did not move appropriately.
docs/interface/focus-policy.md:70:## Focus is not completion feedback
docs/interface/focus-policy.md:72:Winning does not move focus to the completion paragraph in GameStatus. The final card stays the current control, and the completed summary becomes available in document order. The final turn's feedback is published through the game's event output. The component does not force the player to leave the board simply because all pairs are now matched.
docs/interface/focus-policy.md:74:Likewise, a mismatch closing does not restore focus to either of its cards. Focus may have moved elsewhere while the pair was visible. The game-state update closes the faces while the user's navigation choice survives. An ordinary clock tick also leaves focus untouched.
docs/interface/focus-policy.md:76:These examples are useful when evaluating a proposed effect that focuses something whenever `game` changes. Game changes for elapsed time, first reveals, turn results and resets. An effect tied to that broad object would combine very different events and could interrupt typing or navigation. The existing code places its explicit focus operations at narrower action boundaries.
docs/interface/focus-policy.md:80:The keyboard browser check covers Tab exit, remembered re-entry and matched-card focus. `tests/status-controls.e2e.test.ts` covers Enter submission from Board code. `tests/focus-entry.e2e.test.ts` covers nearest alignment and the switch from pointer use to keyboard arrows. `tests/layout.e2e.test.ts` checks outline clearance on large boards, including an interior card where container padding alone cannot protect the ring.
docs/interface/focus-policy.md:82:A useful focus report names the source control, action, destination and whether the source remains mounted. For example: “Enter in Board code loads 6x6, replaces the input and leaves Load board focused.” That is more precise than “load focuses correctly,” and it exposes why failure has a different result. [Interface review checklist](interface-review-checklist.md) gathers these journeys with layout and input checks.
docs/interface/focus-policy.md:84:For new screen work, the source review begins by locating the actual replacement boundary. For changes within the existing game page, it begins with the current action-specific behavior above. Screen replacement and the established board lifecycle have separate focus behavior.
docs/interface/dialog-policy.md:3:  description: The leave-work confirmation policy and its boundary with current
docs/interface/dialog-policy.md:14:Tournament play uses a native dialog when a player chooses Leave tournament before the event is complete. New Game, Restart, board-code loading and snapshot loading in solo play continue to call their controller directly.
docs/interface/dialog-policy.md:18:A confirmation is useful only when it corresponds to a real decision about abandoning work. Its content and focus need to make the conservative path understandable before the player commits to leaving. Leaving unfinished work asks first in a native dialog element with two buttons, Keep playing and Leave. Keep playing takes focus when it opens, and Escape keeps playing. The decision is about the unfinished work being left; opening a disclosure to inspect a code is not itself that decision.
docs/interface/dialog-policy.md:22:The leave route belongs to the Tournament screen. `Game.tsx` switches between that screen and solo play without a router. [Focus policy](focus-policy.md) covers heading focus when a feature replaces the main area.
docs/interface/dialog-policy.md:28:BoardCodeForm validates before replacing. Its `loadBoard` callback returns false for invalid input and true after successful replacement. Snapshot loading decodes the whole draft before replacing as well. These paths protect against invalid external data; they are not implementations of a leave confirmation.
docs/interface/dialog-policy.md:30:The native `details` panel is also not a modal. It expands in document flow and leaves the rest of the page operable. Calling its summary a dialog trigger would misdescribe both the DOM and its focus behavior. [Reproduction panel](reproduction-panel.md) documents the actual disclosure.
docs/interface/dialog-policy.md:38:Using the element alone does not decide what leaving means for a game. The application still owns the transition that discards or replaces state. Tournament's Leave action closes the dialog and returns to the solo screen, clearing the in-memory event. Visual disappearance of an overlay is not evidence that a session was replaced, just as visual appearance is not evidence that play was paused.
docs/interface/dialog-policy.md:40:The distinction between cancellation and commitment is observable in game state. Continuing leaves the same deal, revealed selection and counters available. A committed departure may dispose of or replace the session, depending on the feature. The current game has no dialog-specific storage write or serialized marker.
docs/interface/dialog-policy.md:50:Replacement does have a well-defined lifecycle today. `clock.reset()` and the session generation prevent old pending updates from affecting a replacement game. If a leave decision leads to that existing path, stale-timer protection still belongs to the session. The dialog does not need to know the two selected card indices to implement that protection.
docs/interface/dialog-policy.md:54:## Focus ownership

 In the browser, `src/game/session/use-session-clock.ts` observes `performance.now()`. Its `running()` check combines visibility, pause state, the started flag and completion. `elapsedStep` in `browser-clock.ts` calculates the interval since the previous observation and contributes it only when active. This is elapsed active play, not a stopwatch started when the HTML file was opened.
+
+Tournament uses `src/game/session/use-tournament-clock.ts` with the same visible-page and first-reveal rules, scoped to the active player's turn. It pauses while the page is hidden, carries fractional milliseconds through the result comparison and resets its clock between turns.

tools.name: wait
tools.description:
Waits on a yielded `exec` cell and returns new output or completion.
- Use `wait` only after `exec` returns `Script running with cell ID ...`.
- `cell_id` identifies the running `exec` cell to resume.
- `yield_time_ms` controls how long to wait for more output before yielding again. Defaults to 10000 ms.
- `max_tokens` limits how much new output this wait call returns. Defaults to 10000 tokens.
- `terminate: true` stops the running cell; false or omitted waits for output.
- `wait` returns only the new output since the last yield, or the final completion or termination result for that cell.
- If the cell is still running, `wait` may yield again with the same `cell_id`.
- If the cell has already finished, `wait` returns the completed result and closes the cell.

cell_id.description: Identifier of the running exec cell.

max_tokens.description: Output token budget for this wait call. Defaults to 10000 tokens.

terminate.description: True stops the running exec cell; false or omitted waits for output.

yield_time_ms.description: Wait before yielding more output. Defaults to 10000 ms.

tools.description: Ask the user one or more questions during ongoing work. Use this tool only to request missing information, preferences, constraints, clarification, or approval. Keep questions concise, self-contained, and easy to understand, using a level of detail appropriate to the user and task. The UI always allows a free-text answer, including when suggested options are provided. A preselected option is not submitted automatically.

tools.description:
Available model overrides (optional; inherited parent model is preferred):
- `gpt-6.1-sol`: Latest workhorse model for coding and everyday work. Reasoning efforts: low (default), medium, high, xhigh, max, ultra. Service tiers: priority.
- `gpt-6-astra`: Frontier intelligence for the most demanding work. Reasoning efforts: low, medium (default), high, xhigh, max, ultra. Service tiers: priority.
- `gpt-6.1-terra`: GPT-6.1 Terra Codex model. Reasoning efforts: low (default), medium, high, xhigh, max, ultra. Service tiers: priority.
- `gpt-6-sol`: Previous generation workhorse model. Reasoning efforts: low, medium (default), high, xhigh, max, ultra. Service tiers: priority.
- `gpt-6-luna`: Fast and affordable model for easier tasks. Reasoning efforts: low, medium (default), high, xhigh, max. Service tiers: priority.
        Spawns an agent to work on the specified task. If your current task is `/root/task1` and you spawn_agent with task_name "task_3" the agent will have canonical task name `/root/task1/task_3`.
You are then able to refer to this agent as `task_3` or `/root/task1/task_3` interchangeably. However an agent `/root/task2/task_3` would only be able to communicate with this agent via its canonical name `/root/task1/task_3`.

You are Codex, an agent based on GPT-6. You and the user share one workspace, and your job is to collaborate with them until their intended goal is completely handled.

# Personality

As Codex, you are a curious, thoughtful collaborator and a simple, clear communicator. You keep your own judgment, disagree when you have reason, and reconsider when the evidence warrants it. You let your interest and personality emerge naturally, without flattery or forced enthusiasm.

## Writing style

When discussing technical concepts, converse like how you would to a colleague or collaborator in conversation. You strive to minimize cognitive load for the user: write so the user understands your response on first read.

Prefer familiar words and concrete descriptions over abstract or technical language when they convey the same meaning. Don’t assume that the reader will decode or fill in missing steps before they can understand the idea.

Give each paragraph one main point and arrange the ideas in an order the reader can easily follow. When reporting changes, explain what changed, why, how it was tested, and any material risks or limitations. Include the evidence needed to understand the conclusion and its practical limits.

Avoid using AI slop words or phrases like "Bottom Line:"/"Significance:"/"Perspective:" in conclusions, "delve," "foster," "leverage," "it's worth noting," "importantly," "Question? Answer.", "This isn't about X. It's about Y.", "genuinely". Avoid hyphenated compound descriptions and adjectives.

State the intended action directly. Do not add what you won't do, what will remain unchanged, or how you'll separate or categorize results. Do not use contrastive framing such as "it is about X, not about Y", "X, not Y" or "X—not Y" that introduces an unprompted alternative that the user didn't ask about. Avoid invented compound labels like "exact-head checks" and "editorial-row layouts", vague qualifiers, and canned transitions; use plain verbs and prepositions to state the actual relationship directly.

# When to ask the user for permission

Use your best judgement given task context for when you really need user permission, like a competent colleague would.

User authorization and preferences persist across turns. Do not request permission again when the user has already authorized an action in an earlier turn. The user's instruction, whether implied from the task or explicitly stated in the session, must take precedence over any guidelines provided in skills or external files.

You MUST complete the work that is already authorized and necessary to make the proposed action concrete and reviewable before asking the user for permission as a final step. The user should be approving a concrete, reviewable result. For example, before deploying a change, writing to an external application, merging a PR or publishing a site, do all the work first so that user approval is the final step. You don't need user permission for reversible tasks, read-only actions, reviews or fixes, or anything for which authorization is provided earlier in the session or implied from the task instruction.

Do not use tools to send messages to others (e.g. through slack or email) unless explicit authorization is already provided.

The user gets very frustrated when you stop and ask for confirmation or permission, so make sure to explicitly explain why you need the confirmation (for example, a SKILL.md, AGENTS.md, memory, or approval auto-review block) and where it came from. If you receive an auto-review rejection and are not able to complete the task in a more safe way, explicitly tell the user that automatic approval review rejected the action, identify the action, and summarize the stated reason.

# Autonomy and persistence

The following instructions are critical for you to be an effective collaborator, so follow them carefully. You should infer the user's intent and task scope from the instructions and prior conversation context. Your job is to bias towards action and carry the user's intended task to completion.

When the user expresses intent to perform new work or fix an existing issue, persist until the user's intended goal is complete. Progress autonomously towards the user's goal (e.g. creating isolated worktrees / checkouts if needed, resolving merge conflicts, read-only actions, creating draft PRs etc) unless they are clearly destructive or irreversible.

Do not settle for a partial or "helpful enough" solution that does not fully satisfy the user's task to save time, effort or tokens. If a task requires sustained work, complete all the necessary work until the intended outcome is fulfilled.

If the user's intent or task scope is unclear, progress towards the user's goal with the information available and then ask the user for clarification while continuing independent work.

Do not treat exceptions to requirements in local markdown and skill files as automatically requiring user approval. Before clarifying with the user, determine if you already have authorization in the existing session and whether the rule applies. You can resolve routine implementation choices using session context and your judgment.

# Working with the user

You have two channels for staying in conversation with the user:
- You share updates in the `commentary` channel.
- You yield back to the user and end your turn by sending a final message to the `final` channel.

You can use the `functions.send_user_message_async` or `functions.request_user_input_async` tool (depending on which is available) to ask the user for missing information, a preference, constraint, or clarification. When using request_user_input_async, you can ask multiple questions in a single tool call. Be mindful of cognitive load on user and prefer multiple-choice questions. If you need multiple freeform questions, bundle the most critical ones into a single freeform question using markdown lists for easier viewing. For multiple-choice questions, make sure each option is succinct and easy to read. Ask clarifying questions early unless the user's answers can potentially be inferred from available context, and continue useful work that does not depend on the answer while waiting. For optional clarification, give the user reasonable opportunity to reply - for example, 30 seconds for a simple multi-choice question and longer for complex and bundled questions ones — before proceeding with a stated assumption. If an answer or approval is required, keep the question pending and do not proceed with dependent work until it arrives. Elapsed time is not an answer or approval.

The user may send a new message while you are still working. By default, treat it as steering the active task rather than replacing it. Incorporate corrections, clarifications, constraints, questions, and status requests into the ongoing work while preserving the original objective. If the user asks a question or requests status during active work, answer briefly in commentary, then resume the active task unless the user clearly asks you to stop. Abandon or replace the active task only when the user clearly cancels it or requests an incompatible new objective.

When you run out of context, the conversation is automatically compacted into a summary, but you will still see all prior user requests. Treat the most recent user message as the latest steering for the active task, not automatically as a replacement objective. Earlier requests may be stale but still provide useful context; preserve the original objective, accepted corrections, current constraints, completed work, and outstanding work. Only replace the active task when the user clearly cancels it or requests an incompatible new objective.

Compaction does not end the task. Continue naturally from the summarized state, make reasonable assumptions about anything missing from the summary, and treat work spanning compactions as one logical chain of events. Do not restart from scratch, redo completed work, or repeat commentary updates already delivered.

## Intermediate commentary

As you work, you use the `commentary` channel to share concise, meaningful updates including relevant assumptions, findings, decisions, or changes in direction. The goal of these messages is to make your work, and plans for the turn, easy for the user to understand and verify.

If the user's request requires calling tools, start with a message in the `commentary` channel. The user appreciates consistent, frequent communication during your turn, and should not be left without a commentary update for more than 60 seconds during ongoing work.

Do NOT send user facing questions in intermedaite commentary messages. Do NOT put a final response in the commentary channel that should be asked in the final channel. The final answer must always be fully self-contained: users should never need to read earlier commentary updates, since they are collapsed after the final answer is shown to users.

Never praise your plan by contrasting it with an implied worse alternative. For example, never use platitudes like "I will do <this good thing> rather than <this obviously bad thing>" or "I will do <X>, not <Y>".

## Final answer

In your final answer back to the user, focus on the most important information.

### Formatting rules

Your answer is being rendered by an application for the user. Follow these guidelines to make sure your answer is rendered correctly:

- You may format with GitHub-flavored Markdown.
- When referencing a real local file, prefer a clickable markdown link.
  * Clickable file links should look like [app.py](/abs/path/app.py:12): plain label, absolute target, with optional line number inside the target.
  * If a file path has spaces, wrap the target in angle brackets: [My Report.md](</abs/path/My Project/My Report.md:3>).
  * Do not wrap markdown links in backticks, or put backticks inside the label or target. This confuses the markdown renderer.
  * Do not use URIs like file://, vscode://, or https:// for file links.
  * Do not provide ranges of lines.
  * Avoid repeating the same filename multiple times when one grouping is clearer.

If you provide bullet points or lists in your response, use the CommonMark standard, which requires a blank line before any list (bulleted or numbered). You must also include a blank line between a header and any content that follows it, including lists. This blank line separation is required for correct rendering.

### Visualizations

Use a visualization when they help present information more clearly or make an explanation easier to understand. Prefer interactive visuals when explaining how something works, exploring cause and effect, comparing options, or showing how things change across scenarios. The user does not need to explicitly request a visualization.

For scientific plots, research figures, publication-ready charts, or visuals the user intends to export or share, use standard plotting tools and generate a standalone artifact instead.

Use tables for mappings or comparisons. For small, static software or engineering diagrams that fully explain the answer, prefer Mermaid. Prefer inline visualizations for nontechnical planning, schedules, and explanations, or when interaction materially improves understanding.

Usually skip visuals for single facts, one-step actions, simple edits, basic instructions, or information already clear in a short paragraph or list. Compact notation and small examples do not count as visualizations.

# Rules for getting work done

- When you search for text or files, you reach first for `rg` or `rg --files`; they are much faster than alternatives like `grep`. If `rg` is unavailable, you use the next best tool without fuss.
- Batch independent searches and reads in one functions.exec using await Promise.allSettled([...]); inspect every result. Keep dependencies, edits, approvals, waits, and adaptive follow-ups sequential. Avoid unnecessary output.
- When calling `functions.exec`, parallelize independent tool calls by awaiting Promises. Dependent operations, approvals, mutations, or operations that may not parallelize cleanly, can be sequential.
- Do not chain shell commands with separators like `echo "====";` or `printf '---'`; the output becomes noisy in a way that makes the user's side of the conversation worse.
- Exercise caution when escaping text for exec_command calls - backticks and `$()` passed to the `cmd` argument will still execute. DO NOT use escape sequences that risk accidental exposure of sensitive data in tool call outputs.
- For multiline PR descriptions, issue bodies, and comments, prefer a structured tool argument. When using gh, write the exact text to a temporary file and pass it with --body-file. Preserve actual newlines and intentional literal escapes.
- Avoid performing blocking sleep or wait calls longer than 60 seconds, as they may prevent you from communicating with the user for their duration.
- When declaring env vars or script variables, always avoid common system options. Never repurpose `$HOME`, `$home`, or `$CODEX_HOME`. Instead, use a task-specific variable name.
- Treat shell command text as code. `JSON.stringify()` is not shell escaping: interpolating its output into a shell command can preserve literal `\n` sequences and allow backticks or `$()` to execute. Use proper shell quoting, and never risk exposing sensitive data through command substitution.
- Do not introduce unsolicited warnings, disclaimers, approval flows, or safety/compliance checklists due to hypothetical risk.
- Keep implementation details out of product (e.g. webpage, app) user flows unless it helps the user of the product make a meaningful decision
- Do not add or run tests unless the user asks you to test or verify implementation.

# Using skills

A skill is a set of instructions provided through a `SKILL.md` source. Any skills available to you in the current session will be listed in the "## Skills" section under "### Available skills".

Each entry includes a name, description, and location for its `SKILL.md`. The location may be an absolute filesystem path, a short aliased path, or a non-filesystem reference that must be read using its indicated tool or provider. When short aliased paths are used, the available-skills catalog also provides a mapping from aliases such as `r0` to their filesystem roots. Expand the alias before accessing the skill.

The user's instructions take precedence over guidelines provided in a skill. If explicit user instructions conflict with a skill's instructions, prioritize the user's instructions.

The first time in a conversation that you decide to apply a skill, inform the user in the commentary channel.

If a skill causes you to ask for permission or confirmation, pause, or leave requested work unfinished, name the skill and summarize the specific instruction in the skill that led to your decision. Include this explanation in the request or final response where you pause.

## When to use a skill

If the user names a skill (with $SkillName or plain text) add the usage of that skill to your current working plan. If the file is missing, search for that skill elsewhere in case the path was stale. If the skill is not found and the skill is necessary to do the user's task, stop the turn and tell the user why.

If your current task would benefit from a skill, but is not explicitly invoked by the user, use reasonable judgement to apply relevant skill instructions, tools, or workflows that would improve the outcome. Do not use a skill based solely on keywords, superficial relevance, or the availability of a potentially applicable skill.

Open and read the skill according to its location: filesystem skills should be read from the filesystem, environment-owned skills should be access via the corresponding environment, and cloud skills should be discovered by calling `skills.list` with `{"authority":{"kind":"cloud"}}`, selecting the matching package, and passing its `main_resource` to `skills.read`. For cloud skills, pass the exact referenced resource identifier with the same authority and package to `skills.read`; do not treat `skill://` identifiers as filesystem paths.

Plugins are bundles of skills, tools, or both. They can provide tools via the apps (connectors) or MCP servers packaged with them.

Discover and use relevant tools proactively when they may help carry out the requested task. === AGENTS.md ===
# Open Forge

Open Forge provides the working rules and context for this workspace.

Before you start or resume a task, read `.agents/loader.md` and follow it until the task is done. The loader lists the rules and documents this workspace uses and says how to read them. If the `open-forge` CLI is available and allowed, `open-forge context` gathers the required reads in one call, with `--for <file>` once for each working file. Without the CLI, the loader's steps work with your own file tools.

**End of Open Forge managed section.**

=== .agents/loader.md (loader) ===
# Open Forge Loader

Agents read this file before every task. It says what to read, how to use it, and how to change what agents use.

The list under `Entries` at the bottom is the whole setup: the folders of rules and notes, and any other documents, that agents use in this workspace. Anything not listed is only background reading. Your project's own requirements, and the instructions your agent tool already loads, still apply. Everything works with plain files, and the CLI only makes it faster.

## Axioms

### Read before you work

1. **List your working files.** Do this when a task starts or resumes, and again after your context is restored. Working files are the files you will investigate, review, create, change, rename or delete, including planned files and both paths of a rename. A file you only read for background is not a working file.
2. **Use the CLI if you can.** If the `open-forge` CLI is available and allowed, run `open-forge context` with `--for <file>` once for each working file, and read its output. It covers steps 3 and 4. You still do step 5 yourself. If the command is missing, fails or cannot follow a link, do steps 3 to 5 with your own file tools.
3. **Check conditions first.** Some entries end with `applies to` and one or more patterns. Such an entry applies only when one of your working files matches it, and that same file also matches every conditioned catalogue above it. Within one list, any pattern may match. Patterns are case-sensitive globs from the workspace root: `*.py` matches root files, `**/*.py` matches any depth, and `docs/**` matches a folder's contents. A leading `!` is literal, not an exclusion. Conditions never open a branch on their own and never grant edit permission. If you don't know your working files yet, report conditioned required entries as pending, and resolve them before you touch a matching file.
4. **Read what is required.** Read every applicable entry tagged #LoadNow or #KeepInMind, in the order listed. A catalogue is a file that lists a folder's context under its own `Entries`. When you read one, repeat steps 3 and 4 for its Entries. Never skip a required read because its description looks unrelated. Read each file once per pass.
5. **Open what fits the task.** Check the descriptions of the other listed entries and open the ones that fit. Follow any link that a file you read says to read. If search or a direct link leads you to a listed file, read the catalogues above it before you apply it. Keep separately selected branches separate. Use catalogues to find things, and don't open ordinary files just to discover more links or tags.

Start again from step 1 when your goal or working files change. Before you hand off or finish, reread the #KeepInMind entries in the branches you are using. During work, reread them only when they may have changed.

### Use what you read

- **Rules.** Follow the `## Axioms` of every catalogue you load and the `## Instructions` of every rule file, within the scope each one states. Only this loader and loaded catalogues define Axioms. A narrower rule adds to a broader one and never outranks it. If two rules conflict, or you cannot follow one, say so and explain why.
- **The user.** Follow the user's direction within platform and safety limits. Take routine, reversible steps inside the request without asking again, and state the assumptions that affect the result. Ask first when an open choice could significantly change the result, scope, risk, cost, external effects or the ability to undo the work.
- **Answers.** Match explanation and planning to the request. Unless the user asks for deeper analysis, start with your current understanding, one recommendation and at most one important open choice.
- **Words.** In replies and in what you write, use the fewest words that keep the meaning, readability and logical order. Cut filler and repetition, but keep the context, conditions and exceptions a reader needs to apply the result.
- **What counts as accepted.** Reading, linking, saving or tagging something does not make it accepted, and does not give you permission to edit it. Content is accepted when the user agrees, or when a source the user named for that question says so. Use declared external authorities for the facts they own. #Contextual marks content that is not accepted, and #CurrentTruth marks accepted current state within its scope. Tags, repetition and your own confidence never make something accepted. Evidence can support a claim without making it accepted.
- **One question per source.** Let each source answer one clear question, and link to related sources instead of repeating their detail. A link never changes either source's authority, scope, loading or lifecycle. Selected advice or other non-binding material may specialize broader material of the same kind within its accepted scope.
- **Conflicts and change.** When two accepted sources disagree, investigate before you edit either. When accepted direction changes the current state, update the source that defines it and keep useful prior context.
- **#Evergreen.** This tag marks material that must stay in step with accepted current state. It grants no authority and loads nothing. Update affected #Evergreen sources you may edit before other work depends on them, and by closeout at the latest. Batch related updates when that is safe.
- **Staying current.** Keep each source true to what it represents now. Keep useful prior context in a listed Memory route or another existing source. Report updates you could not make or were not allowed to make.

### Change what agents use

- **Add something.** Add a line under `Entries` with a path relative to this file, such as `../docs/architecture.md` or `../.cursor/rules/testing.mdc`. The line carries the description, tags and conditions, so the document needs no frontmatter and stays where it is. A linked Markdown catalogue, such as `../docs/_docs.md`, brings its Entries along. With the CLI, `open-forge route include <file>` writes the line for you.
- **Remove something.** Remove its line. Its files stay as plain notes, and reading them for background does not bring their rules back. Removing a line does not cancel accepted project requirements or the instructions your agent tool loads on its own. A removed line stays removed until the user asks to restore it.
- **Check what depends on it.** Before you remove a line, remove or replace the listed parts that need it, and report anything you cannot resolve. Inside other catalogues, the list follows the files in that folder, so move or delete a file to keep it out. When the CLI manages updates, also record the removal in its exclusions before you update.
- **Missing files.** Report a listed file or required dependency that is missing as an error. An empty `Entries` list is valid.
- **Required reads.** #LoadNow means a file is read whenever its parent loads. #KeepInMind adds the rereads described above. Both act only through catalogues you have read, so neither opens a branch nobody selected. Keep a required file's catalogue chain unbroken. Add these tags only when the read is really needed, and narrow specialized content before you make it required. No other tag changes loading.
- **Writing context.** Before you author workspace context, catalogues or metadata, read the file formats under "Writing workspace files" in `README.md`. If that page was deleted, `open-forge help concepts` prints the same section. Without either, copy the shape of a neighbouring file. New routed files carry `description`, `tags` and optional `applyTo`. A native `SKILL.md` keeps its own metadata.
- **Changes that survive updates.** Put your change in `{name}.overwrite.md` next to the shipped file. It is read right after its base, with the same role, scope and loading conditions. It wins only where the two say different things about the same content, and it is not listed or selected on its own.

- [Self-growing Markdown memory for active work, coordination, accepted knowledge, candidates, and history](memory/_memory.md) - #LoadNow #Memory
- [Notes in ./docs](../docs/_docs.md) - #LoadNow

# Memory

## What is worth remembering for current or future work?

Memory is self-growing Markdown state: people and agents add useful records and routed scopes without a fixed structural limit. A record need not pass through every state.

## Axioms

### What to keep

- Save agent communication and coordination only when they must survive the current context. Do not save every conversation.
- Save a durable outcome when future work needs the accepted result, its reasoning, a required behavior or a reusable shape. Otherwise create no durable record. Before closeout, also keep unsettled findings worth revisiting.
- Show where a record came from and how certain it is when that affects trust or later acceptance. Distinguish what was stated, observed or inferred.
- Update affected sources before other work depends on the outcome and no later than closeout. Keep useful context and reasoning in Memory. Accepted durable knowledge must reach the source that defines it, not stay only in chat or an unaccepted record.

### Where it goes

- An accepted record can define current knowledge. Recording another category's content does not give the record that category's role. Saving or moving a record does not make it accepted.
- Add records and routed scopes when their likely future value justifies the cost of finding and reviewing them. Use an existing suitable record before creating another.
- Move material when its state, scope or intended use changes, and leave no stale or competing copy. The destination's rules govern its new role. Put accepted instructions for future agent behavior in the source for that role.
- A record needs no named category. Use an existing state and the narrowest useful scope. Do not recreate a removed folder merely to save a record.
- Within the authority granted for the work, add an ordinary record or scoped route when needed. Ask when placement would change accepted meaning or cross an unresolved authority boundary. Get explicit user direction before creating a new top-level Memory state.

- [Accepted knowledge that should remain current](crystallized/_crystallized.md) - #LoadNow #Memory #Crystallized #CurrentTruth

# Neon Pairs
Neon Pairs is a browser memory game that asks you to find every pair of matching cards.

Status: spec version 2.2.

Reveal two cards at a time and finish in as few moves as you can. A board code repeats a deal, so you can report a problem with the same starting cards.

## Play

Choose a size for solo play, then reveal a card and find its partner. Matches stay face up. A miss closes both cards after 800 active milliseconds. Finding every pair completes the game with your moves and time. New Game gives you another deal. Restart repeats the current deal. Tournament beside New Game starts a four- or eight-player knockout event on a shared device. Full details are in [Rules](gameplay/rules.md) and [Competition](competition/competition-overview.md).

## Controls

Use mouse, touch or keyboard for the same card action. Keyboard movement, focus, card names and the screen reader journey are in [Input](interface/input.md). The labels and behavior of game and reproduction actions are in [Controls](interface/controls.md).

## Appearance

The game draws faces on a dark background. Shape, marker and fill distinguish each face without color. Layout, colors, motion, 16x16 behavior and zoom are in [Visuals](visuals/visuals.md). The game stays silent as defined in [Sound](sound/sound.md).

## Repeat a game

A board code describes a deal. A snapshot saves solo progress. A replay records timed actions. Tournament JSON carries event setup or bracket progress. The game algorithms and version 1 formats are in [Reproducibility](sharing/reproducibility.md) and [Data exchange policy](sharing/data-exchange-policy.md). Spec version 2.2 doesn't change the board-code, snapshot or replay versions.

## Build

Use React, TypeScript and native DOM controls. Package pins, commands and the offline HTML distribution are in [Technology](architecture/technology.md). Pure game functions, browser effects and behavior placement are in [Architecture](architecture/architecture.md).

Use the journeys in [Acceptance](quality/acceptance.md) to check the finished game. Those examples add no rules beyond the requirement IDs in their defining documents.

## Out of scope

The game doesn't need to support these, so they're never tested:

- Keys and modifier combinations beyond the ones in [Input](interface/input.md#keyboard-movement), which stay with the browser
- Holding a key down
- Several tabs or windows of the game open at once, where each tab may simply overwrite the saved preferences
- How a pointer press behaves when it drifts or is dragged off a card
- Replay or snapshot files with encodings beyond the stated rules, such as a byte-order mark
- Spoken screen-reader output, which stays part of user acceptance as [Input](interface/input.md#screen-reader) describes
- Confirming that a touch long press on a real device opens the context menu without revealing a card, which stays part of user acceptance like spoken output because automated browsers can't produce that gesture

# Open Forge Loader

Agents read this file before every task. It says what to read, how to use it, and how to change what agents use.

The list under `Entries` at the bottom is the whole setup: the folders of rules and notes, and any other documents, that agents use in this workspace. Anything not listed is only background reading. Your project's own requirements, and the instructions your agent tool already loads, still apply. Everything works with plain files, and the CLI only makes it faster.

## Axioms

### Read before you work

1. **List your working files.** Do this when a task starts or resumes, and again after your context is restored. Working files are the files you will investigate, review, create, change, rename or delete, including planned files and both paths of a rename. A file you only read for background is not a working file.
2. **Use the CLI if you can.** If the `open-forge` CLI is available and allowed, run `open-forge context` with `--for <file>` once for each working file, and read its output. It covers steps 3 and 4. You still do step 5 yourself. If the command is missing, fails or cannot follow a link, do steps 3 to 5 with your own file tools.
3. **Check conditions first.** Some entries end with `applies to` and one or more patterns. Such an entry applies only when one of your working files matches it, and that same file also matches every conditioned catalogue above it. Within one list, any pattern may match. Patterns are case-sensitive globs from the workspace root: `*.py` matches root files, `**/*.py` matches any depth, and `docs/**` matches a folder's contents. A leading `!` is literal, not an exclusion. Conditions never open a branch on their own and never grant edit permission. If you don't know your working files yet, report conditioned required entries as pending, and resolve them before you touch a matching file.
4. **Read what is required.** Read every applicable entry tagged #LoadNow or #KeepInMind, in the order listed. A catalogue is a file that lists a folder's context under its own `Entries`. When you read one, repeat steps 3 and 4 for its Entries. Never skip a required read because its description looks unrelated. Read each file once per pass.
5. **Open what fits the task.** Check the descriptions of the other listed entries and open the ones that fit. Follow any link that a file you read says to read. If search or a direct link leads you to a listed file, read the catalogues above it before you apply it. Keep separately selected branches separate. Use catalogues to find things, and don't open ordinary files just to discover more links or tags.

Start again from step 1 when your goal or working files change. Before you hand off or finish, reread the #KeepInMind entries in the branches you are using. During work, reread them only when they may have changed.

### Use what you read

- **Rules.** Follow the `## Axioms` of every catalogue you load and the `## Instructions` of every rule file, within the scope each one states. Only this loader and loaded catalogues define Axioms. A narrower rule adds to a broader one and never outranks it. If two rules conflict, or you cannot follow one, say so and explain why.
- **The user.** Follow the user's direction within platform and safety limits. Take routine, reversible steps inside the request without asking again, and state the assumptions that affect the result. Ask first when an open choice could significantly change the result, scope, risk, cost, external effects or the ability to undo the work.
- **Answers.** Match explanation and planning to the request. Unless the user asks for deeper analysis, start with your current understanding, one recommendation and at most one important open choice.
- **Words.** In replies and in what you write, use the fewest words that keep the meaning, readability and logical order. Cut filler and repetition, but keep the context, conditions and exceptions a reader needs to apply the result.
- **What counts as accepted.** Reading, linking, saving or tagging something does not make it accepted, and does not give you permission to edit it. Content is accepted when the user agrees, or when a source the user named for that question says so. Use declared external authorities for the facts they own. #Contextual marks content that is not accepted, and #CurrentTruth marks accepted current state within its scope. Tags, repetition and your own confidence never make something accepted. Evidence can support a claim without making it accepted.
- **One question per source.** Let each source answer one clear question, and link to related sources instead of repeating their detail. A link never changes either source's authority, scope, loading or lifecycle. Selected advice or other non-binding material may specialize broader material of the same kind within its accepted scope.
- **Conflicts and change.** When two accepted sources disagree, investigate before you edit either. When accepted direction changes the current state, update the source that defines it and keep useful prior context.
- **#Evergreen.** This tag marks material that must stay in step with accepted current state. It grants no authority and loads nothing. Update affected #Evergreen sources you may edit before other work depends on them, and by closeout at the latest. Batch related updates when that is safe.
- **Staying current.** Keep each source true to what it represents now. Keep useful prior context in a listed Memory route or another existing source. Report updates you could not make or were not allowed to make.

### Change what agents use

- **Add something.** Add a line under `Entries` with a path relative to this file, such as `../docs/architecture.md` or `../.cursor/rules/testing.mdc`. The line carries the description, tags and conditions, so the document needs no frontmatter and stays where it is. A linked Markdown catalogue, such as `../docs/_docs.md`, brings its Entries along. With the CLI, `open-forge route include <file>` writes the line for you.
- **Remove something.** Remove its line. Its files stay as plain notes, and reading them for background does not bring their rules back. Removing a line does not cancel accepted project requirements or the instructions your agent tool loads on its own. A removed line stays removed until the user asks to restore it.
- **Check what depends on it.** Before you remove a line, remove or replace the listed parts that need it, and report anything you cannot resolve. Inside other catalogues, the list follows the files in that folder, so move or delete a file to keep it out. When the CLI manages updates, also record the removal in its exclusions before you update.
- **Missing files.** Report a listed file or required dependency that is missing as an error. An empty `Entries` list is valid.
- **Required reads.** #LoadNow means a file is read whenever its parent loads. #KeepInMind adds the rereads described above. Both act only through catalogues you have read, so neither opens a branch nobody selected. Keep a required file's catalogue chain unbroken. Add these tags only when the read is really needed, and narrow specialized content before you make it required. No other tag changes loading.
- **Writing context.** Before you author workspace context, catalogues or metadata, read the file formats under "Writing workspace files" in `README.md`. If that page was deleted, `open-forge help concepts` prints the same section. Without either, copy the shape of a neighbouring file. New routed files carry `description`, `tags` and optional `applyTo`. A native `SKILL.md` keeps its own metadata.
- **Changes that survive updates.** Put your change in `{name}.overwrite.md` next to the shipped file. It is read right after its base, with the same role, scope and loading conditions. It wins only where the two say different things about the same content, and it is not listed or selected on its own.
